title: Odisha: Culture, Memory and Living Traditions
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
description: Odisha lives in its languages and landscapes, its songs and stories, its kitchens, workshops and shared spaces. This book follows the people and practices through which culture is remembered, made and renewed.

Across forty-eight chapters, it explores history and faith, literature and performance, textiles and crafts, food and everyday life. Adivasi knowledge and regional voices meet cinema, archives and the digital worlds reshaping cultural expression.
For curious readers and those reconnecting with home, this is an invitation to discover the many ways people carry their inheritance into the present.
authorBio: Ahimanikya Satapathy is the founder of Project Odisha. His work brings together technology, art and a long-standing commitment to Odia language and culture. Through Project Odisha, Kabita Live and A Poem Without Borders, he creates spaces for stories, poetry and shared knowledge to reach readers across places and generations.

chapters.title: Many Odishas
chapters.subtitle: Landscapes, languages and ways of belonging
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A photograph of Chandipur holds the evening light on wet sand. In another image, two Chhau performers occupy a darkened stage. A weaver sits before the patterned cloth emerging from his loom; farther south, fields lie among hills. Each is a recognisable view of Odisha. None can carry the whole place by itself.

To begin with many Odishas is to make room for these different scales of belonging: a home, a neighbourhood, a language, a working landscape, a remembered journey. This book approaches them through particular people, objects and practices. A regional name helps us find our bearings, but it should not decide in advance what everyone within that region must share.

The following pages offer an orientation rather than a set of cultural boundaries. Coast, north, west and south are directions in which to look. The stories we encounter will cross them, just as a language, a textile or a performer’s repertoire can lead beyond a district or state border.

sections.heading: Water and the work around it
paragraphs: Chilika brings freshwater and the sea into a coastal brackish-water lagoon. The Chilika Development Authority describes a place important both for migratory birds and for fishing livelihoods. These are connected ways of understanding the same waters: an ecological habitat and a place in which people make a living. A cultural account needs room for both.[1]

Elsewhere on the coast, a river mouth offers another perspective. In his 2019 account of Balaramgadi near Chandipur, Jitu Mishra describes the Budhabalanga reaching the Bay of Bengal and records boats, unloading and fish auctions. It is a dated writer’s account, but its attention to work takes us beyond the view of the beach. The water is also a route, a workplace and a place of exchange.[2]

Such accounts suggest a way to read the coast throughout this book. A boat may enter a chapter as an object of craft, a means of earning, or part of a festival’s remembrance. Those meanings deserve to be followed separately before we connect them. A beautiful shoreline can draw our attention; the people who work beside it give us more to understand.

sections.heading: Northern forests and performing worlds
paragraphs: In Mayurbhanj, Similipal offers a different landscape from the coast. UNESCO’s biosphere-reserve profile places its forests within a wider ecological account. For this opening journey, it is enough to notice the change in setting and to ask what kinds of knowledge a forest landscape invites us to learn. Its appearance alone cannot tell us the histories or daily lives of those associated with it.[3]

Mayurbhanj is also a name in the history and practice of Chhau. UNESCO describes three regional styles: Seraikella, Purulia and Mayurbhanj. The shared listing matters. Odisha’s contribution can be recognised precisely without claiming the entire tradition as its own.[4]

The photograph here records two performers whose names are not supplied by its source. It gives a moment of a performance, not the years of training behind it. As we turn to dance later in the book, the movement on stage will be only one part of the enquiry. Teachers, musicians, learning spaces and audiences also belong in its story.

A forest and a performance do not add up to a complete portrait of Mayurbhanj. They are two entrances into it. Keeping that distinction in mind lets us enjoy the clarity of an example without asking it to represent an entire region.

sections.heading: Western occasions and skilled work
paragraphs: The Sambalpur district account introduces Nuakhai and the gatherings called Nuakhai-Bhet Ghat alongside Bhaijiuntia and Dalkhai. Together, these references open questions about the agricultural year, family relationships, celebration and performance. Their value lies in the occasions they name; a district summary does not prescribe how every household observes them.[5]

Kalahandi’s cultural account identifies Ghumura among its art forms. Setting it beside the western traditions described around Sambalpur gives us a more varied picture than a single label such as folk dance. The next questions concern the particular performers, instruments and occasions of each practice. A shared place in a festival programme does not make their histories interchangeable.[6]

Skilled production offers another route into western Odisha. The handloom department lists Bargarh for cotton tie-dye, silk and furnishing textiles. In the photograph of Sambalpuri weaving, attention rests on a person at work and the fabric stretched before him. The later chapter Threads of Place follows the preparation of yarn and the choices that become visible in cloth.[7]

These examples bring celebration and livelihood into the same account. One chapter may follow a song; another may follow a thread. Both should leave us asking who carries the knowledge, how it is learned and what makes its continuation possible.

sections.heading: Southern landscapes as lived places
paragraphs: The photograph of hills in Koraput was made on a journey towards Rayagada. It shows land seen from a traveller’s position. To understand a lived landscape, we must go beyond the distant view and turn to accounts of particular activities and people. Neither scenery nor the broad word Adivasi can supply that detail.

At Kotpad in Koraput, the Development Commissioner for Handlooms associates weaving with the Mirgan community and describes aul-root dyeing. That is a specific connection among place, skilled work and material knowledge. It does not describe every community in the district.[8]

A situated study provides another kind of detail. Sujatarani Dandapat’s research centred on Kurli in 2017–18 describes finger millet, pulses, sesame and tubers, alongside crops including pineapple and banana. It also records cooperation between households when work exceeds the labour available within one household. This account of Dongria cultivation brings decisions, relationships and changing demands into view.[9]

Niyamgiri’s Dongria communities receive a fuller treatment elsewhere in our collection. Here, the study offers a reminder about scale: knowledge gained in a named place should retain that place, its date and its people. A detailed case can deepen our understanding without becoming a substitute for all the communities of southern Odisha.

sections.heading: Languages do not stop at the border
paragraphs: The Central Institute of Indian Languages describes Kuvi as a Dravidian language spoken in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and notes its use of Odia script in writing. One language therefore leads us across a state boundary and into questions about the relationship between speech and script. Kuvi and Kui must also be kept distinct rather than treated as interchangeable names.[10]

SCSTRTI’s catalogue of trilingual booklets offers another practical entrance into multilingual Odisha. Its separately labelled language resources make difference visible within educational publishing. A catalogue cannot tell us how every child learns or how a particular classroom works, but it shows why a single-language account of the state would be inadequate.[11]

In later chapters, Odia appears alongside other languages and regional ways of speaking. Their names and classifications sometimes require careful attribution. The useful question is not only which language belongs on a list. It is also who speaks, reads, writes, translates and teaches it, and whose account we are hearing.

sections.heading: Cities with more than one history
paragraphs: The cities belong in this cultural landscape as fully as the hills and villages. Cuttack’s district profile connects the surviving remains of Barabati with the city’s silver-filigree tradition. These lead to different kinds of history: one through a gateway, moat and palace mound, another through skilled making. The palace remembered in historical accounts should not be mistaken for an intact building.[12]

Bhubaneswar similarly asks us to look across periods. The Mukteswar photograph gives one view of its carved architecture. The municipal City Disaster Management Plan identifies Otto Konigsberger as the planner of the modern city. The two references belong to different chapters of urban history, but both belong to Bhubaneswar.[13]

A cultural edition should be able to move between an older building and a modern institution without treating one as more authentic simply because of its age. It should also ask how people inhabit and interpret those places now. The photograph of a temple can begin that enquiry; it cannot finish it.

sections.heading: A way into the book
paragraphs: The examples gathered here are deliberately incomplete. They do not rank districts or assign each community a representative craft. They establish a habit of attention: start with something particular, keep its context, and follow the connections that the evidence allows.

That habit also makes space for questions a celebratory survey can leave aside. Who has access to a place of learning or worship? Whose labour is named when an object is admired? How do women describe work that an outside account calls tradition? What do younger people want to retain, revise or leave behind? The chapters that follow must make room for answers that do not always agree.

Odisha can be approached through a famous monument, a familiar song or the food remembered from home. Any of these may be a beginning. This book asks us to keep going: from the image to the practice, from the practice to the people, and from one known place towards others we have yet to understand.

chapters.title: Kalinga, Utkala and Odisha
chapters.subtitle: How names and territories shaped a province
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: An elephant emerges from the rock at Dhauli. In Cuttack, a gateway survives where a fort once guarded royal power. A printed government order names the day a new province would begin. These objects belong to different worlds, yet each offers a way into the history behind the name Odisha.

The names Kalinga, Utkala and Odisha carry memories of kingdoms, sacred places and political demands. They do not describe one unchanged territory passing neatly from one name to the next. To follow them, we must ask who used a name, when they used it, and what country or community they meant. This chapter follows a few of those changes, from inscriptions to the making of a language-based province.

sections.heading: Kalinga in the rock
paragraphs: Dhauli preserves a material encounter with Ashoka’s rule in the third century BCE. Its inscriptions are in Prakrit, written in the Brahmi script. The carved elephant stands above them. The National Monuments Authority’s description makes an important distinction: Dhauli does not contain the complete sequence of fourteen major rock edicts. Numbers XI, XII and XIII are absent, while two separate edicts appear there. Related inscriptions survive at Jaugada in southern Odisha.[1]

That detail matters when telling the familiar story of Kalinga and Ashoka. We should not place a passage on the Dhauli rock merely because it belongs to the wider body of Ashokan edicts. The stone has its own text, arrangement and history. Looking closely gives the monument more meaning than a photograph used simply as a symbol of an ancient battle.

Kalinga’s history also reaches beyond Ashoka. At Udayagiri, the Hathigumpha inscription names another ruler, Kharavela. The neighbouring Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves preserve Jain religious architecture, with work extending across more than one period.[2] Together, these sites open different questions about power, patronage and religious life. They cannot be compressed into a single founding moment for everything that followed.

sections.heading: Utkala and the language of kingdoms
paragraphs: In her study of inscriptions, epigraphist Bharati Pal follows Utkala through royal grants and accounts of conquest. Her examples include the Bhaumakaras and Somavamsis, followed by the expansion of Ganga power. She also points to the Dirghasi inscription of 1075, where Utkala occurs in Sanskrit and Odda or Odra in its Telugu portion.[3] Names could overlap across languages even as their political meanings changed.

This is a richer history than a list of synonyms. A name in a grant may locate a monastery or village; in a royal title it may announce sovereignty. A conqueror’s claim also needs to be read as a claim. The surviving text tells us something about how authority was presented, without automatically supplying the precise boundary that a modern map requires.

The buildings of the Ganga period give this history another scale. UNESCO associates the Sun Temple at Konark with the thirteenth-century reign of Narasimha Deva I. Its chariot form, carved wheels, musicians and dancers bring royal patronage into the history of skilled work and religious imagination.[4] For a cultural history, the ruler’s name is a starting point. The stone also directs our attention towards the people who designed, carved, maintained and used these places.

sections.heading: Cuttack and changing rule
paragraphs: Barabati’s surviving gateway brings political change into a place that can still be recognised. The Government of Odisha’s account of Cuttack traces its passage to Afghan rule in 1568, Mughal rule in 1592, Maratha rule in 1751 and British rule in 1803.[5] These dates describe changes in control at Cuttack. They should not be stretched into a claim that every part of present-day Odisha experienced the same transition at the same moment.

From the gateway, it is possible to think about history at two scales. One follows rulers and administrations. The other asks how people worked, worshipped, traded and learned in the city across those changes. Political chronology helps locate cultural life, but cannot replace its history. Nor does a surviving fort tell us equally about everyone who lived beyond its walls.

The nineteenth-century story therefore needs more than a succession of governments. It needs the language of schools and public discussion, the circulation of print, and the organisations through which people began to argue for a different administrative future.

sections.heading: A language becomes a public cause
paragraphs: Historian Pritipuspa Mishra describes the 1860s campaign against proposals to replace Odia with Bengali in the Orissa division. Utkal Dipika, edited by Gourishankar Rai, became an important forum. Newspaper discussion connected language with education, government policy and the condition of the people. The issue was practical as well as literary: which language would carry learning and public argument?[6]

The movement acquired an organisational centre when the Utkal Sammilani first met in Cuttack in December 1903. Mishra places Madhusudan Das among the leaders working towards an organisation that could represent Odias across provincial divisions. Its early leadership included princes and educated government employees.[6] Remembering these participants helps us see both the movement’s reach and the limits of who could speak through its institutions.

A memorial can keep a leader visible long after the immediate arguments have faded. The statue reproduced here belongs to that later work of remembrance. Its book and raised hand offer a public image of Madhusudan Das; the history of the movement still needs meetings, writings and competing proposals to explain how change was pursued.

sections.heading: The province made in 1936
paragraphs: The Government of India (Constitution of Orissa) Order, 1936 gives the change a precise administrative form. Paragraph 4 appoints 1 April 1936 as the operative date. Paragraph 3 and the First Schedule specify territory transferred from Bihar and Orissa, the Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces.[7] The language movement had helped make a province possible; the order defined what that province legally contained.

This distinction prevents two familiar confusions. The province was established under British rule, before Indian independence. Its formation was also not the completion of every later territorial change. Mayurbhanj, for example, merged with Odisha on 1 January 1949.[8] A map labelled simply “Odisha” needs a date if it is to explain these different political geographies.

The reproduced Gazette page makes the transition tangible. Its formal paragraphs turn a political demand into administrative instructions. Read beside the older inscriptions, it shows how different kinds of authority addressed territory: a royal statement cut in rock and a colonial order printed for circulation. Each must be understood within the institutions that produced it.

sections.heading: Odisha and belonging today
paragraphs: In 2011, the Orissa (Alteration of Name) Act changed the state’s name to Odisha. A separate constitutional amendment substituted Odia for Oriya in the Eighth Schedule.[9][10] These measures changed official naming; they did not establish a new state. Older publications retain the spellings under which they appeared, allowing us to find and identify their records accurately.

The achievement of a linguistic province also leaves a question about belonging. Mishra argues that a regional language could resist marginalisation while gaining power over communities that did not speak it. Her discussion of Adivasi inclusion challenges an uncomplicated account of linguistic unity.[6] This is an invitation to ask whose language and knowledge a public institution recognises.

Our opening chapter approached Odisha through several landscapes and ways of living. Its history asks for the same breadth. Kalinga and Utkala help us read particular pasts; Odisha names a shared political home whose people need not tell an identical story. The chapters that follow can hold those histories together while giving their differences room to remain visible.

chapters.title: Ports, Boats and Ocean Crossings
chapters.subtitle: Maritime archaeology and cultural memory on the Odisha coast
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Odisha’s maritime past comes into view at several scales. There is the small boat released in a festival, the wooden hull assembled by skilled hands, the fragment of an imported bowl and the stone once used to hold a vessel in place. Together they invite us to look outward from the coast, while keeping our attention on the work that made a crossing possible.

This chapter follows those connections through ports, boat making and seasonal sailing. It also asks how journeys become part of a community’s memory. Archaeological finds and living celebrations illuminate different parts of that story. Read together, they give the ocean a place within Odisha’s cultural history without requiring every remembered voyage to become a documented itinerary.

sections.heading: Where rivers meet the sea
paragraphs: At Khalkattapatna, near the mouth of the Kushabhadra, the surviving evidence includes pottery made locally and ceramics brought from elsewhere. Rudra Prasad Behera’s study describes porcelain and celadon, including bowls and plates, alongside other finds. These objects give the port a material presence: trade becomes something that could be handled, used, broken and left behind.[1]

The pottery also changes the direction in which we look. A maritime history told only through departing ships misses the arrival of goods. Imported wares make Odisha a destination within wider circuits of exchange. Their presence does not by itself identify a captain, a direct route or a single origin for every cargo. It does establish that an account confined to local production would be incomplete.[1]

For a reader standing before a ceramic fragment, the most useful question may be a modest one: what can this particular object tell us? Its fabric, glaze and form can be compared with other finds. Its archaeological context can help place it in time. A port history is assembled through such connections, rather than recovered as one continuous narrative.

sections.heading: A stone that travelled
paragraphs: A broken stone anchor from the Manikapatna coast supplies a different kind of clue. In a 2022 study, Sila Tripati and colleagues examined its rock through petrography, chemical analysis and strontium–neodymium isotopes. Their results point most strongly to basalt from Palitana in Gujarat’s Saurashtra region, rather than a local Odisha source.[2]

The finding extends the view beyond the Bay of Bengal. Material found on the eastern coast can preserve a connection with western India. The researchers identify the object as an Indo-Arabian type associated with medieval maritime activity. Its missing upper portion makes the accompanying reconstruction particularly useful, provided we keep the surviving stone separate from the proposed outline.[2]

An anchor’s rock can outlast the vessel it served. Here, scientific comparison helps recover a material journey; it does not recover the crew’s names or a complete sailing route. That distinction leaves us with a substantial discovery: a physical object connecting distant coastal worlds, with more of its history still to be understood.

sections.heading: Knowledge in the hull
paragraphs: The boat-building display at the Odisha State Maritime Museum in Jobra, Cuttack, offers another point of entry. The photograph shows a partly built hull and posed figures. It invites attention to assembly: the boat is something made through a succession of decisions, before it becomes a shape moving across the water.[3]

Swarup Bhattacharyya’s later field study of the patia describes that decision-making in detail. The owner specifies the desired length; other dimensions are worked out proportionately. Heated planks are bent with a wooden device called merry kath, and the shell is built before the internal supporting timbers are added. Such knowledge joins measurement with a practical understanding of the material.[4]

The study also records fisherman Arjun Behera of Pashchim Gadadharpur in West Bengal explaining the advantage of lighter arjun timber for boats brought ashore. The discussion follows craft practices across the Odisha–Bengal coastal region. It reminds us that a boat’s usefulness includes what happens when it leaves the water: handling and shelter matter alongside movement at sea.[4]

These observations concern later working craft. They offer a way to appreciate boat builders’ skill, without turning a photographed display or a modern patia into a replica of every vessel that once crossed the Bay. For this cultural history, the valuable continuity is a question worth pursuing: how do communities teach and adapt the knowledge on which work at the water’s edge depends?

sections.heading: Sailing with the seasons
paragraphs: A long crossing required an understanding of when movement was possible. Sila Tripati and L. N. Raut’s study of monsoon winds and historical evidence reconstructs journeys from Odisha towards Southeast Asia with the northeast monsoon and returns with the southwest monsoon. Their account treats wind and current as conditions that shaped maritime trade.[5]

This seasonal reading gives time a different weight. An ocean route was more than a line between two named places. Its possibilities changed through the year. A discussion of departure therefore belongs beside a discussion of waiting and return. The monsoon study offers a broad explanation of sailing opportunities, rather than a timetable for every ship or proof that all voyages followed one pattern.

Bali enters this history both as a place across the sea and as a powerful name in Odisha’s public memory. Archaeology on the Indonesian side deserves its own place in the account. I. Wayan Ardika and Peter Bellwood’s study of Sembiran identifies finds in Bali as evidence of contact with Indian traders. The available abstract supports that wider connection; it does not establish an exclusively Odishan origin for the traders or their goods.[6]

To write about ocean crossings is therefore to make room for more than one shore. A fuller history would ask what people in the receiving ports sought, selected and made of their encounters. Odisha’s place in that history becomes more interesting when the other coast is allowed its own perspective. A connection is a relationship, not simply the extension of one region’s story overseas.

sections.heading: The journeys we remember
paragraphs: In Boita Bandana, miniature boats carrying lamps are set afloat. The Ministry of Culture’s account of Bali Jatra describes this observance alongside the Cuttack festival’s commemoration of maritime connections with Southeast Asia, especially Bali. The contemporary fair includes crafts, performance and food, bringing remembered journeys into a shared public occasion.[7]

The small boat makes an immense distance imaginable. It can be prepared and released by someone who has never crossed an ocean. That is one way a cultural practice works: participation gives a historical theme a place in ordinary life. The meaning of the gesture need not depend on assigning each miniature vessel to one excavated port or one dated voyage.

For the cultural edition, these scales belong beside one another. A ceramic sherd asks for comparison; an anchor asks what its stone can reveal; a working boat asks how skill is learned. A festival asks how people choose to remember. The surviving evidence remains uneven, but the questions bring a coast of makers, traders and commemorating communities into view. The ocean becomes part of the inhabited world of Odisha, with connections still open to research.

chapters.title: Cities, Villages and Cultural Landscapes
chapters.subtitle: Neighbourhoods work and shared spaces in Odisha
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A city is remembered through routes as well as buildings: the way to a market, the turn towards a tank, a street that becomes a performance space. A village can hold a workplace within a home and carry its name into exhibitions far away. These relationships make a cultural landscape. They connect the visible setting with the people who use and change it.

This chapter looks at selected places rather than offering a tour of every district. Bhubaneswar, Cuttack, Puri and Raghurajpur show how worship, planning, work and performance give spaces their character. A final turn towards Koraput opens the view beyond the coastal cluster. The question throughout is how to read a place while leaving room for the lives that a photograph cannot show.

sections.heading: Bhubaneswar around the tank and the neighbourhood
paragraphs: India’s 2014 Tentative List submission for Ekamra Kshetra describes the old town through water bodies, temples, shrines and ritual routes. Lingaraj is a sacred centre, while Bindusagar is a focus of the settlement. This account invites us to see relationships between places: the route and the tank belong in the picture beside the temple tower. The submission is a proposal on UNESCO’s Tentative List, not a World Heritage inscription.[1]

The twentieth-century capital added another way of organising urban space. The Bhubaneswar City Development Plan records Otto Koenigsberger’s 1948 plan, designed around neighbourhood units for an initial population of 40,000. Administrative buildings, housing and a town centre containing markets and a bus station formed parts of its arrangement. Later residential units accommodated growth.[2]

The two accounts offer different starting points for looking at the same city. One follows ritual connections; the other follows an administrative and residential plan. Neither alone describes present-day Bhubaneswar. Reading them together helps us ask what a neighbourhood needs and how successive generations fit their lives into an inherited layout. A temple precinct and a planned unit both become meaningful through repeated use.

sections.heading: Cuttack through streets and work
paragraphs: Cuttack’s municipal history locates the old city on the strip between the Mahanadi and Kathajodi. It describes a dense pattern of streets and lanes, remembered in the expression Baban Bazaar, Tepan Galee, or fifty-two markets and fifty-three lanes. The phrase gives the city an intimate scale: a place known through successive turns, destinations and encounters.[3]

The same account associates Cuttack with silver filigree and commercial activity. These are useful reminders that cultural identity is also made at work. A finished object may travel beyond the city, while its place-name continues to point back to a concentration of skill. To understand that connection fully would mean following the object into particular workshops and recording the people who make it.[3]

The photograph on this page takes a smaller approach. It records dahibara-aludam served in Cuttack in 2011, with a bowl of food occupying the frame. It cannot explain the whole food economy or establish who first made the dish. It can remind us that an urban memory may be held in a meal as readily as in a landmark. A history of streets needs room for both.

sections.heading: Puri when the street becomes a stage
paragraphs: In Sahi Jatra, the neighbourhood enters the performance. IGNCA and Sangeet Natak Akademi’s Akhyan account describes processions through Puri whose crossings become arenas for dancers, acrobats and costumed figures. Rama, Ravana, Parasurama and Hanuman are among the characters it names. The familiar story gains a local setting through the places in which it is performed.[4]

Preparation also has a geography. Bimal Prasad Mohanty’s 2015 account describes akhadas and their associated jagas as neighbourhood institutions, linking physical practice with social and cultural activity. Wrestling and stick practice appear alongside music and drama. His description makes visible some of the institutional life behind a public appearance.[5]

The portrait here records one costumed figure, identified in its source as Parasurama of Harachandi Sahi. Its close framing cannot show the procession or the audience. Placed beside the written accounts, it suggests two necessary scales of attention: the performer’s appearance and the neighbourhood that makes performance possible. Puri’s cultural landscape includes that preparation, as well as the moment when a crossing fills with spectators.

sections.heading: Raghurajpur between home and workshop
paragraphs: In Sucharita Sahoo’s 2014 account of Raghurajpur, painted house walls stand alongside work on cloth and palm leaves. Pattachitra, other crafts and Gotipua performance form part of the village’s cultural life. The account also describes artists taking their work to fairs and exhibitions. The village is therefore both a setting for making and a point of departure into wider circuits of exchange.[6]

The doorway in the photograph helps bring those connections into view. A woman holds a work for the camera, with paintings around her. We can see the encounter between a maker and a visitor, although the source leaves her unnamed. That omission matters: a village’s collective reputation should not make individual practitioners disappear from its record.

Raghurajpur’s connections extend into the history of dance. Srjan’s chronology identifies Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra as the son of chitrakara painter Chintamani Mohapatra, records his early Gotipua training under Balabhadra Sahu, and follows his work in Puri and Cuttack theatre. One life joins village, town and city through learning and employment. These movements complicate any easy division between a rural tradition and an urban stage.[7]

sections.heading: A town can connect many landscapes
paragraphs: Koraput offers another starting point. The district’s account of the town places its Jagannath temple and adjoining tribal museum within the hill setting. Its art-and-culture overview also draws attention to weekly markets where people from different communities meet. These official descriptions are brief, but they point towards connections between a town and the surrounding region.[8][9]

A market is worth approaching as a place of exchange and work. What is being sold, who has made it and how it has arrived are more useful questions than treating the people present as part of a picturesque scene. The published overview does not answer those questions for individual traders. Doing so would require conversations, names and attention to the terms on which people wish to be represented.

A museum presents a related challenge. Its collections can introduce objects and practices, but a display cannot stand in for the continuing lives of all the communities it describes. The regional town is a place from which to begin learning, rather than a substitute for those communities’ own accounts. The next chapter takes up that need for named, particular perspectives.

sections.heading: Keeping places open to life
paragraphs: These examples suggest a practical way to read Odisha’s settlements. Look at a building, then follow what connects it to water, work or a route. Notice where a domestic doorway becomes a place to show a painting, or where an ordinary crossing becomes a stage. Ask whose activity gives the space its importance, and whether their names have entered the record.

Preserving such places raises questions beyond the survival of a facade. Can people continue to work there? Can a neighbourhood prepare and hold its performances? What happens to shared spaces as their uses change? This chapter does not settle those questions. It places them beside the photographs, so that beauty and historical interest remain connected to the people whose lives make a landscape cultural.

chapters.title: Adivasi Worlds and Community Knowledge
chapters.subtitle: Seeds cloth stories and the work of language
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: An account of Odisha’s culture changes when its starting point is a seed keeper, an embroiderer or someone making a language usable on a phone. Each brings a different understanding of what deserves to be remembered, and of the work remembrance requires. Knowledge has a place, a language and people who practise it. It also has a future that those people should be able to shape.

This chapter follows several named encounters recorded by researchers and reporters: Dongria Kondh seed keeping and embroidery, Ho language work online, Santali writing and a Saora artist’s storytelling. These are distinct histories, not interchangeable examples of a single Adivasi culture. The accounts offer points of entry into living worlds; they cannot stand in for every household or community.

sections.heading: Seeds that travel between households
paragraphs: In a 2015 report from the Niyamgiri hills, Manipadma Jena described priestesses who were also searching for seeds. Dasara Kadraka of Kadaraguma spoke about millet varieties that were becoming difficult to find. The bejuni priestesses’ work joined cultivation to journeys, conversations and obligations between neighbours.[1]

The report describes seeds shared among five families and priestesses returning twice the amount of grain they had received as seed. News of surviving varieties travelled through weekly markets and ritual gatherings. Dom neighbours helped carry that news. The network therefore crossed household and community boundaries: finding a seed depended on knowing whom to ask, and keeping it depended on growing and sharing it.[1]

This is an account from 2015, not an inventory of what survives today. Its value lies partly in the practical detail. A seed collection is sustained through relationships as well as storage. The work involves attention to other people’s fields, willingness to travel and the possibility that something lost in one place remains in another.

A later account complicates any picture of an unchanged farming world. In 2022, Deepanwita Gita Niyogi reported on Singari Jakesika of Gandili. Jakesika described her husband’s turn towards horticulture for greater income, less land under millet and a household diet that included more subsidised rice.[2] The two accounts show different pressures and choices; they do not establish one uniform trajectory for all Dongria families.

For a cultural edition, the question is not simply which crop is traditional. It is who has the time, land and incentive to keep cultivating it. Remembering a seed keeper’s name brings those decisions into view. It also prevents an attractive phrase such as “community knowledge” from hiding the labour that makes knowledge available.

sections.heading: The time inside an embroidered cloth
paragraphs: In interviews conducted in November 2017, Kanak Rajadhyaksha recorded how Dongariya Kondh women learned and fitted embroidery into their lives. Kumri Sikoka recalled learning at about nine or ten from her paternal aunt. Learning was a relationship between people, carried through demonstration and practice.[3]

Binjo Jakesika and Sukri Kadraka described embroidery alongside fieldwork and housework. Their accounts included bodily strain associated with prolonged work during training. Site Jakesika spoke of earnings and independence, while also recognising the convenience of buying a gift rather than spending the time to embroider it.[3]

A finished cloth can conceal these negotiations. Looking closely should mean attending to the maker’s choices as well as the stitches. An inherited skill may be valued, tiring, economically useful and difficult to make time for—all within the same life.

sections.heading: A language on a phone
paragraphs: Ganesh Birua’s route into digital language work began with learning. In Karishma Mehrotra’s 2022 report, Birua, from Dighiabeda in Odisha, recalled encountering Warang Citi through the Ho Society India Facebook group while studying in Baripada in 2014. He began learning the script and sharing letters and words, using Odia and English equivalents to help readers.[4]

His work grew into a blog, “Elabu Etona Warang Citi”, and online videos and posts. The report’s interview scene is especially telling: Birua spoke from a tree where he could obtain a phone signal. Digital work was already taking place, but the means of reaching it were uneven. The same report described Subhashish Panigrahi’s interest in word lists and other foundational tools for languages online.[4]

A script needs more than an image of its alphabet to function on a screen. Unicode’s standard describes Warang Citi as a distinct script, with uppercase and lowercase letters.[5] Encoding gives characters agreed identities that software can use. Teaching materials, readable fonts and people who want to write remain necessary parts of the larger task.

The significance of Birua’s work is not that a language becomes valuable when it reaches the internet. Its speakers already give it value. The change is in what they can do with it: explain a letter to someone far away, circulate a lesson, or leave material that another learner can return to.

This is community knowledge being deliberately extended. It is also individual initiative, with an identifiable author and a particular history of learning. A responsible archive should preserve that authorship alongside the material, so that a useful resource does not become an anonymous example of “tribal content”.

sections.heading: Writing and the right to be remembered
paragraphs: Raghunath Murmu’s creation of Ol Chiki in 1925 offers another history of language work. It concerns Santali, not Ho, and a different script. The date is recalled in the President of India’s account of the script’s centenary celebrations.[6]

Unicode records Ol Chiki as an alphabet with independent vowel letters, written from left to right. It also notes that Santali has been written in Devanagari, Bengali, Odia and Latin scripts.[5] The history of a language is therefore larger than the history of any one writing system.

A commemorative bust makes Murmu visible as a named cultural worker. In this chapter it stands for that public remembrance, not for all Santali experience. Beside the story of a young Ho learner, it opens a longer view of people making tools through which others can learn and write.

sections.heading: A story with a painter attached
paragraphs: An illustrated Sahapedia account presents Enam Gomango, a Saora painter and teacher from Odisha, narrating a tale of a man and a snake through a sequence of paintings. M. D. Muthukumaraswamy draws attention to the main characters and actions that carry the story from image to image.[7]

The important editorial choice is to keep the painter’s name attached. A picture can be approached as an act of narration by a particular person, rather than detached from its story and treated only as a decorative pattern. That reading does not require us to assign a universal meaning to every motif or to make claims about practices the source does not document.

sections.heading: Keeping knowledge with its people
paragraphs: These encounters suggest a way of building an edition. Name the people who explain a practice. Record when their words were gathered. Keep languages and communities distinct. Let accounts of changing livelihoods sit beside accounts of continuity, without forcing either into a story of inevitable loss or effortless preservation.

The pictures need the same care. A landscape cannot identify its inhabitants by itself; an embroidered object without a maker’s name leaves an important gap. A commemorative sculpture is evidence of remembrance, not a photograph of the person in life. Captions should make these distinctions visible.

Knowledge is carried through the ordinary work of growing, teaching, stitching and telling. Its future depends partly on whether people can continue that work on terms they choose. An Odisha cultural edition can help readers notice it, trace its sources and seek out its makers. It should leave room for those makers to correct, extend and reshape the account.

chapters.title: Odisha Beyond Its Borders
chapters.subtitle: Work language and belonging across distance
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Odisha does not end at the state boundary. Its cultural life also takes shape in a worker’s room in Surat, an association meeting in North America and a language lesson in Chennai. These places belong to different histories of movement. A journey made for wages, one made for education and a childhood spent outside Odisha do not produce the same relationship with home.

What connects them is the work of making a life across distance. People find accommodation and employment through others, create occasions to gather, and decide what to teach their children. Sometimes return remains a plan; sometimes belonging grows in more than one place. Following these relationships reveals a cultural geography made by people as well as by borders.

sections.heading: The route to Surat
paragraphs: In Aishwarya Mohanty’s 2024 reporting from Kalamba in Ganjam, Kamallochan Sahoo recalled first travelling to Surat at eighteen. An uncle had gone before him. The presence of people he knew helped make the journey imaginable: work, accommodation and food did not have to be found entirely alone. He also remembered the attraction of the clothes and goods that returning workers brought with them.[1]

The same report recorded another experience. Mitika Nayak, from Bada Badangi, described caste discrimination during his two years in Surat, including being made to eat and live separately. Migration had not left the village’s hierarchies behind. Taken together, the accounts show how a network can offer security to some while leaving others excluded.[1]

The cultural meaning of a journey lies partly in these unequal possibilities. A familiar language can help someone find their way, but shared regional origin does not guarantee equal treatment. The words “Odia community” become more useful when they leave room for those differences.

Reetika Revathy Subramanian’s 2019 reporting for the People’s Archive of Rural India brings women’s work into this picture. Renuka Pradhan, from Sanabaragam in Ganjam, removed loose threads from machine-embroidered sarees in her home in Surat. The work required care: damage to the cloth could be charged to her. Production entered the same small space in which family life took place.[2]

The report also described Shanti Sahu working with her daughter Asha. Asha had left school after the available Odia-medium schooling ended at Class 8 and private education proved unaffordable. Elsewhere in the neighbourhood, Ranjita Pradhan organised work for other women after approaching factory owners directly.[2] These are dated accounts of particular lives, but they widen the story of migration beyond the male mill worker.

Home, in these accounts, is both a remembered place and a room where income has to be earned. The making of a life away from Odisha includes the organisation of work and schooling, as well as the festivals through which that life becomes publicly visible.

sections.heading: Finding one another far away
paragraphs: An association begins with a practical discovery: other people nearby share something that matters to you. The New York and New Jersey chapter of the Odisha Society of the Americas remembers the late 1960s through small gatherings in houses and apartments. Its account places the home of Krushna Mohan Das in Cambria Heights among the settings where an organisation took shape.[3]

That chapter history also describes the gathering of names for a North American directory in 1970. It dates the first OSA convention to 17 October that year, in Hartford, Connecticut. A list of addresses and a meeting place helped turn scattered acquaintances into a wider association.[3]

The modest objects in this history deserve attention. A directory makes someone reachable. A programme gives a meeting a sequence; a souvenir preserves names that might otherwise disappear. Cultural institutions need these ordinary forms of organisation before they can present a performance or sustain an annual gathering.

The Odisha Society of New England’s own history traces the wider organisation’s beginnings to a New England initiative in 1969. It recalls a community puja in an apartment in 1976, a public-park picnic in 1982 and the formation of the regional society in 1983.[4] These dates describe different stages of association building, rather than a single moment when a complete institution appeared.

Gatherings do more than recreate a familiar occasion. They give people reasons to meet repeatedly, allow newcomers to enter a circle and create experiences that children can remember for themselves. The place of celebration becomes part of the memory: an apartment or park in America can acquire a family significance alongside places in Odisha.

Association histories are accounts of the people who organised and participated. They illuminate a substantial part of life abroad without representing everyone who migrated. Those who did not join, could not attend or expressed belonging in other ways remain part of the larger story.

sections.heading: A language learned beyond home
paragraphs: Chennai offers a reminder that living beyond Odisha need not mean living outside India. The Prabasi Odia Cultural Society describes itself as an organisation for Odia families and individuals in Chennai and Tamil Nadu, founded in 2008. Its Ama Chatasali initiative teaches children to speak, read and write Odia, alongside cultural material that includes stories, music and dance.[5]

The society’s own description places attachment to Odisha alongside participation in Chennai’s life. That pairing matters. A child can belong to the city where they grow up while learning a language associated with parents or grandparents. The lesson need not ask them to choose one home and surrender another.

In North America, the Odisha Society of the Americas describes both remote and in-person Odia teaching. Its language programme also uses songs, speeches and plays around community celebrations, and vocabulary and speaking competitions at conventions.[6] The language is being given occasions for use, as well as being taught as a subject.

These activities suggest a distinction between inheritance and access. A language may be described as someone’s mother tongue even when that person has had little opportunity to learn it. A class can provide an entry point without treating difficulty or hesitation as a failure of belonging.

There is also a difference between rehearsing a performance and being able to sustain an ordinary conversation. Both have value, but neither automatically supplies the other. The strongest cultural learning leaves space for questions, mistakes and changing interests. Children need opportunities to make something with a language, not only to demonstrate that they have received it.

Placed beside Asha’s account in Surat, organised heritage teaching raises a further question: who can continue learning, and under what conditions? Language attachment is shaped by time, income and available schools. Celebrating it is most meaningful when those practical conditions remain in view.

sections.heading: A chariot in another city
paragraphs: A photograph of a Ratha Yatra chariot in London offers a different kind of crossing. ISKCON’s account of its fiftieth London festival traces the first procession to 1969, from Hyde Park to Trafalgar Square. It credits the initiative to the movement’s early American devotees in London.[7]

This is a history of religious circulation as well as migration. A festival strongly associated with Jagannath and Puri can gather people whose ties to Odisha differ, or who have no family origin there. The London event should therefore not be treated as a photograph of an exclusively Odia diaspora.

The chariot’s presence among London buildings makes that distinction visible. The festival enters a new urban setting, with its own organisers, audience and devotional history. The connection to Odisha remains significant, but the public life built around it also belongs to the people and city in which it takes place.

sections.heading: More than one place to belong
paragraphs: The worker’s room, the association directory, the language class and the street procession reveal different ways of carrying attachments across distance. None is a complete measure of cultural belonging. Public celebration is easier to photograph than care, work or an unfinished conversation; an organisation’s archive is easier to find than the memories of someone who never joined it.

Keeping these forms together changes what counts as a cultural history. The person who arranges work, the woman who fits paid production around domestic life and the volunteer who prepares a lesson all help make collective life possible. Their circumstances differ sharply, but their labour belongs in the account alongside the stage and the festival.

Home can remain a village or neighbourhood in Odisha without making every other place temporary. It can also become a relationship that changes across generations. Some people return; others build lasting lives elsewhere. Their children may inherit a name, learn a language later or discover a tradition through friends rather than family.

Odisha beyond its borders is therefore an open history of relationships. Its continuity depends on people finding ways to meet, learn and support one another. Its richness also lies in the new experiences they bring to those relationships: experiences that enlarge what home can mean.

chapters.title: Jagannath and the Many Worlds of Puri
chapters.subtitle: Devotion service and the life of a sacred city
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: The temple tower is Puri’s most recognisable landmark, but the worlds gathered around Jagannath extend beyond its outline. They include the daily work of service, the public road along which the deities travel, the preparation of food and the songs through which a devotee addresses the Lord. Each offers a different way into the city.

Jagannath is worshipped with Balabhadra and Subhadra. The district’s account places the present great temple in the twelfth-century world of the Ganga ruler Anantavarman Chodaganga.[1] That historical association is one part of the story. Sacred narratives, inscriptions and continuing practices preserve other kinds of memory. Reading them together allows the temple to appear as a living institution, sustained by people as well as stone.

sections.heading: Sacred narrative and historical time
paragraphs: In the Purushottama Kshetra narrative of the Skanda Purana, King Indradyumna seeks a place where he can behold the deity. Vidyapati travels on his behalf and encounters Visvavasu, a Sabara devotee, in a forest setting. In G. V. Tagare’s translation, Visvavasu welcomes the traveller and offers hospitality; Vidyapati asks to see Nilamadhava.[2]

This meeting gives the forest devotee a central place in the telling. Knowledge of the deity is already present before the royal seeker arrives. It would diminish the narrative to reduce Visvavasu to a passing figure on the way to the king’s achievement. It would also ask the text to do something different from its purpose if its sacred chronology were turned directly into a modern historical date.

Inscriptions provide another kind of evidence. D. C. Sircar edited four records in the Patalesvara shrine within the temple complex. His discussion distinguishes the Madala Panji’s construction tradition from Ganga dynastic records crediting Chodaganga, and notes the scholarly interpretation that Anangabhima completed work begun by Chodaganga.[3] The question concerns stages of building and patronage, rather than a simple choice between a true story and a false one.

One record, dated by Sircar to 1225, concerns land granted to support offerings of milk, ghee, rice and curds to Purusottama. Here the historical record brings cultivation into the sacred centre. Worship required continuing material provision, and a donor made arrangements for that provision to endure.[3]

The sacred story and the inscription answer different questions. One makes a divine presence known through a journey and an encounter; the other records an act of support. Neither, by itself, establishes the first moment of worship at Puri. Their value grows when their differences remain visible.

sections.heading: Service as knowledge and livelihood
paragraphs: The temple’s ritual life depends on sevayats, or servitors, whose responsibilities form an organised system of service. A study published in 2019 by S. Samanta, R. K. Nanda and P. Rautaray examined the social and economic circumstances of these ritual functionaries. Its fieldwork took place from October to December 2017.[4]

The researchers found variation in earnings according to the kind of service and the days allotted to it. They also described younger family members seeking other employment while continuing to take their turn in ritual service. Their study acknowledges that permission and access shaped the selection of participants.[4]

These findings invite attention to the household behind the ritual role. Devotion and livelihood can coexist without the latter cancelling the former. The continuity visible to a pilgrim depends on people maintaining knowledge, organising their time and earning enough to sustain their families.

sections.heading: Food and the material life of worship
paragraphs: Mahaprasad brings worship into the act of receiving and eating food. Incredible India’s temple account describes daily cooking in earthen pots and identifies the food as a sacred offering.[5] The vessel matters as well as the dish: material, handling and preparation belong to the practice, not merely to its presentation.

The thirteenth-century land grant offers a historical counterpart to that present description. It records resources directed towards offerings; it does not establish that today’s recipes or kitchen arrangements have remained unchanged.[3] Continuity can be understood through the recurring commitment to feed the deity, even while the detailed history of ingredients, labour and supply needs its own evidence.

A meal also changes the scale at which a pilgrimage is remembered. The great tower may be seen from a distance, while food is received and shared at close quarters. In that movement from monument to meal, the institution becomes part of bodily experience: waiting, hunger, taste and the company in which one eats.

To write about this world only through quantities would miss much of its meaning. Claims about the largest kitchen or the greatest number of meals can obscure more useful questions: who prepares the food, how work is organised, and how devotees understand what they receive. The servitors’ livelihood study reminds us that institutional grandeur does not imply identical circumstances for everyone who serves.[4]

The history of food at Puri therefore belongs beside the history of patronage and skill. A grant of agricultural land, a cooking pot and an allotted turn of service illuminate different parts of the same relationship. Sacred value is made present through material work, repeated from day to day.

sections.heading: When the deities take the road
paragraphs: Ratha Yatra changes the relationship between the temple and the city. Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra travel on three wooden chariots along Bada Danda, the Grand Road, towards Gundicha Temple. The return journey is known as Bahuda Yatra.[6] Worship becomes visible through movement across a public urban space.

The finished chariot can seem a single magnificent object. The construction photograph on the preceding pages shows a different state: exposed timber, wheels and painted components before the covering is complete. Incredible India’s account of Puri identifies Akshaya Tritiya as the occasion when master carpenters begin making the chariots.[7] The festival thus has a season of preparation as well as a day of departure.

A road ordinarily understood as a route through town becomes a place towards which people direct their attention. That transformation depends on the workers who prepare the vehicles, the servitors who conduct the rites and the people who gather to witness them. The public spectacle joins forms of effort that are less easily seen.

The photograph below records the chariots before the return journey in 2015. It captures one moment in a particular year, with the crowd filling the foreground. It lets us see the scale of gathering without making every person in it stand for the same experience or reason for being there.

sections.heading: A voice beyond the threshold
paragraphs: Salabega’s devotional voice complicates any easy equation between access to the temple and attachment to Jagannath. In his essay “Songs of Salabega”, Subas Pani places the poet in the first half of the seventeenth century and recounts his exclusion from the temple because he was the son of a Muslim. Pani describes his devotion to Jagannath, identified with Krishna, and his view of Patitapabana from Bada Danda.[8]

The account places longing at a threshold. The poet’s place in devotional memory does not erase the boundary he is said to have faced. Instead, it asks the reader to hold belonging and exclusion in the same view. A song can address a deity intimately even when the singer cannot enter the institution associated with that deity.

The distinction remains relevant to a present account of Puri. Odisha Tourism’s published guidance identifies restrictions on non-Hindu entry to the Jagannath temple.[9] Public participation in a procession, devotion expressed in song and admission to the interior are different forms of relationship. They should not be collapsed into a general claim that everyone participates on the same terms.

sections.heading: Reading the many worlds together
paragraphs: The many worlds of Puri meet without becoming identical. A donor’s inscription records provision; a sacred narrative tells of revelation; a servitor maintains a responsibility; a pilgrim waits for a glimpse. The maker’s skill and the poet’s longing each bring something that a view of the building alone cannot explain.

This is why the temple belongs in a cultural history as both a sacred centre and an institution of work, memory and encounter. Respectful attention can hold devotion and historical inquiry together. It can recognise the force of a shared celebration while asking whose labour supports it and how people’s access differs. Puri becomes richer to read when none of these questions is allowed to stand for the whole.

chapters.title: Temples, Goddesses and Local Shrines
chapters.subtitle: Sacred places in the life of Odisha
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: At Hirapur, a ring of sculpted goddesses faces an enclosure open to the sky. At Tara Tarini, the view extends from a hilltop towards the Rushikulya. In a photograph of Samaleswari, electric light washes a temple tower pink against the evening. These are three different ways of encountering a sacred place: through its arrangement of images, its surrounding landscape, and the changing life around its walls.

Odisha’s temples reward attention to all three. A building can be read through stone, proportion and carving; a place of worship also asks us to follow water, offerings, stories and journeys. Alongside the famous sanctuaries are temporary centres of devotion, assembled for a season or carried through a street. Moving between them gives us a fuller cultural geography, one in which the smallest gathering deserves as careful a description as the tallest tower.

sections.heading: Water and worship in Ekamra
paragraphs: In old Bhubaneswar, Lingaraj stands at the centre of a sacred geography extending beyond its enclosure. India’s 2014 submission for the UNESCO Tentative List describes Ekamra through temples, small shrines, tanks and prescribed ritual routes. It places Lingaraj at the religious centre and Bindusagar at the focus of the old town. The submission draws on sacred texts to explain these relationships; its account is a cultural map as well as a description of buildings.[1]

This changes the scale at which we look. A tank is part of the sacred setting, and a route between shrines belongs to the history of a temple town. The smaller structures beside water or along a wayside become legible as parts of a larger place. Their importance cannot be measured simply by comparing heights.

Ekamra also offers a useful discipline for looking: begin with the celebrated monument, then turn towards its neighbours. What connects the shrines? Where does water gather? Which paths make the separate buildings into a place that can be traversed? Such questions keep architectural appreciation close to the ground.

sections.heading: A remembered offering at Remuna
paragraphs: At Remuna, the name Khirachora Gopinath carries a devotional story. The fourth chapter of the Chaitanya Charitamrita’s Madhya-lila tells of Madhavendra Puri travelling towards Jagannath Puri for sandalwood. At Remuna, Gopinath sets aside a pot of sweet milk for him. The narrative explains the deity’s name through this act: Gopinath becomes the one who steals the milk offering for a devotee.[2]

The story belongs to Vaishnava devotional literature. Its miracle is part of the text’s religious meaning, rather than an event that an architectural survey can establish. Read on those terms, it brings a different kind of evidence into view: affection between deity and devotee, a remembered food, and a journey connecting Remuna, Puri and Govardhana.

A temple’s cultural life can therefore reside in a name as much as a façade. To hear the name explained is to encounter a particular understanding of generosity and devotion. Remuna invites us to read an offering as a story-bearing object, while keeping the text’s account distinct from claims about today’s kitchen or ritual schedule.

sections.heading: A circle at Hirapur
paragraphs: Hirapur’s Chausathi Yogini sanctuary changes the architectural encounter again. The heritage inventory hosted by the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts describes a circular, open-air temple, with Yogini images and a central mandapa associated with Bhairava figures. It distinguishes the sandstone structure from the black-chlorite images inside. Goddess and Shaiva imagery meet within the same small enclosure.[3]

The inventory assigns the building to the early tenth century on architectural and sculptural grounds. This is a stylistic assessment, not a foundation date supplied by an inscription. It also records renovation, conservation and weathering. The sanctuary we see has passed through care and damage; its material history continues after the moment of construction.

In the photograph, the curved wall gathers the figures into a company. Differences of posture remain visible within the repeated niches. Above them are sky, palm fronds and wires: the old sculptures inhabit a present-day setting. Looking closely lets us appreciate the arrangement without pretending that a photograph reveals the full history of the rites once practised here.

sections.heading: Samaleswari and the western horizon
paragraphs: Samaleswari shifts the chapter’s centre towards western Odisha. The Sambalpur district account identifies her as the city’s presiding deity and describes her importance across western Odisha and neighbouring Chhattisgarh. It locates the sanctuary beside the Mahanadi and records several names of worship, including Jagatjanani and Adishakti.[4]

This regional reach matters. A cultural map centred only on the coastal temple cities would leave a major devotional centre at its edge. Following Samaleswari instead allows Sambalpur to become the point from which a wider sacred region is understood. The river and the city belong in that picture alongside the sanctuary.

Aditya Mahar’s 2015 photograph records an evening view: a white tower, coloured illumination, railings and people near the entrance. It is a dated glimpse of a working place of worship. The ordinary fittings deserve to remain in the frame. They remind us that a temple is encountered through movement and maintenance as well as through the silhouette that represents it in a guidebook.

sections.heading: Tara Tarini above the river
paragraphs: In southern Odisha, Tara and Tarini are worshipped together at a hilltop sanctuary overlooking the Rushikulya. The Ganjam district description identifies them as sister goddesses and marks the Tuesdays of Chaitra as especially significant occasions of worship.[5] The hill, river and recurring month give this sacred place both a setting and a rhythm.

The opening photograph looks out from the temple precinct towards the river below. It is a useful counterpoint to a frontal architectural view. Here the surrounding country enters the image, while carved and painted forms occupy the foreground. We see something of what makes an ascent memorable: a change of level and a widening horizon.

The district’s festival account also describes devotees fulfilling vows at the Chaitra gathering.[6] This gives the journey a personal dimension. A place on a map can become the destination of a promise, with a return visit carrying meaning that no photograph can fully show.

sections.heading: When the shrine enters the street
paragraphs: Budhi Thakurani’s yatra offers another relationship between deity and place. Ganjam’s cultural account describes the goddess being taken to a temporary temple during the festival and visiting different streets in procession. It also records decorated festival spaces and displays with religious and contemporary themes.[6]

A temporary shrine changes what we might otherwise understand by permanence. The festival’s importance does not depend on its setting remaining in place throughout the year. For its duration, a route and a gathering space become central to the encounter with the goddess. The devotional landscape is made through movement as well as through construction.

This is why local shrines need to be studied with their streets and calendars. A photograph taken on an ordinary day and a photograph taken during a yatra may describe very different arrangements of the same neighbourhood. Both belong to its history.

sections.heading: Under the shade of a tree
paragraphs: J. C. Mahanti’s Fading Festivals of Odisha describes Chaitra Mangala worship on Tuesdays of the lunar month. In his account, worshippers, mostly married women, gather beneath a tree and prepare an image of Mangala on sand or earth, decorating it with cloth and flowers. Seasonal fruit and pana are offered around midday, accompanied by conch, bells and ululation.[7]

The description brings materials and actions into focus: a shaded place, a prepared image, offerings and a gathering. It gives us a particular account of practice, rather than a rule for every household or locality. Its value lies partly in the scale of attention it permits. We can recognise religious making without first looking for a monumental building.

The women who assemble the worship are central to this scene. A history concerned only with royal patrons and surviving stone would struggle to make their work visible. Cloth, fruit and prepared earth ask for another kind of record, attentive to those who arrange, remember and repeat the observance.

sections.heading: Learning to see the smaller place
paragraphs: These encounters suggest a way of reading Odisha’s sacred landscapes without flattening their differences. A devotional narrative at Remuna, a sculptural inventory at Hirapur and a description of seasonal worship each answer different questions. Together they make room for buildings, remembered journeys and acts of preparation.

The next time a temple tower draws the eye, there is reason to look around it too: towards the tank, the approach, the neighbouring shrine and the place where people gather. There is also reason to ask who can explain what happens there, and to listen for differences between their accounts. Local knowledge gains depth when it is attached to particular people and places.

An adequate cultural portrait must hold the monumental and the intimate in the same field of view. Stone survives unevenly; so do stories and practices. Giving each its proper source and scale is one way to keep a small shrine from disappearing behind a famous skyline.
