chapters.title: Buddhist and Jain Histories
chapters.subtitle: Religious life through places and objects
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A doorway cut into a hillside and a small name impressed in clay offer very different entrances to Odisha’s past. The first can be seen from a distance; the second may fit in a hand. Both preserve traces of religious communities: where people stayed, what they honoured, and how they named the institutions to which they belonged.

This chapter follows Jain caves at Udayagiri and Khandagiri near Bhubaneswar, then the Buddhist remains of Ratnagiri, Lalitgiri and Udayagiri farther north. The two Udayagiris are distinct places. Keeping their identities clear is the beginning of a larger task: allowing different histories to emerge from particular sites and objects.[1][9]

The surviving evidence includes royal inscriptions, residential spaces, images, relic containers and travellers’ accounts. Read together, these sources reveal religious landscapes repeatedly built, used and altered. They also leave gaps. A carefully preserved uncertainty can tell us more than an attractive story that joins every ruin into one institution.

sections.heading: Rooms cut into the hill
paragraphs: The Jain caves of Udayagiri and Khandagiri bring architecture close to the shape of the rock. In its historical account, the National Monuments Authority associates their early cutting with Kharavela and his successors around the first century BCE. It also records work continuing into the Somavamsi period, many centuries later. The hills hold an accumulated history rather than a single building campaign.[1]

Rani Gumpha makes that architectural ambition especially visible. Its two storeys open towards a court, with a rhythm of columns, entrances and carved surfaces. The National Monuments Authority singles it out among the larger caves and describes the flowers, creepers and animal motifs decorating the cave façades. Scale varies across the complex: a monumental frontage and an individual cell ask for different kinds of looking.

In Bernard Gagnon’s photograph, the horizontal openings remain part of a rough, uneven hill. The court gives space from which to take in the whole arrangement; the smaller entrances draw attention back to the rooms. Stone has been removed to create a place that people could enter and inhabit. The landscape itself has become architecture.

sections.heading: Royal memory and later images
paragraphs: At Hathigumpha, Kharavela’s inscription adds a royal voice to the site. Sahapedia’s account by Adrija Ghosh describes its seventeen lines and the expeditions and recovery of Jain images that it records.[2] Such an inscription preserves a ruler’s presentation of his actions. It deserves to be read as a historical text with a speaker and a purpose, alongside the physical setting in which it was placed.

The same guide points to another period of Jain image-making at Khandagiri. It assigns additions in Navamuni and Barabhuji caves to the eleventh century, describing Tirthankaras and their attendant Sasana Devis. Tirthankaras are the liberated teachers central to Jain tradition; the accompanying goddesses are part of the caves’ religious imagery. These later carvings extend the story well beyond Kharavela’s reign.

Ghosh also describes Hindu worship of Chakreswari at Barabhuji. This is a useful, specifically attributed example of a sacred image receiving attention across religious boundaries. It invites a history of particular objects and their changing reception. The guide’s account does not establish that every cave followed the same course, or that the original meanings of its images disappeared.

sections.heading: Ratnagiri in brick and clay
paragraphs: At Ratnagiri, excavation allows us to move from an impressive ruin towards a named community. The Archaeological Survey of India’s report for 1958–59 describes work under Debala Mitra that exposed two neighbouring monasteries. Monastery 1 included a large court, a shrine and twenty-four cells. The report also records major rebuilding: older rooms were filled, new floors raised, and parts of the complex adapted while other spaces remained in use.[3]

Clay sealings supplied the name Ratnagiri Mahavihara and referred to its community of monks. Their lettering connects a physical site to the way an institution represented itself. The count of rooms tells us about the excavated plan; it cannot by itself become a count of students.

The same season’s report records five plaques bearing dharanis, sacred Buddhist formulas, inside another stupa. Religious writing was placed within a structure as part of its devotional life. Together, the sealings and plaques give clay more than one role: it could identify a community or carry a sacred text. The stupas in Satyabrata Nanda’s photograph belong to this wider setting of buildings, deposits and images.

sections.heading: What Lalitgiri kept within
paragraphs: Lalitgiri’s most intimate evidence lay inside its hilltop stupa. Excavations in December 1985 and January 1986 recovered three outer khondalite containers. Two held nested containers of steatite, silver and gold, with bone fragments inside the innermost vessels. The published report distinguishes a gold-wrapped fragment in one set from an unwrapped charred fragment in another; the third outer container lacked the complete inner set.[4]

The care given to these tiny remains is palpable in the sequence of materials. Each container enclosed another, protecting what the community had chosen to preserve. Their religious significance is clear, but the identity of the individuals is unresolved: the report states that the two relic-bearing sets have no inscriptions and presents attribution to the Buddha or disciples as speculation.

Elsewhere at Lalitgiri, the evidence becomes more explicit. Snigdha Tripathy’s study of the monastic sealings reads the name Chandraditya Vihara. The difference is instructive: one object preserves a name, while another preserves remains without naming their owner. Both deserve their full importance. Neither needs an invented certainty to make it compelling.

sections.heading: The other Udayagiri
paragraphs: The Buddhist Udayagiri in Jajpur has its own institutional identities. Bimal Bandyopadhyay’s excavation report distinguishes the earlier excavated complex, identified through seals as Madhavapura Mahavihara, from Udayagiri-2, where work in 1997–2000 recovered evidence for Simhaprastha Mahavihara. The inscription readings were contributed by Snigdha Tripathy.[5]

The second excavation revealed a monastic complex, shrines and a water reservoir. These details bring the practical needs of residence into the archaeological picture. A monastery required places for worship and arrangements that supported people living together. The surviving walls and paved spaces can be approached with both functions in mind.

A sealing can recover a name that a large building no longer announces. Udayagiri names the place we visit; Madhavapura and Simhaprastha name communities identified through the archaeological record. Preserving that distinction gives the landscape a more precise history.
The photograph presents the Buddhist complex as it appeared in 2005. It is a view of exposed remains in a wooded setting, not a reconstruction of the complete monastery or its vanished upper parts.

sections.heading: A traveller and a difficult identification
paragraphs: In the seventh century, Xuanzang described the country of Uda as a place of learning with more than a hundred monasteries and over ten thousand monks. Li Rongxi’s English translation then introduces Pushpagiri Monastery among the mountains. The large numbers belong to Uda as a whole; they are not an enrolment figure for Pushpagiri.[6]

The account combines observations of religious life with reports of marvellous happenings at stupas. Its descriptions of shining light and offerings belong to the devotional world that the traveller recorded. They should remain visible as religious testimony, with a different evidential status from a measured wall or a legible sealing.

Identifying Pushpagiri with a particular excavated site requires further argument. Bandyopadhyay’s 2007 report discusses the proposed identification at Langudi and records scholarly reservations.[5] That dated discussion should not be made into a claim that the question can never be resolved. It does, however, caution against treating Ratnagiri, Lalitgiri and Udayagiri as the campuses of one proven ancient university simply because they form a modern visitor circuit.

sections.heading: The work of keeping histories legible
paragraphs: Modern care is part of the story now visible at these places. At Lalitgiri, the site museum was created to protect and display excavated antiquities, including the nested caskets. The Ministry of Culture’s 2018 announcement described six galleries of sculpture and architectural fragments; the Prime Minister’s Office subsequently confirmed the museum’s inauguration on 24 December.[7][8] Display brings the small object back into conversation with the landscape from which it came.

India’s 2025 Tentative List submission groups Lalitgiri, Udayagiri and Ratnagiri as Buddhist heritage sites. Their place on that list is a step in a heritage process, not World Heritage inscription.[9] The modern grouping makes it easier to consider their relationships while leaving each site’s excavated identity intact.

Jain caves and Buddhist monasteries also need to remain distinct in a cultural edition. Their histories meet through a shared region and through the work of people who record, conserve and interpret them. A cave entrance, a damaged image and an impressed name each carry something different. Looking closely enough to preserve those differences is how a broad history gains human scale.

chapters.title: Mahima Dharma and the Poetry of Bhima Bhoi
chapters.subtitle: The formless divine and the suffering world
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: What does a prayer ask for? Relief, forgiveness, perhaps a place beyond suffering. In Bhima Bhoi’s poetry, the request becomes more difficult: how can the speaker accept deliverance while others remain in pain? The question brings the intimate voice of devotion into contact with the widest imaginable community of living beings.

The nineteenth-century poet gave Mahima Dharma an enduring literary voice. Its founder, Mahima Gosain, and its poet should be distinguished, even as their histories meet. The movement’s commitment to a formless divine and its challenge to inherited religious authority open another route through Odisha’s sacred landscape.[1] At Joranda, that landscape includes the buildings pictured below. At Khaliapali, it includes a place of poetic memory. Between them lies a history carried by words, communities and competing understandings of faith.

sections.heading: A divine beyond the image
paragraphs: Mahima Dharma’s language asks the worshipper to think beyond a deity contained in a visible image. Alekha names the indescribable; nirakara, the formless. Sunya belongs to this vocabulary too. In his study of Bhima Bhoi, Sitakant Mahapatra places these expressions within a longer Odia religious and literary conversation about ultimate reality.[2] Their presence does not, by itself, establish that Mahima Dharma and Buddhism are the same tradition.

The challenge for poetry is immediate. How can language approach what it calls indescribable? A poem must still address someone, ask something and make feeling audible. Bhima Bhoi’s prayer offers a way into that difficulty: an appeal to the guru, a confession of weakness, a demand that suffering be heard. Reading him, we encounter a relation of dependence and urgency rather than a detached list of divine attributes.

Formlessness also does not mean that believers live without gathering places. The Dhenkanal district administration identifies Joranda as a religious headquarters, with Mahima Gosain’s samadhi and the Sunya, Dhuni and Gadi mandiras. It records the annual gathering at Magha’s full moon.[3] These places locate a shared religious life. The photograph cannot explain their practices by itself, but it makes one important point visible: a faith directed towards the formless has a material history of buildings, care and assembly.

sections.heading: The prayer that widens
paragraphs: The twenty-seventh boli of Stuti Chintamani offers a concentrated encounter with Bhima Bhoi’s poetic method. In the English selection printed by Mahapatra, the speaker imagines the weight of wrongdoing gathered into a basket and placed at the guru’s feet. The plea then expands from the burden of one person to the distress of devotees and, finally, to the suffering of the living world.[2]

That movement matters. The basket gives an abstract moral burden the weight and familiarity of something carried. The widening address prevents the poem from resting in private relief. Its culminating willingness to endure condemnation for the sake of others makes compassion costly. In this reading, the poem asks whether salvation can be satisfying when it leaves everyone else behind. The force comes from the change in the scale of concern, from a troubled self to lives beyond it.

sections.heading: Khaliapali and the work of community
paragraphs: Khaliapali belongs to the poet’s later religious life. Mahapatra dates the ashram’s emergence as a centre of his activity to 1877 and identifies Ma Annapurna as supervising it.[2] Remembering her changes the emphasis of the story. A community cannot be sustained by the fame of a single voice alone; it also requires people who hold its daily life together.

The memorial photograph is from 2012. It records a later commemorative landscape, not the appearance of the ashram during Bhima Bhoi’s lifetime. Its towers and grounds offer a setting in which to think about remembrance: what a community chooses to build, preserve and associate with a poet. Joranda and Khaliapali should therefore remain distinct points on our map, connected by faith but carrying different associations.

sections.heading: Weakness as a poetic resource
paragraphs: Compassion is only one register of this writing. In an extract from the thirty-first prayer, reproduced by Nishamani Kar in Odisha Review, the speaker seeks refuge while acknowledging depleted strength and patience. The translation is credited to Saubhagya Kumar Mishra.[4] Here, the voice does not claim mastery of spiritual practice. It asks for help because its resources are failing.

Read alongside the twenty-seventh boli, this admission gives the poems an arresting tension. The person who feels unable to secure his own spiritual footing can still care about the fate of the world. Smallness does not cancel ethical imagination. Nor does anguish disappear when the prayer turns outward. The reader hears vulnerability and an extraordinary reach of concern occupying the same voice.

These observations concern the selected English passages, not a new translation or a line-by-line study of the complete Odia text. Translation gives access, but also shapes cadence, emphasis and the relation between ordinary and sacred language. Keeping the translator visible is part of reading responsibly. A familiar saying detached from its prayer can retain its moral beauty while losing the sequence of images and appeals that gave it force.

sections.heading: Equality and differing authorities
paragraphs: Historian Ishita Banerjee-Dubey places Mahima Dharma among religious movements that worked against caste hierarchy through their practices. She also warns against treating challenges from lower-caste poets and saints as merely a response to the silence of elite intellectuals.[5] This perspective allows us to recognise religious thought as an arena of social argument in its own right.

Yet a movement’s egalitarian promise does not make all its communities identical. Johannes Beltz, drawing on fieldwork in western Odisha in 2000–2001 and documentary sources, examines differing claims to Bhima Bhoi. In the Joranda controversy he discusses, Kaupinadhari and Balkaladhari positions assigned different degrees of authority to the poet’s writings.[1] These are historically situated observations, not a description of every believer today. They remind us that a poem can become a source of institutional argument as well as devotion.

sections.heading: A life remembered in many ways
paragraphs: Bhima Bhoi’s biography requires care. Mahapatra begins by acknowledging uncertainty about his birth and the history of his sight. Beltz treats stories about him as evidence of how a saint is remembered, rather than accepting every episode as a recoverable event.[1][2] A responsible account can respect devotional memory without turning it into an exact chronology.

This matters for the way we picture the poet. An invented face would offer an easy sense of recognition while concealing how little it could establish. The photographs in this chapter instead show places of religious and commemorative life. They leave room for the reader to meet Bhima Bhoi through the work, without mistaking a modern visual reconstruction for a historical record.

sections.heading: The voice beyond its first listeners
paragraphs: On 2 March 2024, addressing a Mahima gathering in Sambalpur, President Droupadi Murmu presented Bhima Bhoi’s writings as a resource for social equality and human welfare, and called for wider translation.[6] This is a documented moment of public reception: a religious poet being addressed to readers far beyond his immediate community.

Such recognition creates an opportunity to return to the poems. Their value is not exhausted by the idea that they convey a good message. They make a reader experience changes of scale: the weight of personal wrongdoing, the need for shelter, the suffering of others, the possibility of concern without limit. The person praying remains vulnerable throughout.

In an edition devoted to Odisha’s cultural worlds, Bhima Bhoi asks us to attend to what words can do within those worlds. Buildings make a tradition visible; communities sustain its practices; a poem can unsettle the boundaries of the self. The question with which we began remains open at the end: what should one ask for, once the suffering of others has entered the prayer?

chapters.title: Muslim and Christian Lives in Odisha
chapters.subtitle: Places of worship and the work of belonging
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A shrine courtyard in Cuttack, a church entrance in Bhubaneswar, a hospital serving Nabarangpur: each opens a different view of Odisha. Muslim and Christian histories belong within the region’s cultural life, alongside the temple landscapes, festivals and literary traditions through which it is often introduced.

This chapter follows selected places and institutions to explore worship, learning, craft and public service. Its subjects are communities with their own religious commitments and internal differences. Their lives cannot be gathered into one story of harmony, nor reduced to episodes of conflict. The buildings pictured here offer starting points; schools, books and personal testimony take us further into the work of belonging.

sections.heading: A courtyard in Cuttack
paragraphs: The National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities records Kadam Rasul in Cuttack, on Jail Road, dating the site broadly to the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and noting a Persian inscription from Aurangzeb’s time.[1] Such a record places Islamic heritage within the city’s historical fabric. It also gives us a useful discipline: attach claims to a particular site, rather than treating every mosque or shrine as interchangeable.

The courtyard photograph shows patterned surfaces, a shaded approach and a doorway into the shrine. These details suggest how much a religious place contains beyond the silhouette of a dome: spaces for arrival, waiting and attendance. A picture cannot tell us the beliefs of the person within it. It can, however, encourage a closer way of looking at a building that remains part of an inhabited city.

A heritage itinerary is only one route into Muslim life. The history of learning offers another. According to its institutional account, the Odisha State Board of Madrasa Education was established in 1971; earlier, students’ examinations had been administered through the Bihar board. Its functions include examinations, courses of study and recognition of affiliated madrasas.[2] This history concerns the practical organisation of education as well as religious learning: where students obtain credentials, who sets examinations and how institutions connect with the state.

sections.heading: The craft beyond a single community
paragraphs: Pipili’s appliqué offers a different connection. In a 2015 Odisha Review essay, Manoj Mishra describes chandua’s relationship with Jagannath’s processional traditions and its expansion into domestic and decorative products. He also records participation by young Muslim makers beyond the craft’s earlier association with the Darji caste.[3] This is a dated observation about a particular craft, not a count of its workforce today.

The connection deserves attention without being turned into a fable in which difference disappears. Cloth has to be selected, cut, stitched and sold. Recognising Muslim participation means recognising labour and skill within a familiar Odishan art. A buyer who sees only the finished umbrella or wall hanging may miss the people whose livelihoods give the object its continuing life.

sections.heading: Christian words in an Odia world
paragraphs: Christian printing forms part of the history of modern Odia reading. Historian Pritipuspa Mishra dates the establishment of the Orissa Mission Press at Cuttack to 1838. Earlier Odia Christian texts had been printed at Serampore. The Cuttack press produced religious tracts and editions of the Bible, but also a dictionary and school textbooks.[4]

The evangelical purpose of this work matters. These publications sought to persuade, and some directly criticised established religious practices. Their contribution to print culture therefore belongs to a history of argument as well as education. Odia became a medium through which Christian teaching addressed readers; the expanding world of print also served needs extending beyond conversion.

The photograph of the Church of Christ in Bhubaneswar brings the relationship between faith and language into a later cityscape. English names the institution at the gateway; Odia lettering appears on the church behind it. The visible coexistence of scripts is a modest but concrete reminder that religious identity and a regional language need not occupy separate worlds.

sections.heading: A southern Christian landscape
paragraphs: Christian life in Odisha also has a substantial southern geography. The National Council of Churches in India traces the Jeypore Evangelical Lutheran Church to the Breklum mission’s work in the former undivided Koraput district, identifying 1882 as its founding year.[5] This Lutheran history differs from the Baptist printing story in Cuttack and from Catholic institutions elsewhere. The church photograph locates one strand of that history in Jeypore.

A personal account makes the institutional story more tangible. In a 2023 Lutheran World Federation interview, Dr Santosh Kumar Nag described himself as a fourth-generation Lutheran from a rural, lower-middle-class family. He had initially wanted to study engineering; after entering medicine, he chose to serve at Christian Hospital Nabarangpur. He explained affordable care and the training of healthcare workers as expressions of faith.[6] His account joins professional decisions to local responsibility. It is testimony from a participant, rather than an independent assessment of the hospital’s services.

sections.heading: Schools and shared aspirations
paragraphs: A school can maintain a religious character while serving pupils from different communities. New De Paul School in Berhampur describes itself as a Catholic institution, primarily serving Christian educational needs but open to other communities. It explicitly retains a Christian identity and worship.[7] Its own account allows us to see openness and religious distinctiveness together, without assuming that one requires the other to vanish.

Institutions also face material difficulties. Elizabeth Gangmei and Gowramma I.P., writing in the Journal of Indian Education in 2018, examined selected Muslim and Christian elementary schools in Odisha. Their purposively selected study identified problems involving infrastructure, teacher appointments and access to professional development.[8] Its findings should not be applied to every minority school or treated as a present-day census. They nevertheless bring teachers and classrooms into a story too easily confined to founders and monuments.

The everyday questions are consequential: whether a classroom has the facilities it needs, whether a teacher can learn new methods, whether a school can take part in wider educational networks. Such matters belong in a cultural account because institutions help shape the opportunities through which children enter public life. Religious communities are also communities of parents, pupils and workers.

sections.heading: Remembering harm and rebuilding trust
paragraphs: Shared life has also been damaged by violence. In October 2009, a World Council of Churches report described its team’s visit to Christians displaced by the 2008 attacks in Kandhamal. Survivors spoke about destroyed homes, lost relatives and fear of returning. The report also documented efforts to rebuild houses and relationships, including local committees and cooperation among church bodies.[9]

This account should be read as a dated report from a visiting church delegation, with testimony from affected people. It cannot stand for every experience in Kandhamal. It does establish why rebuilding cannot be measured only in repaired walls. Home also requires confidence that one can remain, practise a faith and live alongside neighbours without coercion.

The sites and accounts gathered here do not exhaust Muslim or Christian Odisha. They show why neither community belongs at the margins of its cultural history. A shrine, a printed page, a stitched textile, a classroom and a hospital each reveal a different kind of participation. Attending to them means making room for religious conviction, skilled work, unequal conditions and the patient effort required to sustain a shared place.

chapters.title: The Seasonal Calendar
chapters.subtitle: Fields, households and the occasions that shape an Odisha year
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: An Odisha year can be remembered through things held in the hand: a length of swing rope, the first rice of a crop, a little grain measure, a miniature boat lowered onto water. Each object belongs to an occasion. Together they suggest a calendar made through repeated acts, with time felt in food, work, worship and visits.

This chapter follows several of those rhythms. Raja, Nuakhai and Manabasa offer different ways of connecting a household to the agricultural year. Boita Bandana turns a seasonal gathering towards the sea. They belong within a much larger field of observances, whose meanings and dates need to be understood in particular places.

sections.heading: Reading the year
paragraphs: A printed festival list can make Odisha appear to share one uninterrupted round of celebrations. A closer view reveals overlapping calendars. Fields have their rhythms; families remember obligations; temples and public gatherings bring people together on another scale. A holiday may be widely recognised without being observed in the same way by every household.

Even the relationship between festival and date needs care. Raja is associated with Mithuna Sankranti, while the Nuakhai described in western Odisha follows a lunar date in Bhadraba. A season, a calendrical rule and a Gregorian date are different kinds of information. The broad months in this chapter orient the reader; they are not an annual schedule.[1][2]

The distinction matters when we read the landscape. A festival associated with the rains does not certify that rain has arrived in every village. An offering of first rice does not announce that every crop has been harvested. Ritual time gives agricultural experience a shared form, while actual fields remain subject to differences of place and circumstance.

sections.heading: Raja and the work of rest
paragraphs: In Pravukalyan Mohapatra’s account, Raja is especially associated with coastal Odisha. Its three principal days fall around Mithuna Sankranti in June. The earth is understood within the festival’s sacred idiom as menstruating and resting; cultivation is paused. Swings, songs, visits and the sharing of cakes make the interval visible beyond the field.[1]

The swing is an especially expressive object. It takes an ordinary place and gives it a temporary purpose: people gather, wait their turn and watch one another move. Poda pitha and other preparations similarly turn ingredients and kitchen labour into the taste of an occasion. Celebration acquires a texture that a date alone cannot convey.

Raja also asks for a careful account of gender. The literature describes leisure and sociability for girls and women alongside ritual restrictions. Neither side should erase the other. A cultural history can recognise the pleasure of the festival while asking who prepares the food, who receives a respite and how participants understand its rules.

sections.heading: First rice and shared belonging
paragraphs: Nuakhai places new grain at the centre of an encounter between fields, deities and kin. Indhubala Kesavan’s ethnography of a village in Bargarh district describes its observance on the fifth day of the waxing moon in Bhadraba, usually August or September. The offering uses the first ripened paddy, rather than marking the completion of the entire harvest.[2]

In that account, new rice is offered to deities and ancestors and distributed within the family. Greetings and visits extend the occasion beyond a single home. Unmarried sisters have important ritual roles, and gifts accompany their relations with brothers. Rice becomes a means of recognising both dependence on cultivation and obligations between people.[2]

This is a situated account, based on fieldwork, rather than a script for all western Odisha. Kesavan also examines the tension between sisters’ ritual importance and their structural position. Honour within a ceremony should not automatically be read as equality in everyday life. The value of the study lies partly in holding those experiences together.

Public performance adds another setting. The photograph below records Dalkhai at a Nuakhai Bhetghat gathering in Burla. It shows how an occasion can enter a stage programme; it does not show the household offering of first grain. Keeping that distinction helps us see a festival’s several forms without collapsing them into one.

sections.heading: A Thursday inside the home
paragraphs: Manabasa Gurubara brings the seasonal calendar across the threshold. Observed on Thursdays in Margasira, broadly November and December, it is associated with Lakshmi, grain and household prosperity. The mana, a grain measure, gives the observance its distinctive material focus. Women’s worship and the preparation of the domestic space are central to descriptions of the practice.[3]

The photographed jhoti at Sergarh in Baleswar makes that preparation visible through a few white lines: feet, a floral form, an offering. The image is small in scale, but its setting matters. Here the calendar is marked on the surface of a home, rather than only through a procession or a crowded public ground.

The Lakshmi Purana, attributed to Balaram Das, gives this devotional world a powerful narrative dimension. Lakshmi’s departure from Jagannath and Balabhadra brings hardship; the story places hospitality, food and social exclusion within a moral argument. Its challenge to hierarchy deserves attention without treating a sacred narrative as evidence that discrimination disappeared.[3]

Osha and brata invite this kind of close reading: an observance has participants, preparations, stories and obligations as well as a name. The household is therefore an essential place for understanding the cultural year. What may be almost invisible to an outside visitor can be central to the person keeping the occasion.

sections.heading: Small boats and a public memory
paragraphs: At Kartika Purnima, miniature boats give water a ceremonial role. Odisha Tourism describes Boita Bandana as recalling Odisha’s maritime voyages, while the Ministry of Culture places it alongside Cuttack’s Bali Jatra. The little vessel and the large fair work at different scales, joining an intimate gesture to a public commemoration.[4][5]

The photograph from a village pond in Baleswar keeps that smaller scale in view. Flowers, floating craft and the edge of the water make a setting that can be approached without an ocean voyage. The occasion connects participants with a remembered seafaring past; it does not, by itself, establish the route or date of a particular historical expedition.

This distinction allows memory to retain its own importance. Archaeology asks what survives from a port or a ship. A festival asks how a community gives the past a recurring place in the present. Both questions belong in the cultural edition, but they call for different kinds of evidence.

sections.heading: A seasonal guide
paragraphs: These are selected points of orientation, not a complete festival inventory. Gregorian months are approximate; local calendars and organisers should be consulted for a particular year.

March–April: Sarhul. The Kendujhar district account describes sal flowers brought to a sacred grove in Munda observance. This is a community-specific example, not a calendar for all Adivasi peoples.[6]
June: Raja. Rest, swings and sociability gather around Mithuna Sankranti, with a particularly strong coastal association in the account used here.[1]
August–September: Nuakhai. First rice, offerings and kinship come together in the western Odisha field study discussed above.[2]
October–November: Sohrai. The Kendujhar account describes a Munda observance concerned with cattle, including feeding them and tending their shelter.[6]
Kartika Purnima, usually October–November: Boita Bandana. Miniature boats recall maritime journeys; Cuttack’s Bali Jatra gives the commemoration a major public setting.[4][5]
November–December: Manabasa Gurubara. Thursdays in Margasira place Lakshmi, grain and domestic preparation at the centre of the observance.[3]

The gaps are part of the guide’s meaning. A household’s year may also be shaped by observances explored elsewhere in this edition, including temple festivals and Muslim and Christian religious life. The examples here cannot stand for everyone. They offer a way of asking better questions: whose calendar is being described, what work sustains it, and what does returning to the occasion make possible?

Read this way, a seasonal calendar is more than a list of attractions. It is a record of relationships renewed through action. A person prepares, offers, shares, visits or remembers. Repetition gives those acts familiarity, while each new year gives them another setting in which to matter.

chapters.title: A Land of Many Languages
chapters.subtitle: Names scripts and the languages of learning in Odisha
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A sign at Bhubaneswar airport announces a service in Odia, Hindi and English. The same practical message appears in three forms, offering different readers a way into a shared space. It is an everyday glimpse of multilingual Odisha, though only a small part of its linguistic life.

Beyond such public writing are languages learned in families, used among neighbours, carried into classrooms and chosen for poems. Odia, Sambalpuri/Kosali, Desia, Santali, Ho, Kui, Kuvi, Sora, Juang and Koya belong in this account. Their histories cannot be reduced to one script, one administrative category or a set of neatly separated territories.

This chapter offers an orientation to that diversity. It follows names and classifications into questions of writing and learning, asking what becomes visible when we attend to speakers as well as to language labels.

sections.heading: Names on a page
paragraphs: The Census of India’s 2011 C-16 table for Odisha records population by mother tongue. In its published arrangement, Desia and Sambalpuri appear within the broader ODIA heading. That arrangement is important when interpreting the table: a total for the heading is not the same thing as a total for the individual entry named Odia. Nor is either a measure of everyone who can speak it.[1]

The census has a separate C-17 table for bilingualism and trilingualism. Reading the two together makes the difference clear. A mother-tongue return and the ability to use another language answer different questions. The figures describe a dated enumeration; they should not be silently turned into present-day estimates or counts of ethnic communities.[2]

A census category also does not settle what a writer should call their language. Sambalpuri and Kosali occur in public discussion with different emphases. Sahapedia’s indexed introduction to its Haldhar Nag interview identifies his writing as Kosali. That named literary usage deserves to remain visible beside the census term Sambalpuri, without making one source decide every question of identity.[3]

For this edition, the paired form Sambalpuri/Kosali keeps both names in view. It is an editorial aid, not a declaration that every speaker uses them interchangeably. In an interview, poem or performance record, the name preferred by the person concerned should take priority, accompanied where necessary by an explanation for readers.

sections.heading: Relationships beyond the state border
paragraphs: Languages can also be compared through their historical relationships. Odisha’s Academy of Tribal Language and Culture places Kui, Kuvi and Koya within the Dravidian family. The Central Institute of Indian Languages likewise describes Kuvi as Dravidian and locates its speakers in both Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. A state boundary is therefore only one line in a much wider language geography.[4][5]

For another set of relationships, CIIL’s Sora and Juang collections place those languages in the Munda branch of the Austroasiatic family. Unicode’s script documentation identifies Santali as Munda and Ho as North Munda. These descriptions help explain linguistic kinship; they do not imply that the languages are interchangeable or that their speakers share one undifferentiated culture.[6][7]

Kui and Kuvi need particular care because the similarity of their names can encourage confusion. The academy lists them separately, and educational catalogues also provide separate entries. A resource labelled for one should not be reassigned to the other merely because both are associated with Kandha communities.[4][8]

The Koraput landscape below supplies a regional setting for thinking about southern Odisha. It cannot tell us which language a household uses. For that, a photograph must give way to people’s accounts, recordings and carefully located research. A hill range can be shared by several linguistic histories.

sections.heading: A language and its writing
paragraphs: Raghunath Murmu’s commemorative bust honours a named maker of a writing system. Unicode identifies him as the creator of Ol Chiki for Santali. It describes an alphabet written from left to right, with independent vowel letters. It also records Santali’s use of Devanagari, Bengali, Odia and Latin scripts. One language can have more than one history of writing.[7]

Ho offers a related but distinct example. Warang Citi, devised by Lako Bodra, is used for Ho; it is not Ol Chiki. Unicode also notes other scripts used for Ho in different settings. Remembering the separate names matters, both for cultural attribution and for the practical task of finding a suitable book, font or learning resource.[7]

The relationship works in the other direction too: sharing a script does not make two languages identical. CIIL describes Kuvi as using the Odia script. A reader may recognise the written characters yet still need to learn the vocabulary and grammar. Familiar letter shapes are an opening into a text, not a guarantee of understanding.[5]

Writing can extend what speakers do with a language, from keeping a lesson to circulating a poem. It does not confer value on speech for the first time. A story told aloud already has a teller, an audience and a setting. An archive should retain those relationships when it adds a transcription or translation.

sections.heading: When the classroom listens
paragraphs: A dated account from Kumbhitangari in Keonjhar brings the question of language into a child’s school day. In February 2026, UNICEF reported on Savitri Pingwa, a Ho-speaking pupil who had struggled with unfamiliar Odia classroom language. The report describes bilingual materials, familiar settings in stories and support for teachers as part of a multilingual approach.[9]

The same account describes words in children’s languages placed beside Odia equivalents, with Odia script retained in the materials discussed. This is one educational use of a shared script, rather than a statement about the only way Ho or Santali should be written. UNICEF reports increased participation in this school setting; its feature is not an independent evaluation of every classroom in Odisha.[9]

A different document records work before a book reaches learners. A June 2023 Ministry of Education release describes a workshop at the Central University of Odisha preparing materials in Kui and Desia. Participants considered listening, speaking, reading and writing, selected vocabulary and planned illustrated alphabet books. Local trials and subsequent revision were still part of the stated process.[10]

That sequence deserves attention. Preparing a manuscript, trying it with speakers, revising it and making it available to teachers are different achievements. The workshop report documents the first steps and plans; it does not establish later distribution or learning outcomes. Its account of community interaction also makes clear that educational material is made through people’s contributions.

sections.heading: The work behind a resource
paragraphs: SCSTRTI’s trilingual-booklet catalogue gives this labour a visible shelf. It includes separately labelled resources for Ho, Juang, Koya, Kui, Kuvi, Santali and Saora, as well as an entry labelled Bhatri-Desia. The catalogue preserves particular institutional names. It should be read as a guide to publications, not as a definitive classification of every language or variety.[8]

A useful reading practice follows from this. Keep the source’s title, identify its intended readers and ask which variety and script it uses. A catalogue entry confirms that a resource is listed; inspecting the book is a further step. Classroom use and a learner’s response require further evidence again. Each stage adds something that the previous one cannot supply.

For the cultural edition, this means allowing both connection and difference to remain audible. Odia’s public presence belongs beside the literary name Kosali, the educational use of Desia and the distinct histories of Santali, Ho and the southern languages. None needs to disappear so that another can be described clearly.

A land of many languages is made through people addressing one another. Its future lies partly in whether children can learn through familiar words, writers can find readers, and speakers can name their own experience. The sign, the commemorative bust and the learning booklet offer different entrances into that larger conversation.

chapters.title: Odia in Manuscript, Print and Public Life
chapters.subtitle: Copying reading and the making of a literary public
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A manuscript leaf, a newspaper’s subscription notice and a school anthology all put words before a reader. Yet each depends on a different arrangement of work. Someone copies a text; someone pays for printing; someone decides which book belongs in a classroom. The history of written Odia is also a history of these decisions.

This chapter follows that history from the continued use of palm-leaf manuscripts into the presses, newspapers and literary arguments of the nineteenth century. Its focus is how writing circulated and acquired public authority. The making of palm-leaf art receives fuller treatment later in this edition; here, the material page helps us ask who could produce, encounter and judge a text.

sections.heading: The leaf and the listening reader
paragraphs: In her history of language and regional politics, Pritipuspa Mishra describes palm-leaf manuscripts as an important part of Odisha’s textual life even after printing had begun. Copying depended on patronage and the labour of scribes. An author’s composition and a scribe’s surviving copy were different acts, sometimes separated by a considerable interval.[1]

That distinction changes how we look at a museum display. The age of a literary work cannot simply be assigned to every manuscript bearing its title. A photograph may record a leaf clearly while leaving the copyist, copying date and history of ownership unknown. The opening picture is therefore identified as a manuscript photographed at the Odisha State Museum, without supplying a title or date that its source does not establish.

Mishra also describes Bhagabata Ghara or Bhagabata Tungi as places where manuscripts were housed and readings of Jagannath Das’s Bhagabata were heard. A written text could reach listeners as well as people able to read it themselves. The social life of a book extended beyond the person holding it, through a voice and a gathering.[1]

This makes a simple progression from manuscript to print misleading. New presses entered a world with existing ways of copying, reciting and sharing literature. Their arrival changed the means of reproduction, but it did not make those earlier relationships disappear on a single date.

sections.heading: More than one language on a leaf
paragraphs: Odia script and Odia language also need to be distinguished. CIIL’s catalogue describes a palm-leaf Gita Govinda in Odia script. The National Museum’s account identifies Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda as a Sanskrit work and dates its own illustrated palm-leaf example to the eighteenth century. The composition, writing system and physical manuscript each have a history.[2][3]

The photograph below shows a different Gita Govinda display, at the Odisha State Museum in 2013. The source identifies the work, but does not establish the copying date. It should not be called Jayadeva’s autograph or assigned the National Museum object’s date. Keeping objects separate is essential when an image travels beyond its original caption.

For a reader, this is a useful pause before the history of printing. A script connects texts that need not be in the same language. A familiar title can survive in many copies. The cultural world around Odia writing includes these crossings, while the task of identifying a particular manuscript still requires its own evidence.

sections.heading: The press and the schoolbook
paragraphs: Mishra dates the establishment of the Cuttack Mission Press to 1838. Before that, Odia publications including a Bible translation and a grammar had been printed at Serampore and brought to Odisha. The press in Cuttack served missionary purposes and also produced dictionaries and educational material. Its place in print history should retain that religious and institutional setting.[1]

Later presses depended on other forms of support. Mishra describes the Cuttack Printing Company’s funding through shareholders and patrons, while its routine business included government forms and schoolbooks. Her account of its third annual report records 12,500 schoolbooks among 18,200 books printed. Those are production figures reported by the historian, not evidence that every copy reached a separate reader.[1]

Textbooks made repeat demand possible. They also made choices about language consequential: which vocabulary to teach, which poems to select, and whose account of the world children would encounter. Printing was not only a new way to preserve old works. It provided employment, required investment and made particular kinds of writing commercially useful.

The classroom was already a site of political argument. Mishra traces proposals in 1864–65 to replace Odia with Bengali as the language of instruction in Odisha division schools. Officials invoked shortages of suitable Odia books and qualified teachers. Opposition challenged the proposed change and connected the production of books with the standing of the language itself.[4]

This was not a conflict in which every person’s position followed their mother tongue. Mishra notes Bengali as well as Odia participation in the Utkal Bhasha Uddhipani Sabha formed in 1867. The history is best understood through particular institutions, arguments and participants, rather than inherited antagonism between today’s language communities.[4]

sections.heading: A newspaper makes its offer
paragraphs: Utkal Dipika began publication in 1866, during the devastating famine remembered as Na’anka. Odia Bibhaba’s collection introduction identifies Gourishankar Ray as its founder and editor and describes the newspaper’s role in bringing public concerns before government. Alongside news and argument, it carried essays, poetry, reviews and notices of other publications.[5]

The reproduced page offers a closer encounter with the business of circulation. In the archived reprint of the 1866 volume, printed page 9 sets out prices and conditions for the newspaper, postal provision, advertising and printing work. It addresses people as possible subscribers and customers. These are offers on a page; the notice alone cannot tell us how many accepted them.[6]

This modest distinction is important. A newspaper could imagine a dispersed readership and provide a means of reaching it. Demonstrating actual circulation would require further records. The terms nevertheless show the practical arrangements behind public discussion: payment, delivery, available space and work for the press.

The image is taken from a later reprint digitised by Srujanika, rather than photographed directly from an original 1866 sheet. That transmission history stays with the illustration. The page can be studied as evidence of the reproduced terms without being mistaken for an untouched original issue.

sections.heading: Who decides what belongs in a book
paragraphs: The growth of print also opened disagreement about literary value. In Mishra’s account of the 1890s, arguments about Upendra Bhanja’s poetry spread through newspapers and journals. One question was whether older poetry was suitable for schoolchildren; another was whether its place in the literary inheritance should depend on that suitability. Those questions did not always lead to the same answer.[1]

A school selection could therefore become a judgment about the past. Defending an earlier poet did not necessarily mean wanting every work taught in a classroom. Equally, demanding new writing could involve a particular idea of what readers ought to become. The history of print includes argument over the purposes of reading, as well as the multiplication of pages.

Utkal Sahitya, launched in 1897 under Biswanath Kar, provided another setting for this expanding literary life. Odia Bibhaba describes a monthly whose contents ranged across culture, politics, economics and science, alongside travel writing, biography, fiction and poetry. Its publication history brings several kinds of knowledge into the same reading space.[7]

The widening ambition of print should not be confused with universal access. Mishra emphasises the limited urban and educated constituency of the early public sphere. Editors could speak in the name of a much larger public than the group actually producing or reading their journals. Questions about class, gender and participation belong beside the achievements of the press.[1]

Today, digitised collections let us return to some of these pages. Their gaps and condition remain part of the evidence: an archive’s index helps locate a text, but does not guarantee that every issue survives. The reader’s task is to keep the date, edition and source attached. In doing so, we can follow written Odia through its changing public life while still noticing the people and work that made a page available.

chapters.title: Poets, Storytellers and the Changing Literary World
chapters.subtitle: Who speaks and who is heard
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A girl listens to her father sing. An exiled queen wakes to a forest that welcomes her. Another queen looks back on the cost of a life remembered chiefly through other people’s victories. Literature brings these experiences into view by deciding whose feelings deserve our attention.

This chapter follows a small group of works across Odisha’s literary world. It moves from Sarala Das’s epic imagination through Fakir Mohan Senapati’s short fiction and Gangadhar Meher’s poetry to Pratibha Ray, women’s writing in translation and Haldhar Nag. The selection offers a route into reading, rather than a complete history. Its central question is how an inherited story changes when its centre of attention moves.

sections.heading: An epic open to argument
paragraphs: Sarala Das’s fifteenth-century Mahabharata invites us to think of retelling as an act of authorship. A familiar narrative can acquire different moral pressures in another poet’s hands. B. N. Patnaik’s account of Sarala’s work offers a particularly striking example in Sakuni, a character often remembered chiefly for intrigue.[1]

In Patnaik’s reading, Sakuni recognises his responsibility for the deaths of his nephews and of innocent soldiers. He chooses death on the battlefield over returning to rule. The interest lies in the burden of responsibility that this interpretation gives him. A figure associated with manipulation becomes capable of judging the consequences of his own actions.

This is a useful way to enter an epic without reducing it to a set of exemplary heroes and villains. Ask what a retelling makes newly difficult to judge. The discussion here follows Patnaik’s interpretation; it does not claim to settle every episode or manuscript reading in Sarala’s vast work.

sections.heading: Rebati and the wish to learn
paragraphs: Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Rebati begins inside a household. The child already participates in a world of words: she hears her father’s devotional singing and reading, learns songs and sings them herself. Her wish for lessons grows within this existing intimacy with language. Her father and the teacher Basudev support her, while her grandmother insists on the domestic skills expected of a girl.[2]

The opening makes the conflict painfully concrete. Rebati wants to learn; the adults disagree about what a girl should be allowed to know. Reading the story through that exchange keeps her desire in view before later suffering threatens to overwhelm it.

A close reading can pause here, at the household argument, rather than hurry toward a moral extracted from the ending. Who recognises the child’s eagerness? Who sets the boundaries of her future? The short story makes such ordinary speech worthy of sustained attention. A cultural history of literature needs this domestic scale alongside the great events of epic.

sections.heading: A forest receives Sita
paragraphs: In Gangadhar Meher’s Tapasvini, the Ramayana’s aftermath becomes the setting for Sita’s life in exile. Canto IV, available in Harekrishna Meher’s English translation, opens with dawn approaching her dwelling. Dew, leaves, birds and breeze participate in a welcome that grants the abandoned queen dignity.[3]

The scene is tender without being free of pain. Sita rises with Rama still in her thoughts and asks that he be blessed. Later, the river Tamasa receives her with the intimacy of an embrace. Speaking of her own journey, the river links perseverance to the water she gives those along her banks.

Nature here does more than furnish a beautiful background. It becomes a company of attentive beings around a woman who has suffered. That reading should retain the poem’s particular understanding of devotion: Sita’s fidelity remains central. Reading through a translation also means hearing the translator’s choices of rhythm and vocabulary. Harekrishna Meher’s rendering gives access to the scene without replacing the sound of Gangadhar’s Odia.

sections.heading: Draupadi looks back
paragraphs: Pratibha Ray’s Yajnaseni returns to the Mahabharata through Draupadi’s consciousness. In the English excerpt published on Ray’s website, the approach to the end of life becomes an occasion for questioning attachment, desire and the meaning of what has been endured.[4]

The Himalayan ascent supplies a stark image. Draupadi falls; her husbands continue. Her reflections make the cost of the journey personal. The reader meets a consciousness measuring its own experience, rather than simply a figure moving toward an ending already known from epic.

Placed beside Tapasvini, this passage suggests a rewarding comparison. How does each work allow a woman to speak from within a sacred story? Where does tenderness lead, and where does questioning begin? These are distinct literary projects, not interchangeable statements on womanhood. Their differences make the comparison worth pursuing. The website does not identify the translator of this excerpt, so its English wording is not attributed here to a named translator.

sections.heading: A larger circle of readers
paragraphs: A literary world also changes through the work of selection and translation. Spark of Light, edited by Valerie Henitiuk and Supriya Kar and published by Athabasca University Press in 2016, brings together short stories by women writers of Odisha in English. Its contents place Reba Ray, Binapani Mohanty, Pratibha Ray, Sarojini Sahoo and many others within one reading journey.[5]

The anthology’s range matters. Women’s writing becomes visible as a field of differing voices, periods and concerns. The publisher identifies class, poverty, violence and family among its themes. Readers can follow these concerns across stories while resisting the temptation to make any single author speak for all women. The open-access edition also provides a practical next step: begin with a story, read its contributor information and notice who translated it.

Haldhar Nag widens the linguistic frame. A Lehigh University literary profile identifies his language as Kosali, also called Kosali-Sambalpuri or Sambalpuri. It describes poetry that reworks mythological stories while also addressing land, agriculture and environmental concerns. Its discussion points readers to Surendra Nath’s English translations in Haldhar Nag: Selected Poems, published by Black Eagle Books in 2020.[6]

This is a reminder to keep Odisha’s literary geography open. A chapter centred on Odia should not absorb every neighbouring voice into that label. Language names, local audiences and the conditions of translation deserve attention in their own right. A translated collection is an invitation to seek the poet’s spoken and written language, as well as an opportunity to encounter the work in English.

sections.heading: Returning to the works
paragraphs: The most useful next step is to read slowly. Begin with the family conversation in Rebati; then compare the welcome offered to Sita with Draupadi’s recollection of abandonment. Return to an epic character whose motives once seemed settled. In each case, attend to the person speaking, the person listening and the experiences left outside the frame.

Odisha’s literary world grows through the making, reinterpretation and translation of stories. Each encounter can lead us toward another writer, another language and another experience that deserves to be heard.

chapters.title: The Craft of the Poem
chapters.subtitle: Sound comparison and the voices within a song
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A poem gives us more than a subject to remember. A consonant returns; a comparison turns joy into something imaginable; a name enters a lyric just as we think we know who is speaking. These small decisions shape the experience of reading and listening.

This chapter brings together three ways into Odia poetic craft: the alphabetic and dramatic design of Champu, sound and comparison in Upendra Bhanja, and the poet’s signature within a song. Brief original phrases appear beside literal English glosses. The glosses explain a local meaning; they do not recreate the music of the verse.

The pictures invite a related kind of attention. Who listens, who persuades and what does a printed page preserve? Following these questions makes craft visible without turning the poem into a catalogue of technical terms.

sections.heading: The alphabet becomes a composition
paragraphs: Kavisurya Baladeva Rath’s Kishorachandrananda Champu joins literary design to a sung tradition. In his account of Odissi music, Kalicharan Pattanaik describes Sanskrit prose alongside verse governed by raga and tala, and songs organised through initial letters from ka to ksha. He also recalls arranging Champus for his stage in 1932. A composition and a later dramatic presentation are connected, but distinct.[1]

The alphabet supplies a constraint, not the entire experience. It cannot tell a singer where to place every emphasis or a listener how to understand every reply. The digital contents on Odia Wikisource offer a practical route into individual songs. Its editorial note also explains an exception to alphabetical sequence, placing sa before sha with the retroflex sound, in order to preserve the emotional progression. That explanation belongs to this edition and should be read as such.[2]

A confidante can change the direction of a scene by listening or persuading. The painting below makes that agency visible in a different work, Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda. The Cleveland Museum identifies Krishna twice: preparing leaves at the right and watching Radha from among the trees. Beside Radha, her sakhi urges a meeting. The image shows how several actions can occupy one painted space; a song must unfold them through time.[3]

sections.heading: Hear the returning consonant
paragraphs: Begin with a small observation in the eighteenth chhanda of Upendra Bhanja’s Baidehisha Bilasa. In the consulted transcription, its first two lines open with the following words:[4]
ବନ୍ୟା  ·  ବିଟପ

Both begin with the consonant conventionally named ba. The attached vowels differ, so these are not identical spoken syllables. The pattern is something the reader can see before the whole sentence is understood. Read the openings aloud, then return to the passage and notice how sound accompanies the developing scene.

A constraint can become a resource for invention. It asks a poet to find words that satisfy the pattern while carrying an action or feeling. Yet the discovery of repetition does not settle every technical classification. Bhandaram Vani’s introduction to Dandin’s Kavyadarsha distinguishes figures operating through sound from those working through sense; it treats yamaka as a more specific pattern of repeated sounds. A returning initial consonant should not automatically receive that label.[5]

sections.heading: A comparison makes feeling tangible
paragraphs: Later in the same chhanda, amid reunion involving Rama, Bharata and their assembled company, stanza 36 offers a compact comparison:[4]
ଦରିଦ୍ର ଧନ ଲଭିଲା ପରି
Literal gloss: “like a poor person finding wealth.”

The word pari means “like” in this phrase. It brings the happiness of reunion alongside an experience of gaining something deeply needed. The comparison supplies more than another word for joy: it gives the feeling a situation that a reader can imagine.

This is the usefulness of a term such as upama, or simile. It directs attention to what is compared and what likeness makes the comparison work. Naming the device is only a beginning. We still need the surrounding scene to understand its force, and the Odia words to hear how it is expressed.[5]

sections.heading: When the poem names its craft
paragraphs: Bhanja’s Subhadra Parinaya makes technical vocabulary part of its own speech. On printed page 2 of the 1939 fourth edition, the first chhanda’s stanzas 16–18 include terms such as shlesha, yamaka and anuprasa. The page is evidence that the poem names devices; explaining each one still requires a particular example.[6]

The facsimile also reminds us that a poem reaches us through an edition. The verse, explanatory notes, printing and later digitisation are separate layers of work. Preserve their distinctions when comparing a printed witness with an online transcription.

sections.heading: When the poet enters the song
paragraphs: A character speaks, a poet composes and a performer gives the words a voice. A name inside a lyric asks us to notice another relationship between these roles. In his study of Vidyapati, Ramanath Jha uses bhanita for a poet’s name in a song’s closing couplet. He also describes signatures being altered, added or omitted in that corpus. A signature is therefore useful evidence, but cannot alone settle authorship.[7]

An Odia example appears in Utkal Sangeet’s transcription of Ramani Ratana, attributed there to Bhanja’s Lavanyanidhi. A woman addresses a cloud concerning her absent beloved. The final stanza includes:[8]
ଭଣେ ଉପଇନ୍ଦ୍ର
Literal gloss: “Upendra says.”

The spelling follows this transcription. The phrase places the named poet within the verbal composition, rather than only in a heading above it. The woman’s longing and the poet’s named presence remain distinguishable. Neither should be confused with the biography of the singer who performs the lyric.

Listen again after finding the signature. Does its arrival frame what came before, or invite a change of emphasis? These are questions for an identified rendition. A printed transcription cannot establish that every singer uses the same wording, and a poet’s name cannot supply missing credits for music or performance.

sections.heading: Keep the words within reach
paragraphs: A useful reading begins with a short, located passage. Identify its speaker, notice a repeated sound, and ask what a comparison makes imaginable. Keep the original beside the gloss. An English explanation may clarify the sense while leaving the sound pattern behind.

Access itself has makers. The Centre for Internet and Society’s interview with Prateek Pattanaik documents his work bringing the Champu to Odia Wikisource. Such work allows a reader to locate and revisit a passage; it does not remove the need to compare editions.[9]

The craft of a poem becomes clearer through these returns. Read, listen and look again. A familiar line may disclose a new choice of sound, a different relation between speakers, or a detail that the first hearing passed over.

chapters.title: Dhaga, Dhamali, Riddles and Everyday Wit
chapters.subtitle: The pictures and judgements carried by everyday speech
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A lemon pressed too hard. An answer that volunteers more than anyone asked. A rice-pounder travelling all the way to heaven, only to resume its familiar work. A few words can call an entire scene into a conversation.

The expressions gathered under dhaga and dhamali offer an entry into this compact art. This chapter selects a few sayings from Project Odisha’s Words We Carry collection and follows their credited witnesses. It then turns to a published example of Kui riddling, keeping the language and source distinct. These are selected readings, not a survey of everything spoken across Odisha.[1]

The pleasure lies partly in recognition. We see the object, hear the mismatch or find the answer. But the occasion matters too: the same familiar saying may offer affectionate advice in one conversation and become a cutting rebuke in another.

sections.heading: When too much turns bitter
paragraphs: ଅତି ଲେମ୍ବୁ ଚିପୁଡ଼ିଲେ ପିତା ।
Literal rendering: “If you squeeze a lemon too much, it turns bitter.”[2]

The action begins usefully and ends by undoing its benefit. That reversal makes proportion easy to imagine. In an invented example, someone has agreed to help with a small task, but the requests keep multiplying. The saying could remind the asker to stop before goodwill is exhausted.

sections.heading: The answer arrives before the accusation
paragraphs: ଠାକୁର ଘରେ କିଏ ରେ? ନାଁ ମୁଁ କଦଳୀ ଖାଇନାହିଁ
Literal rendering: “Who is in the shrine room? Well, I have not eaten the bananas.”[3]

The question asks who is there; the reply introduces an act that nobody mentioned. The listener completes the little drama. This is the comic force of excess information, rather than a reliable test of dishonesty. A nervous or defensive answer alone cannot establish guilt.

The saying’s scene is a verbal invention, not evidence of an actual incident or of a particular temple custom. In a new, imagined setting, someone asked who moved a notebook might immediately insist that they never read it. The surroundings change while the mismatch between question and answer remains.

sections.heading: The same work in a new place
paragraphs: ଢିଙ୍କି ସ୍ୱର୍ଗକୁ ଗଲେ ବି ଧାନ କୁଟିବ
Literal rendering: “Even if the dhinki goes to heaven, it will still pound paddy.”[4]

A dhinki is a traditional rice-pounding implement; paddy is rice still in its husk. The joke sends a workaday object to a magnificent destination while leaving its task unchanged. The contrast makes an established habit visible.

Imagine a holiday on which the family organiser is still arranging everybody’s timetable. A friend might recall the saying with a smile. That is an editorial example, not a collected conversation. The image can tease an unaltered habit without declaring that people cannot learn, change work or escape an inherited occupation.

sections.heading: A riddle asks us to look again
paragraphs: A proverb can illuminate a situation; a riddle asks the listener to discover something concealed in a description. Anuja Mohan Pradhan’s study of Kui riddles in Kandhamal and adjoining areas gives this example in Roman transcription:[5]
Badigara tani kradi Dosamane.
His English rendering is: “A tiger is sleeping inside the cave.”

Pause before reading the answer: the tongue, resting inside the mouth. The familiar body becomes a landscape, with the possibility of sudden movement. The wording and answer belong to Pradhan’s published account; this chapter does not present them as an Odia saying or as a newly collected performance.

Another example in the study describes a vessel departing hungry and returning satisfied: a water pot. Both descriptions ask the listener to move between an ordinary object and an unexpected likeness. Pradhan emphasises the roles of tone, gesture and exchange in riddling. On a printed page we receive the puzzle, while much of the encounter remains outside the record.

sections.heading: A saying already in print
paragraphs: A version of the lemon saying appears in Dhagamalika, first part, published in Cuttack in 1893. On the page reproduced below, it occurs in the sixth text line, after the first saying on that line. The page provides a dated witness; it cannot tell us who first spoke the expression.[6]

The title page identifies Gobinda Rath as publisher and Victoria Press as the press. Neither a catalogue heading nor the survival of a printed book should turn the publisher into the inventor of the sayings. The modern wording used earlier follows a separately credited digital witness. We retain that distinction rather than silently modernising the old page.

sections.heading: What we inherit can be questioned
paragraphs: ନାହିଁ ମାମୁଁ ଠଉଁ କଣା ମାମୁ ଭଲ
Literal rendering: “A one-eyed maternal uncle is better than no maternal uncle.”[7]

The practical thought concerns accepting some help when the ideal is unavailable. Yet its bodily comparison treats disability as a deficiency in a person’s worth. Understanding an inherited expression does not oblige us to repeat that judgement. We can explain the historical wording and choose another way to express the useful thought.

This is part of reading with care. A proverb’s age does not make it fair in every situation. Nor should a witty line close a discussion simply because people recognise it. Ask who is being described, who is allowed to laugh, and whether the person addressed can answer back.

sections.heading: Keep the occasion with the words
paragraphs: The lemon image is not an instruction to abandon effort. Nor does it decide how much effort a situation needs. Its compactness leaves that judgement to the people speaking. The English rendering carries the picture; hearing the Odia gives access to the phrase’s own movement and sound.

A family notebook can hold more than a list. Record the exact expression, the person who shared it, the place and date, and the situation in which they would use it. If they remember a different wording, preserve that version beside the printed one. Ask permission before recording or publishing their voice.

An English gloss helps a reader enter the scene, but it cannot preserve every echo or social relationship. A performance note might record a pause before the punch line, a change in tone or an answering joke. Such details should come from an actual encounter, not from an editor’s imagination disguised as fieldwork.

The examples here invite that next encounter. Try a saying on your own conduct before directing it at someone else. Let a riddle remain unanswered long enough for another person to find a different possibility. Everyday wit stays alive when words can be remembered, questioned and used with attention to the people listening.
