chapters.title: Stories Passed from Voice to Voice
chapters.subtitle: Tellers, listeners and the lives of a tale
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A story survives through the person who tells it again. A remembered exchange becomes dialogue; a pause invites a question; a familiar ending acquires the weight of a particular voice. To encounter Odisha’s oral storytelling is therefore to meet people, as well as plots.

Musamoni Panigrahi’s recorded telling in Baleswari Odia offers one such meeting. Filmed by Subhashish Panigrahi in January 2014, it preserves a named speaker and a regional form of speech. The recording lets a future listener return to a particular telling, rather than imagine a single voice speaking for all Odisha.[1]

sections.heading: A widow answers through a riddle
paragraphs: In the recording’s English subtitles, a widow approaches a judge with her baby. Her husband has died, and others have taken their land using a forged impression of his finger. Asked for family names, she must negotiate a convention that prevents her from speaking her husband’s name directly. Her answer turns to arithmetic: fourteen multiplied by four, then four added, produces sixty. The name is explained as Sathia.[2]

The episode places verbal ingenuity beside material vulnerability. A woman seeking help has to make herself understood within a rule that constrains her speech. The puzzle is therefore more than a detachable joke. In this reading, its pleasure comes from watching an apparently blocked conversation become possible.

The subtitles also register a question from the listener, laughter and, towards the end, difficulty recalling part of the tale. These details belong to the encounter. An edition that tidied them all away would give us a smoother plot, but a poorer sense of how remembering happens.[2]

We should keep the teller’s account distinct from documentary history. A story can carry ideas about authority, widowhood and cleverness without establishing that its narrated incident occurred. Equally, an English rendering cannot carry every sound and association of Baleswari Odia. The linked recording and subtitles allow readers to move beyond this brief paraphrase.

That attention to the event has a scholarly counterpart. Sanjaya Kumar Bag’s study of western Odisha brings the kathani, its kathak or teller, and its performance into the same discussion. It asks us to consider social setting alongside narrative content. Here, the widow’s problem and the exchange between speaker and listener are both part of what makes the story worth attending to.[3]

sections.heading: A teller has a name
paragraphs: An archive entry for Shagadiara Katha identifies Ratnakar Sutar as its narrator and Sangram Keshari Senapati as its maker. It dates the recording to 18 January 2025 and preserves a telling lasting more than thirteen minutes. Those particulars give the story a visible human source.[4]

The distinction between narrator and recorder matters. One supplies the telling; the other makes this particular record available. A useful caption keeps both names. It also gives the recording date without suggesting that the story itself began on that day.

For this chapter, the entry documents an act of narration; we do not offer an unverified synopsis of its plot. Readers can follow the source link to hear the performance. Beside Musamoni’s recording, it reminds us that an oral archive need not consist only of anonymous fragments from an unspecified past. It can hold identifiable tellings made in different years, inviting comparison without forcing them into a single standard version.

sections.heading: When words are sung
paragraphs: Voice carries more than prose tales. A recording made by Sangram Keshari Senapati on 3 December 2023 names Shantilata Dwibedi as the reciter of an Odia marriage kandana. It is presented here as a documented recital, not as evidence that the camera witnessed a wedding.[5]

Lullabies and children’s rhymes offer another route into this world. Pratap Kumar Dash discusses nanabaya gita within a wider field of Odia oral expression: words used around feeding, play, comfort and sleep, alongside songs and narrative performances associated with other occasions.[6]

A lullaby need not unfold a complete adventure to give a child a small world to inhabit. Repeated sounds, an address to someone absent, an animal or a familiar household action can sustain attention. Reading these forms beside folktales broadens our idea of transmission: what passes onward may be a rhythm, a relationship or a way of addressing another person, as well as a sequence of events.

sections.heading: The journey into print, and back
paragraphs: A printed collection gives a tale another kind of home. Ram Narayan Das’s Kathalahari, in its 1927 sixth edition, includes Halahal Kumar or Sashisena Abhimanyu. Our existing research on Sashisena distinguishes this collected folktale from Pratap Ray’s literary poem. The printed witness should be named when we use it, rather than silently folded into a universal account of the story.[7]

This is one reason to welcome differences between versions. A changed name, an altered punishment or a different place of reunion may be the very feature that reveals how a story has travelled. Comparison begins by asking which book, which teller and which occasion supplied the passage. It does not require us to decide immediately that one version is right and all the others defective.

The same care can guide a family recording. Ask the teller what they call the story, who they learned it from, and whether they remember hearing it another way. Leave room for an interrupted sentence, a correction or a listener’s question. With the teller’s agreement, keep the original recording beside any edited transcript or translation, and record how it may be shared.

These are editorial practices proposed for this edition, not claims that every storyteller follows the same rules. Odisha’s languages and communities do not fit into one household scene or one inherited repertoire. The examples here open a few doors; they cannot stand for the whole house.

What joins them is the possibility of return: to a speaker’s name, to the words of a particular version, to the person who helped preserve it. A book can offer that route back. The next telling, however, still needs someone willing to listen.

chapters.title: Listening to Odisha
chapters.subtitle: Breath, metal, movement and the sounds of work
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: To listen to a place is to notice more than its best-known songs. A shell sounded by a player, a struck metal disc and the movement of a loom lead towards different kinds of knowledge. Each has a maker, a setting and someone who knows what to listen for.

This chapter opens the musical part of the edition through those relationships. It begins with the conch ensemble, follows the mahuri into another gathering, and turns towards the metalworker and the workshop. Odisha emerges through particular occasions and skills, rather than a single soundtrack.

sections.heading: Breath in company
paragraphs: In the Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre’s account of Thakurani Jatra, published in the 2012 Republic Day programme, Jodi Sankha belongs to Ganjam’s religious processions. Conch playing and bodily movement form a combined presentation. The accompanying instruments named are dhol, changu and mahuri. The shell may first catch our attention, but the account directs us towards a group.[1]

The photograph on the opening page makes that company visible: conch players occupy different levels while drummers stand beside them. It records one arrangement, not a diagram that every troupe must follow. Its energy comes from bodies supporting, balancing and playing together. Looking closely suggests a question for listening: how do musicians coordinate what an audience experiences as one performance?

Mahuri leads us into a second setting. An Indian Council for Cultural Relations programme describes the instrument, also spelt Muhuri, with a double reed, a wooden body and a flared wooden bell. Its Bajasal entry places mahuri with dhol, nishan, tasha and jhanj in a western Odisha dance associated with marriage celebrations.[2]

Another witness is a particular instrument in Berlin’s Ethnologisches Museum. The catalogue records a mahuri with seven finger holes and a decorated metal bell; its reed support and mouthpiece are missing. The contrast with the programme’s wooden bell is worth retaining. These are descriptions of different examples, not competing instructions for one standard instrument.[3]

The museum object also brings absence into view. We can read its dimensions and examine its construction, but a missing mouthpiece and an absent player leave part of the story untold. The museum’s 2019 donation date records an acquisition, not the instrument’s invention. To understand its working life we would need the knowledge of musicians and makers as well as the surviving object.[3]

sections.heading: Metal, hands and occasions
paragraphs: Ringing has a history of skilled work behind it. “Metal Craft of Orissa,” published in 2004, distinguishes ghanta, a gong, among beaten-metal products, from ghanti, a bell, among cast brass objects. The article places their manufacture within Kansari metalworking, alongside utensils, lamps and other objects. Sound-making shares a workshop world with everyday use.[4]

The same account describes ringing during arati and offerings, and rhythmic gong playing during the Car Festival. Kalahandi’s district culture table gives another setting: Ghanta Vadya group performance around Bhawanipatna and Kesinga at auspicious events. An object handled in worship and an ensemble of players call for different kinds of attention.[4][5]

Names help, but the object and its use must stay beside the name. The cowbell pictured here is a separate museum example, not an illustration of a temple ghanti. It widens the chapter’s view of what deserves to be heard.

sections.heading: Beyond the concert platform
paragraphs: Subhashish Panigrahi photographed the cowbell at the Tribal Museum in Koraput in December 2017. The image record identifies it as an artefact collected from a local Indigenous community without naming that community or its maker. Its suspension and sounding parts are visible; its particular history remains a question.[6]

We can let that question lead beyond display cases. Who made the object? Who attached it, repaired it or recognised it at a distance? What mattered to the person who used it? Such questions connect sound with daily responsibilities. They also prevent a museum label from becoming an invented account of village life.

Work offers another way of listening. A loom photograph shows hands, thread and a working position; it does not reproduce the sounds of that moment. To hear a workshop well, we would need to connect a sound with an action and the worker’s explanation. A pause might be an adjustment, a check or simply a rest. The observer cannot decide which by admiring the rhythm.

Film can help make these relationships available to a wider audience. PSBT’s catalogue identifies Biswanath Rath’s Kotpad Weaving: The Story of a Race Against Time as a 2018 documentary, 29 minutes long, in Odia and English. Its subject includes the textile tradition and natural dyeing. The credits name Vinayak Dasgupta as editor and sound recordist, and Sudharshan Lingam as sound designer and mixer.[7]

Those credits remind us that recorded sound has makers too. A documentary offers an arranged encounter, shaped by choices of recording and editing. Its catalogue is a route towards viewing, not a substitute for hearing the film. No account of its soundtrack is claimed here.

sections.heading: A small practice of attention
paragraphs: At a welcomed performance, begin by following one sound. Then notice the people around its player: who enters, who waits, who carries the pulse, who responds to movement? At a workshop, begin with the task. Ask the maker which detail matters, rather than turning useful labour into background music.

These are listening invitations, not reports of field visits. A useful note would preserve the place, occasion, player’s or maker’s preferred name, and what they explained. Recording and public sharing need their own agreement. Sometimes listening and remembering are enough.

The chapters that follow take up songs, dances and theatre in greater detail. Carry this habit into them: attend to the supporting musician as well as the central performer, to the tool as well as the finished object, and to the person whose knowledge makes the sound intelligible. A cultural history becomes richer when hearing is joined to learning.

chapters.title: Odissi Music and Its Literary Worlds
chapters.subtitle: Poetry, melody and the people who carry a song
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A poem becomes a different encounter when someone sings it. Words acquire duration; an address to a beloved can linger; a returning phrase can bring a listener back to an unresolved feeling. Odissi music invites us to hear literary imagination through the choices and knowledge of musicians.

Its vocal life deserves attention in its own right. Utkal University of Culture’s 2023–24 postgraduate syllabus in Odissi Vocal places practical singing beside notation, repertoire and theory. Champu, Chhanda, Choutisha and Gita Govinda appear as subjects for study and performance. The curriculum offers a doorway into a substantial musical world, extending beyond accompaniment for dance.[1]

sections.heading: The poem is part of the music
paragraphs: Writing in the Music Academy’s 1958 journal volume, Kalicharan Pattanaik emphasised the literary character of Odissi song. His discussion attends to the thought carried by a stanza and to the sound of its words. Read as a musician’s historical account, it encourages us to ask what a sung phrase is saying, as well as how it moves.[2]

Kavisurya Baladeva Rath’s Kishorachandrananda Champu provides a meeting place for those questions. Pattanaik describes Sanskrit prose alongside a poetic portion governed by raga and tala, with songs ordered through letters from ka to ksha. The theme centres on Radha and Krishna. He also recalls arranging Champus for dramatic presentation on his stage in 1932: a later act of interpretation, distinct from the composition of the work.[2]

The alphabetic design gives a listener something to recognise, but it cannot supply an entire performance. A written sequence does not tell us how a particular singer will hold a syllable, shape a line or respond to an accompanist. Literary form and musical learning meet in the rendition.

A useful recorded example appears in Prateek Pattanaik’s Odissi Project. The catalogue identifies Balaram Gouda of Naikanipalli, Ganjam, as the lead vocalist for Nua-nata-patali-mukuta He, the nga song from the Champu, in raga Kumbhakamodi. It also names Bhimasen Mahankud and Praphulla Swain for mardala and khola, and Gaurahari Khuntia and Jagannath Dora for gini and other accompaniment.[3]

Follow the linked catalogue to the recording with those names in mind. The encounter is no longer simply with an anonymous “traditional song.” There is a literary work, a named rendition and a company of musicians. This chapter identifies that route for listening; it does not offer a transcription or detailed analysis of the audio.

sections.heading: Longing, persuasion and a new rendition
paragraphs: Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda offers another literary world. In this painting, Radha’s confidante encourages her to meet Krishna. The Cleveland Museum identifies Krishna twice: preparing leaves at the right and watching from among the trees. Persuasion, anticipation and waiting occupy a single picture. A song has to unfold its emotional movement through time.[4]

One documented contemporary interpretation is Virahī, part of Bijayini Satpathy’s ABHIPSAA (2021). Its production credits identify Raghunath Panigrahi’s song composition of a Gita Govinda ashtapadi as the basis. Bindhumalini Narayanaswamy is the singer; Srinibas Satapathy supplies the prelude composition, melodic arrangement and flute; Shivshankar Satapathy supplies rhythm composition, mardala and manjira; Agnimitra Behera plays violin.[5]

The poet, song composer, singer, arranger and choreographer occupy different places in this chain. Keeping their credits together makes interpretation visible: a literary work reaches another audience through several kinds of creative labour. The painting illustrates the literary world, not this particular production.

sections.heading: Raga, tala and the work of listening
paragraphs: For a beginning listener, raga and tala name two different aspects of musical organisation: melodic character and rhythmic cycle. They are useful questions to ask about a rendition, alongside its text and poet. Learning their names begins an enquiry; hearing how a musician develops them requires time and guidance.

The Odissi Music database gives Adatali as fourteen matras, divided 4 + 3 + 4 + 3. A matra is the unit counted within the cycle. Speaking those groups makes their organisation apparent, but does not reproduce the drum syllables, hand gestures or phrasing of a performance.[6]

A song’s occasion is another piece of information. Pattanaik’s catalogue lists Chandramani Lenka’s Jhulibe Ta Aja Kunje Barajaraja as a Jhulana Jatra song in raga Kamodi and tala Adatali. Festival, melody and cycle belong together in its record without becoming interchangeable labels.[3]

sections.heading: What a teacher and an archive preserve
paragraphs: Learning involves more than finding a title. The university syllabus asks for notation, practical presentation and oral examination, and includes study of guru parampara. Its combination of tasks makes an important point: written knowledge and demonstrated musical understanding are related, but neither simply replaces the other.[1]

The Odissi Research Centre’s institutional handbook describes another effort to keep repertoire available. Established in July 1986, the centre worked on music as well as dance. Its publication account records cassette volumes of Kishore Chandrananda Champu, notation with accompanying recordings under the name Champu-Sarani, and work on Chhanda. These are records of institutional activity, not dates when the traditions themselves began.[7]

The handbook also describes listening and viewing with teachers in its archive. That setting matters. A recording can preserve a voice, but a teacher can direct attention to a detail that a newcomer has not yet learned to hear. A notation can help a learner return to a passage, while the recorded rendition supplies information that the page leaves open.[7]

Preservation also involves choices. The centre describes a wish to bring greater uniformity to Champu singing. A reader can recognise that institutional aim while still asking how different teachers and performers shape a song. A reference edition is valuable without being mistaken for every rendition that has existed.

Begin, then, with one work and one credited performance. Read enough of the poem to follow its speaker and situation. Listen once for the voice and again for the surrounding musicians. If an explanation is available, return after hearing it. The same line may now reveal a literary turn, a rhythmic meeting or a detail of expression that passed unnoticed before.

The literary worlds of Odissi music are sustained in this repeated encounter: poets provide words, musicians give them a particular sounded life, teachers make attentive learning possible, and listeners return. A song’s history remains connected to the people who help it be heard.

chapters.title: Odissi, Gotipua and Expressive Performance
chapters.subtitle: Learning to see movement, character and feeling
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A dance photograph holds one instant. Performance asks us to follow what comes before and after it: a transfer of weight, a turn towards another person, a pause that changes the meaning of a gesture. The memorable pose is one part of a larger act of communication.

Odissi and Gotipua invite this patient attention in different ways. Their histories meet through teachers and performers, yet each deserves to be encountered on its own terms. This chapter follows a named route of learning, looks beyond Gotipua’s acrobatic reputation, and considers how abhinaya makes a dramatic situation visible.

sections.heading: Histories carried by people
paragraphs: Srjan’s institutional account connects Odissi with Mahari temple dancers and Gotipua performers, and identifies Pankaj Charan Das, Debaprasad Das and Kelucharan Mohapatra among the major figures in its twentieth-century renewal. Such an account points towards several histories of practice. It should not be reduced to a single unchanged dance passing intact from temple sculpture to the modern stage.[1]

A more specific route appears in Srjan’s chronology of Kelucharan Mohapatra. It records Gotipua training under Balabhadra Sahu from 1929, entry into Mohansundar Dev Goswami’s ras leela troupe in 1932, and subsequent work in theatre. In 1947, it places Kelucharan and Laxmipriya together in a Dashavatara sequence directed by Pankaj Charan Das for Sadhava Jhia.[2]

This sequence brings teachers, a woman performer, theatrical productions and musical experience into the frame. It describes a career made through different working environments. The institution’s dates are attributed evidence; they are not a complete history of every Odissi lineage.

The same chronology records Kelucharan teaching at Kala Vikash Kendra from 1953. Learning moves from one setting into another, carrying remembered skills while creating new opportunities for students and audiences. The relationship between Gotipua and Odissi becomes more intelligible when we follow these people and institutions, rather than treating one form as merely an unfinished version of the other.[2]

sections.heading: Gotipua beyond the difficult balance
paragraphs: The NCPA’s announcement for a March 2025 programme describes Gotipua as performed by boys in female attire and identifies bandha, its acrobatic postures, as part of guru-led training. It names Guru Bijay Kumar Sahoo and Nakshyatra Gurukul Trust, while distinguishing the form’s technique, costume and presentation from Odissi. A programme is evidence of a proposed appearance and its framing, not a review of the event.[3]

The opening photograph offers another view: performers in Raghurajpur hold related positions before an audience seated close by. This particular image does not show an acrobatic formation. It makes room for attention to stance, arms, costume and the relationship between dancers. A tradition’s most spectacular moment need not become its only public image.

An audience can look at transitions as carefully as balances. How does a group arrive at a position? Where does attention move next? What can be heard as the dancers change direction? These are viewing questions, not instructions for attempting a posture. The training belongs with knowledgeable teachers and the people learning it.

Young performers also have lives beyond the performance. Respect for their learning includes respecting rehearsal time, supervision and agreed arrangements for photographs. A visitor’s request for another pose should not become the measure of a successful encounter.

The most useful comparison with Odissi is therefore attentive rather than competitive. Ask how a particular group learns, which songs accompany it and what the teacher calls each part. The answers can reveal connections while allowing local terminology and practice to remain distinct.

sections.heading: When waiting becomes an action
paragraphs: Abhinaya concerns dramatic communication. As introductory distinctions, bhava refers to represented states or feelings, while rasa concerns the aesthetic experience made available through their presentation. Chapter VI of the Natyashastra connects rasa with a combination of circumstances, expressions and accompanying states. This is more than matching one facial expression to one emotion.[5]

Chapter XXIV offers a concrete example: a heroine awaiting her beloved listens for a time signal, approaches the doorway and looks along his path. When he fails to appear, her response changes. Expectation becomes a sequence of actions directed towards someone absent. This is a historical theatrical description, not a prescribed sequence for every Odissi choreography.[6]

A doorway matters because someone might enter; a path matters because an arrival remains possible. The dramatic situation gives an action its weight. A performer can invite an audience to imagine such a space without furnishing a literal room.

sections.heading: A lyric, a pattern, an audience
paragraphs: Srjan’s repertoire account distinguishes Batu and Pallavi as pure-dance items from lyric-centred abhinaya. Pallavi elaborates a raga through music, rhythm and movement; abhinaya gives scope to a song’s situation through glance, gesture, bodily movement and facial expression. Its cited repertoire includes Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda and Odia poets such as Baladeva Rath, Gopal Krishna Pattnaik and Banamali Das.[4]

This distinction changes what a viewer might follow. A patterned passage can hold attention through its development without narrating a specific episode. When a lyric becomes central, questions of speaker and address become especially helpful. “Pure dance” does not mean an absence of feeling, and expressive dance does not set rhythm aside.

IGNCA’s Gita Govinda project reads Radha and Krishna’s union, separation and reunion on both human and divine levels. That interpretation leaves room to attend to the chosen passage, instead of deciding in advance that it must be either love poetry or devotion. A programme note and a credited translation can help locate the scene without exhausting its possibilities.[7]

The nayika, or heroine, is a dramatic figure within such interpretation. Her waiting is not a diagnosis of the dancer’s private feelings, and a photographed gesture cannot establish an entire character. What has happened in the poem, whom the speaker addresses and how the performance develops all matter.

Listen as well as watch. The singer’s phrase and the percussionist’s timing belong to the encounter, even when the dancer occupies the centre of attention. Keep poet, composer, musicians and choreographer in the credits when that information is available. A second viewing after reading the lyric may reveal a relationship that escaped notice the first time.

What we learn to see is not simply a larger vocabulary of poses. It is how a performer makes a situation unfold, how a group shares time, and how an audience’s attention can deepen. The photograph is a beginning; the work lives in the movement between moments.

chapters.subtitle: Movement and music across Odisha
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Four names take us into different worlds of performance. Mayurbhanj Chhau, Dalkhai, Ghumura and Dhemsa bring particular places, occasions and ways of moving into view. Seeing them together helps us recognise the range of Odisha’s dance cultures, provided we keep those differences in focus.

Chhau belongs to a wider eastern Indian tradition. UNESCO’s 2010 inscription identifies Seraikella, Purulia and Mayurbhanj styles; Seraikella and Purulia use masks, while Mayurbhanj does not. Its account connects Chhau with Chaitra Parva and describes a movement vocabulary drawing on martial practice, animal gaits and everyday work. Stories from the epics share this repertoire with folklore and abstract themes.[1]

In the photograph below, two unmasked dancers are airborne together. Their extended arms and folded legs make a striking arrangement, but the landing and the movement that follows also belong to the dance. A still image invites us to notice bodily coordination; it cannot tell us which episode is being performed.

sections.heading: Dalkhai and the gathering of voices
paragraphs: Sambalpur’s district account places Dalkhai at Dussehra, Bhaijuntia and other festive occasions. It describes young women from communities including Binjhal, Soura and Mirdha singing Dalkhai songs in a line or semicircle. The description gives us a starting point in an occasion and a social gathering, rather than a dance detached from its singers.[2]

The Odisha Reference Annual adds detail about accompaniment: dhol, nisan, tamki and wind instruments. In its account, the dhol player moves with the dancers while other musicians remain seated. This arrangement makes the drummer’s movement part of the performance, as well as providing a beat for it. It is a documented description, not a rule for every troupe.[3]

The Burla photograph records a stage presentation associated with Nuakhai Bhetghat. Performers hold decorated trays, while drums and musicians are visible behind them. The image’s title identifies the item with Bhaijiuntia and Dalkhai; the photograph alone does not establish a ritual sequence.

A listener can begin with the song. Follow how a phrase ends and how movement continues into the next phrase. Then watch the spacing between performers. The pleasure of a group dance can lie in these shared adjustments as much as in a single dancer’s skill. Different presentations deserve their own descriptions and credits.

sections.heading: Ghumura and the moving drum
paragraphs: Ghumura has a strong association with Kalahandi. The district’s cultural inventory records troupes performing at Nuakhai, Dussehra and other festivals. Its indicative troupe size of eighteen to twenty artists describes an ensemble practice; it should not be read as a compulsory number for every performance.[4]

The Odisha Reference Annual names Ghumura, Nishan, Taal, Turi and Madal among its instruments. It also remarks on the forceful sound and the impression of a war dance. This is useful evidence for how Ghumura has been described, but it does not by itself establish an ancient battlefield origin.[3]

The government photograph shows a group at an Odisha tribal sports meet. Rounded drums hang in front of several performers; some crouch close to the ground while others raise their arms. Here the instrument remains visibly attached to the moving body. A performance can make the relationship between playing, carrying and balancing an instrument part of what an audience sees.

That relationship offers a useful way to watch Ghumura. Notice where the hands return, how the body changes level, and how one formation gives way to another. A photograph cannot supply the missing rhythm. Recordings and live performances let us hear the ensemble that the image can only suggest.

sections.heading: Dhemsa and the linked line
paragraphs: Koraput Odyssey, published by the District Council of Culture in 2016, describes Dhemsa through dancers joining at waists or shoulders and forming winding chains. It names Paraja, Gadaba, Bhumia, Bhotra and Kondh communities among its practitioners, and associates the dance with festivals as well as recreation. This account locates Dhemsa in relationships between people, music and occasions.[5]

A linked formation makes each person’s timing matter to the next. To look along such a line is to follow small transfers of weight and direction. Apparent repetition can hold considerable variation: a change in pace, the depth of a bend or the way a curve travels through the group. These are ways of attending to a performance, rather than a claim that every community dances identically.

The photograph shows an Odisha contingent presenting Dhemsa at a national tribal festival in 2022. Stage lights and the frontal arrangement make the setting visible. It records one public presentation; it should not stand in for every village gathering or identify unnamed dancers with a particular community.

The Tribal Atlas of Odisha notes that many dances are shared across communities and that patterns can vary within a community from place to place. That observation is especially valuable when reading broad labels. A dance name opens an inquiry into local practice; it does not finish it.[6]

sections.heading: Watching without losing the place
paragraphs: Placed beside one another, these performances invite several kinds of attention. In Mayurbhanj Chhau, the unmasked body can shape a character or an imagined action. Dalkhai directs us towards the relationship between song, musicians and a group. The Ghumura image brings the carried instrument into view. Dhemsa asks us to follow connections along a line. These are useful entry points, not exhaustive definitions.

A district name is also an entry point. Balangir’s cultural inventory includes both Dalkhai and Ghumura among many forms of dance and music. The listing reminds us that the associations used in a short chapter do not draw exclusive boundaries around performance. Artists, songs and occasions need more precise descriptions than a single label can supply.[7]

A festival stage offers a particular encounter with this knowledge. Its duration, lighting and arrangement of audience and performers shape what can be seen. A village occasion may involve relationships and purposes that remain outside the frame of a programme photograph. Neither image nor programme should be asked to document what it does not show.

For a fuller record, begin with the troupe’s own name for the item. Keep the place, date and occasion alongside it, and credit dancers, singers, instrumentalists and teachers where those details are available. Ask which language is being sung and what the chosen song means. Such details make comparison more illuminating and give future readers a route back to the people who performed.

The four photographs here leave room for that further listening. Each catches an arrangement of bodies at one moment. The dancers’ knowledge continues through the next step, the next musical phrase and the practice that makes another performance possible.

chapters.title: Pala, Daskathia and the Singing Story
chapters.subtitle: Poetry in conversation with its listeners
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A story told aloud has more than one route to its listeners. A singer can pause over a verse, explain an unfamiliar word, change character or invite an answering voice. Pala and Daskathia make these exchanges central to the experience of literature. Each joins narrative with music, but their arrangements of performers and rhythm differ.

The Nalconagar photograph brings the gathering into view. Performers stand near seated listeners beneath a decorated canopy. A drum and a fly-whisk are visible within the small performance space. The image cannot supply the song, but it shows something a printed poem does not: the people among whom its meaning is being made.

sections.heading: The voice and the answer
paragraphs: Kalahandi’s cultural inventory describes Pala through the Gayak, Bayak and Palias, with mrudanga, gini and chamar among its instruments and objects. The Gayak leads the narrative; accompaniment and answering voices make it an ensemble undertaking. The district account places this practice around Bhawanipatna, Dharamgarh and M. Rampur. Its six-person description is a local example, not a fixed cast for every performance.[1]

Umesh Patra distinguishes seated Baithaki Pala, standing Thia Pala and competitive Badi Pala. The last brings teams into a contest of wit. These names point to different expectations: a seated recitation and a dramatic exchange before an audience do not ask their performers to do quite the same work.[2]

Patra’s Harischandra example shows how little scenery a story may need. A chamara, or fly-whisk, becomes the king’s crown when it is handed over. Elsewhere the object can suggest a bow or trident. A familiar object acquires a temporary meaning through action; listeners follow the change without requiring a new prop. This example belongs to Patra’s account, rather than to the photographs reproduced here.[2]

The answering performer can also change what a verse seems to mean. Sitakant Mahapatra describes the Palia offering a pun or a deliberately contrary reading after the Gayaka’s explanation. Such a reply opens a space for satire. In his account, pompous learning, corrupt officials and selfish rulers can all become subjects of laughter.[3]

Mahapatra gives a pointed example involving Gopabandhu Das’s poetry. An ideal of bodily sacrifice for the country is turned into a parody of leaders sacrificing other people to their own interests. The force comes from recognition: an audience that knows the earlier poem can hear what has been altered. We can describe the device without treating the parody as Gopabandhu’s own words.[3]

Learning to listen to Pala therefore includes noticing changes in register. The story may remain the same while an explanation, a joke or a gesture moves it into another relationship with the audience. An interruption can be where the argument becomes clearest.

sections.heading: Two performers and wooden rhythm
paragraphs: In his 2012 account of Daskathia, Basista Kumar Behera describes two performers: a Gayak or Gahana, who leads, and a Palia, who repeats the concluding stanza and contributes questions, proverbs and humour. Wooden sticks played with the hands provide a distinctive rhythmic element. The reply gives the principal singer a pause and offers the audience another way into the telling.[4]

Kalahandi’s inventory likewise records a pair performing historical and Puranic narratives at Bhawanipatna. Read beside its neighbouring Pala entry, this gives a useful practical distinction between the two forms. Shared stories do not make their distribution of voices and accompaniment identical.[1]

The Puri photograph shows two performers with hand-held pieces of wood, standing at microphones during the 2022 Ratha Jatra programme. Their names are not supplied by the image record. The microphones belong to this documented setting; they do not establish what an earlier performance would have sounded like.

Behera connects Daskathia with Ganjam and recounts a devotional explanation involving Hanuman’s service to Rama. Such an account belongs to the meanings attached to the practice. His proposed origin chronology requires separate historical evidence and is not used here as a founding date.[4]

sections.heading: Artists who read and interpret
paragraphs: The Sangeet Natak Akademi’s 2009 award citation for Jagannath Behera describes a reader of literary classics in Odia, Bengali, Hindi, Sanskrit and English, despite formal schooling only to middle-school level. It names Harekrushna Nath, Bhagaban Singh and Harekrushna Swain among his teachers. Here performance knowledge includes reading across languages as well as learning from other artists.[5]

A written citation preserves one career; a programme record shows that knowledge put into use. Narthaki’s report of the July 2012 Pala and Daskathia Utsav at Rabindra Mandap names Santilata Sahu presenting Hanuman’s meditation in Dwapara Yuga, and Manorama Panda presenting Naga Jyoti. Their presence makes women’s contributions part of the chapter’s account of Pala, rather than an unnamed exception to it.[6]

The same report identifies the Daskathia pair Sudarshan Padhi and Bhabani Shankar Dash presenting Nilendri Harana from Sarala Das’s Mahabharata. A title, text and pair of names give a reader something more useful than a general claim about epic storytelling: a particular performance to investigate.[6]

These are historical credits. They do not establish current appearances or teaching arrangements. Nor do they identify the artists in the Bhadrak photograph below, whose image record names the photographer and occasion but not the performers.

sections.heading: A story in public life
paragraphs: Literary and devotional narration are not the only settings in which these skills have been used. Odisha’s Information and Public Relations Department, in its 2021–22 activities report, lists Daskathia and Palla among forms employed to communicate government plans and policies. The passage documents an administrative use of performance. It does not measure what audiences understood or how every artist chose a repertoire.[7]

This change of purpose raises an interesting listening question. When a performance carries an assigned message, what room remains for a question, a joke or a local example? A programme’s stated objective cannot answer that by itself. We would need to hear the performers and ask how they prepared the presentation.

The same care helps when watching a recorded epic episode. Keep track of who is speaking: the narrator, a character, or a performer commenting on the story. Note when an old verse is quoted and when an explanation begins. A translation should make these distinctions visible, so that a poet is not credited with a later joke and an artist’s interpretation is not mistaken for the source text.

An archive of Pala or Daskathia becomes more useful when it keeps the surrounding information. The item’s name, the occasion and the source work matter alongside the lead singer’s name. Accompanying artists need credits too. A clear recording of an answering voice may explain an exchange that a camera fixed on the principal performer leaves incomplete.

For the listener, the task is less elaborate. Allow time for the explanation and the response. A familiar story may disclose an unfamiliar comparison; a small shift of wording may carry a sharp social judgement. Pala and Daskathia reward attention to that work of interpretation, where poetry meets the knowledge and expectations of the people hearing it.

chapters.title: The Stage, the Street and the Festival
chapters.subtitle: Prahallad Nataka, Danda Nata, Sahi Jatra, Dhanu Jatra and touring theatre
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A king commands a child from a raised platform. A costumed figure advances through a Puri street. In Bargarh, a river and a neighbouring settlement acquire names from Krishna’s story. These theatres ask us to notice where a performance happens, and how people gather around it.[1][5][6]

Prahallad Nataka, Danda Nata, Sahi Jatra, Dhanu Jatra and touring theatre bring different obligations to their audiences. A devotional vow, a neighbourhood procession and an evening’s entertainment cannot be understood through costume alone. Each needs its own account of place, preparation and participation.

sections.heading: Prahallad Nataka: the king and the child
paragraphs: In Ganjam’s Prahallad Nataka, also called Raja Nata, Hiranyakashipu demands the submission of his son Prahallad. The boy’s devotion to Vishnu brings the confrontation to its resolution through Narasimha. The familiar story becomes musical theatre: songs and spoken passages carry an argument about authority and faith.[1][2]

The gahaka, or lead vocalist, guides the chorus and comments on the action. A raised throne helps make the king’s position visible. Listen to how a declaration acquires weight through the accompanying voices; watch how an entrance establishes a character before the confrontation begins. The theatre’s nineteenth-century courtly history is important, but the sources differ over precise dating and authorship.[1]

Prateek Pattanaik’s documentation names Sri Lakshmi Nrusingha Natya Sansada of Burupada, with A. Rajendra Patro as Raja, Kalia Gouda on mukhabina and Tukuna Swain on mardala. Such credits let us recognise a particular ensemble and its work, beyond the name of a form.[2]

sections.heading: Danda Nata: devotion and dramatic play
paragraphs: The Ganjam District Gazetteer describes Danda observances in Chaitra, with groups travelling between villages and a closing Meru Yatra at Maha Vishuba Sankranti. Devotion to Shiva and Kali frames the occasion. Dhuli, Pani and Agni Danda belong to its ritual vocabulary; the gazetteer also names dhol, mahuri, jhanja and ghanta among the instruments.[3]

Aswini Kumar Mishra distinguishes daytime ritual from the Suanga and Leela of the night. His examples include Shiva and Parvati and the bird-catcher pair, Chadheiya and Chadheyani. Mythological figures enter a world of farming, conversation and dramatic humour.[4]

This shift matters to a reading of the whole event. A demanding observance and a comic exchange may belong to different moments of the same gathering. Isolating one spectacular scene can obscure the changes of mood that make the occasion intelligible. The local sequence deserves attention alongside the individual act.

sections.heading: Sahi Jatra: the neighbourhood performs
paragraphs: In Puri, Sahi Jatra brings performance into the streets around Ramnavami in Chaitra. The IGNCA and Sangeet Natak Akademi’s Akhyan programme describes a procession whose crossings become arenas for dancers, acrobats and costumed figures. It names Rama, Ravana, Parasurama, Hanuman, Sugrib and Angad among the characters.[5]

The photograph below preserves one such local association: its source identifies Parasurama with Harachandi Sahi. A character known across the Ramayana world also belongs to a particular neighbourhood’s presentation. Keeping that place-name in the caption makes the image more informative than a general label such as “festival performer.”

Follow the space around the figure as well as the figure itself. A procession’s approach, a pause at a crossing and the gathering of spectators are parts of the theatrical encounter. The street changes its use as the performance moves through it.

sections.heading: Dhanu Jatra: a landscape becomes a story
paragraphs: Bargarh’s Dhanu Jatra extends the acting space across a town, a river and a neighbouring settlement. Bargarh becomes Mathura, Ambapali becomes Gopapura, and the Jeera represents the Yamuna. Over eleven days, Krishna’s story and the rule and defeat of Kansa unfold across this shared geography.[6]

The district’s account places the festival’s beginning in the harvest season of 1947–48, linking its celebration to the mood of Independence. The story is older than this particular public form. That distinction allows the festival to have a modern civic history as well as a sacred narrative.[6]

The gateway pictured below makes the transformation tangible. An ordinary route is given a theatrical threshold. Read alongside the festival’s geography, it invites us to think about spectatorship as movement: following a story may also mean travelling between the places that represent it. No single stage photograph can contain that experience.

sections.heading: Touring theatre and the work of a company
paragraphs: The word jatra also belongs to Odisha’s popular theatre companies, often called gananatya. This use needs to be distinguished from a festival name such as Dhanu Jatra. Impart’s account traces modern Odia jatra through late nineteenth-century Balasore, exchanges with Bengali theatre, and the musical resources of Suanga and Leela. It describes Baishnab Pani’s Gitabhinay as an important combination of music, verse, humour and familiar speech.[7]

Its history is also a history of support. Early companies could be attached to a local patron; the decline of zamindari patronage changed that arrangement. The same account discusses women’s entry into performance in the mid-twentieth century and the later influence of cinema. Touring theatre should therefore be approached as a changing profession, with artistic choices shaped by changing audiences and institutions.[7]

A useful record of a touring production would follow the company as well as the play. Who writes and revises the dialogue? Who rehearses the music, assembles the acting space and moves the equipment? How does a scene reach spectators on different sides? These questions give the supporting work a place beside the leading actor’s performance.

An older theatre essay preserved by Heritage Odisha argues that an arena and its entrance passages are active parts of performance. It describes actors addressing spectators around them and ceremonial approaches to the playing area. The argument remains a useful way to examine staging: ask what a production needs its space to do.[8]

Across the five traditions, the stage can be a platform, an arena, a crossing or a network of places. Their differences deserve to remain visible. So do the people who teach, sing, organise and perform. A cultural archive becomes more useful when it keeps the company, locality, occasion and version with the story, allowing the next reader to find a particular artistic world again.

chapters.title: Pattachitra and the Painted Story
chapters.subtitle: Cloth, colour, devotion and the learning of a line
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A fine brush touches a surface already crowded with figures and patterned borders. The photograph below records an artist at work in Raghurajpur in 2013. It offers a useful beginning for Pattachitra: a picture takes shape through many decisions, each made at the scale of a line.

The name joins patta, cloth, with chitra, picture. In Odisha, the tradition is closely associated with Jagannath and Puri, while its subjects extend through the stories of Krishna, Rama and other sacred figures.[1] To look closely is to follow both the painted story and the work that makes it visible.

sections.heading: Before the story, a surface
paragraphs: A cloth painting begins before the first figure appears. The Government of Odisha’s process account describes a coating of chalk and tamarind-seed glue that prepares the cloth to receive paint. Borders are completed first; a brush sketch follows, then areas of flat colour and fine black lines. The account also describes a lacquer finish.[2]

This sequence makes preparation part of authorship. The support must receive a delicate stroke without losing its edge. A border must hold together across the whole picture. A small adjustment to an outline can change how an eye, a hand or a fold of clothing is read. The finished surface conceals much of this succession of tasks.

The same official account describes colours from vegetable, earth and mineral sources, including lampblack and shell white. It also records painting on wooden objects, tussar silk and coconut shells.[2] These descriptions establish a repertoire of materials and supports; they do not identify the ingredients of every painting in a shop or collection. The medium of an individual work should remain attached to its own maker’s account or catalogue record.

Looking at a reproduction, begin with the relationship between colour and contour. Where does a dark line separate two neighbouring forms? Where does a repeated ornament make a border seem continuous? These are questions that can be explored without first identifying every character. They give the eye a route into the painting.

A narrative reading can then ask something more precise. Is the composition centred on a deity, arranged in episodes, or built around a single encounter? A picture may invite several kinds of attention: recognition of a familiar subject, delight in a repeated pattern, and slow discovery of smaller scenes. The viewing order need not be settled by the first glance.

sections.heading: A temple carried in a picture
paragraphs: In this Puri painting, dated by LACMA to about 1875–1900, Jagannatha, Balabhadra and Subhadra occupy the central shrine. The museum identifies the conch beneath them with the land of Puri and notes the avatars of Vishnu arranged in a band beside the deities.[3]

The temple is presented through many small compartments. Look from the central figures to the surrounding shrines, then outward to the floral border. The composition makes room for repeated acts of discovery while preserving a clear centre of attention.

LACMA relates this kind of image to the nineteenth-century pilgrimage trade: visitors could take a painted reminder of Puri home with them.[3] A portable picture could therefore carry more than a view of a building. It could preserve a devotional relationship with a place, bringing the remembered shrine into another household.

sections.heading: The centre and the surrounding world
paragraphs: The larger historical painting below, now in the Wellcome Collection, also places the three deities at the centre. Its catalogue dates it to about 1880–1910 and identifies the medium as tempera on canvas. Human and sacred figures, animals and buildings fill the surrounding field.[4]

Compare it with the preceding picture. Both give the temple’s central tower a commanding position, but their smaller spaces are organised differently. Here, dense ranks of figures and buildings encourage the eye to move across the width of the cloth. The comparison reveals choices within a shared subject, rather than a single design mechanically repeated.

Pattachitra’s wider repertoire includes Krishna’s childhood, the encounter with Kaliya, the Dashavatara and episodes of the Ramayana.[1] A title can establish the subject without explaining every scene. For a particular work, a painter’s explanation or a detailed catalogue may help distinguish a sequence of events from figures brought together for another purpose. Recognition is a beginning; the arrangement is part of the story too.

sections.heading: Learning a line, sustaining a livelihood
paragraphs: Joanna Williams’s study describes learning within a family or a master’s household. Pupils began with practice tasks, later filling images drawn by the teacher or working on borders. A large painting could involve several hands. Sketchbooks and retained drawings helped preserve subjects that were not painted frequently.[5]

This is knowledge acquired through practice and correction. A description of family transmission should leave room for the time spent learning, and for the contributions of assistants and collaborators. The border is not merely spare work around a master’s image; it is also a place where control of line and repetition can be developed.

Mamata Tripathy’s 1998 study of Raghurajpur describes painting as household work, with women and men contributing to its preparation and production. She also records training programmes, exhibitions, changing markets and the participation of painters from outside the Chitrakara community.[6] Her account is a historical study, not a census of the village today. It helps show why a craft practice and a community identity should not be treated as identical.

The Puri district profile presents Raghurajpur as a place of several crafts: patta painting, palm-leaf engraving, carving, toys and masks, alongside its Gotipua associations.[7] A visit can therefore open onto several kinds of skilled work. The village name is a useful point of entry, but a fuller account should also identify the artist, teacher, workshop and particular object.

For a new commission, keep the maker’s name, title, date, dimensions and stated materials with the picture. Ask how the subject was chosen and whether others contributed. Such details make it possible to return to the work as a particular creation. They also prevent the story of Pattachitra from ending with an anonymous image: the painted world has makers, and their names belong with it.

chapters.title: Palm Leaf, Paper and the Work of the Hand
chapters.subtitle: Engraving, manuscripts and the shape of a story
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A palm-leaf book asks the reader to notice its construction. Narrow strips, pierced for a cord and protected by covers, hold writing and images in a sequence. The hand that opens the book meets work already done by other hands: preparing, cutting, inscribing and arranging.[1]

This chapter follows those material decisions into visual storytelling. It moves from an engraved leaf to a painted paper page, asking how a surface gives a story its shape. The materials connect literary and craft histories, while each surviving object preserves its own date, makers and history of use.

sections.heading: A line cut into a leaf
paragraphs: In Joanna Williams’s account of Odisha’s illustrated pothis, a lekhani, or stylus, makes a channel in the prepared palm leaf. A darkening substance rubbed into the surface makes the incised marks easier to see. Text was commonly laid out first, with spaces left for pictures and their captions.[1]

A cut line demands attention to a surface that can split. The mark has depth as well as direction. This makes the process different from laying a brushstroke over paper, even when both eventually appear as a dark outline in a reproduction. Material and movement are joined in the act of drawing.

The NID documentation published through D’source describes a living Talapatra Chitra practice in which prepared strips are joined in a folding arrangement. Drawing, engraving, rubbing colour into the incisions and wiping the surface form successive stages. Some examples include additional colour or carefully cut openings.[2]

These folding pictures and the stacked leaves of a book should be examined as distinct objects. Their arrangements permit different ways of opening and viewing. A reader may move through a manuscript leaf by leaf; an unfolding image can gradually reveal a larger composition. A photograph showing only the open front cannot explain all of these movements.

The Government of Odisha’s craft account describes both lettering and pictorial designs on palm leaf, and names epic incidents, deities, animals and plants among its subjects.[3] Such breadth is a reminder to begin with the object in front of us. A leaf bearing writing need not be an illustrated epic, and a recently made engraved picture need not be a manuscript.

For a first close look, follow one contour until it meets another. Notice where the maker leaves space around a figure, where an ornament becomes dense, and where the composition accommodates a hole or edge. Those choices are small, but they determine how much a narrow surface can hold.

sections.heading: A literary world along a narrow strip
paragraphs: The Cleveland Museum of Art identifies the leaf reproduced below with Upendra Bhanja’s romance of Chandrabhanu and Lavanyavati. It dates the object to the late eighteenth century. In the passage illustrated, the romance retells the battle of Rama and Ravana. A literary work can thus hold another familiar narrative within it.[4]

The museum’s description identifies the many-headed Ravana near the right of the battle scene and the army of monkeys and bears extending across the leaf. It explains the black lines as incisions made with a stylus and darkened with charcoal.[4] The technique and the crowded subject can be considered together: each small figure must remain legible within a tightly limited height.

The reproduction presents two views of the leaf. Follow the lower scene horizontally, noting how bows, bodies and raised limbs create a succession of directions. The open binding hole interrupts the field, but the composition continues around it. A practical feature of the book becomes something the image has to work with.

This is an illustration associated with Bhanja’s text, not evidence that the poet drew the image. The writer, the copyist and the illustrator are different roles, even when the surviving record cannot supply every name. Separating them gives artistic interpretation its place beside literary authorship.

sections.heading: Paper gives the scene another shape
paragraphs: In the Met’s Odisha painting dated 1840, Krishna and Balarama arrive at the Yamuna on their journey towards Mathura. The museum identifies the work as a page from a dispersed Bhagavata Purana, made with ink and opaque watercolour on paper.[5]

The picture occupies the upper part of the page, with writing beneath it. A diagonal river, coloured trees and the chariot organise a broad field above the text. Compared with the palm-leaf scene, this page gives the eye more room to move vertically as well as sideways. That is a comparison of these two objects, rather than a rule for every work in either material.

Paper also carried smaller pictures. The British Library catalogues five gouache paintings made by Puri chitrakars around 1960 and acquired near the temple. Their subjects include animals, a milkmaid and Krishna’s encounter with Bakasura.[6] Material alone does not determine whether an image belongs to a book, a devotional purchase or another use.

sections.heading: Keeping the work and its relationships together
paragraphs: A manuscript is more than a succession of attractive pictures. Its order connects words, episodes and pauses. Williams points out that disassembly can disturb that order; original page numbers, where present, can help recover it.[1] A beautiful isolated leaf may therefore preserve a scene while losing part of the reading experience that once surrounded it.

The museum labels used here make this problem visible through words such as “leaf” and “dispersed.” A photograph and an accession number let a reader locate an object, but they cannot by themselves reunite a book. Comparing text, dimensions, ornament and surviving sequence requires more evidence than a shared subject or visual resemblance.

The same care with identity matters for contemporary work. A Talapatra Chitra made for display, an illustrated manuscript copy and a paper painting can share stories while serving different purposes. Recording how an object opens, how its parts are joined and which side is shown helps preserve those differences.

An informative record should keep the maker’s name, the title or subject, the stated materials, the dimensions and the date together. Where a name or date is unknown, leave that uncertainty visible. The date of a poem does not automatically date a copy, and a photograph of a manuscript does not establish that it was written by the poet whose work it contains.

The work of the hand continues in the way these objects are described. A caption can preserve a copyist’s name or erase it; a photograph can retain the edges and binding holes or leave them outside the frame. Looking at the whole object gives future readers more to work with. The story belongs both to the marks on the surface and to the material arrangement that lets those marks be read.

chapters.title: Threads of Place
chapters.subtitle: Weaving traditions across Odisha
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Begin with the end of a sari. In the photograph, peacocks and floral shapes spread across a red pallu, the decorated end panel. Your eye can follow the figures before you know the name of the weave. Looking longer brings another question into view: how did these shapes become part of the fabric?

Across Odisha, that question leads in different directions. It can take us to yarn tied before dyeing, a border built with additional threads, lettering woven into devotional cloth, or the preparation of colour from roots. The place names associated with these textiles offer a useful beginning. Understanding their differences requires attention to the material and the work itself.

This chapter follows selected traditions from the western weaving centres towards Nuapatna and Maniabandha, south to Berhampur, and through Kalahandi and Koraput, before turning to tasar silk. It is a journey through documented practices, with each textile asking us to notice something different.

sections.heading: The pattern begins before the cloth
paragraphs: In bandha, colour is planned while the yarn is still separate. The National Institute of Design’s documentation of Sambalpur weaving describes selected lengths being tied so that they resist dye. Tying and dyeing may be repeated to establish different areas of colour; the prepared yarn is then woven. The image on the finished surface depends on decisions made earlier, when no complete cloth was yet there to see.[1]

Warp names the lengthwise yarns held on the loom; weft is the yarn carried across them. Those simple terms help us follow the work, but a textile’s regional name does not specify every choice of fibre or dye. The Sambalpur process recorded by NID uses cotton and synthetic dyes. Bandha should therefore not be taken as a blanket claim of natural dyeing.[1]

The state handloom department lists Bargarh for cotton tie-dye, silk and furnishing textiles. That range helps us understand Sambalpuri weaving as a production landscape rather than a single design. A sari may first attract us through colour or a familiar motif; tracing its making brings us to the preparation of yarn, the organisation of work and the skill of keeping a design aligned.[2]

sections.heading: Names beside the loom
paragraphs: A description of technique becomes more useful when it also records the person responsible for a particular work. The official Odisha weaver directory credits Swarnalata Meher with a Bapta sari combining silk warp and cotton weft. It credits Debaki Meher with a cotton Dasa Phulia example incorporating calligraphy and supplementary threads. These are individual documented works, not a definition of everything sold under a regional label.[3]

The distinction changes how we read a textile photograph. A caption may identify the tradition while leaving the maker unknown, as in the weaving photograph reproduced here. We can acknowledge the photographer accurately without filling that gap with a guessed name. In future documentation, the name of the person at the loom—and the names of others involved in the cloth—deserve as much care as its colour and pattern.

sections.heading: When words enter the weave
paragraphs: At Nuapatna, cloth also leads into literature. Sakshi Gambhir’s documentation for IDC, IIT Bombay connects calligraphic textiles bearing verses from the Gita Govinda with offerings to Jagannath at Puri. The handloom department lists Nuapatna for silk Khandua and calligraphy textiles. In this setting, writing can become something woven and offered, as well as something read.[2][4]

The accompanying photograph is identified by Prateek Pattanaik as a Gita Govinda Khandua. Rows of lettering occupy the red and yellow textile. Its particular passage has not been transcribed here: identifying a genre of cloth is different from establishing the exact words on an individual piece. Nor does the photograph establish its weaver or the ritual history of this specimen.

The Nuapatna process account describes planning for thread density, tying selected sections of weft, dyeing and weaving. Several people contribute to the sequence. Calligraphy on cloth is therefore both a literary presence and a demanding arrangement of yarn.[5]

Nearby Maniabandha belongs to the wider weaving landscape discussed alongside Nuapatna in Cuttack’s district export plan. Reading the two places together gives a sense of regional connection; it need not erase their distinct identities. A village name is most informative when it accompanies a specific maker, material and account of work.[6]

sections.heading: Three ways to read a border
paragraphs: Bandha does not explain every patterned surface. Bomkai offers a different construction to examine. The India Handloom Brand specification describes a three-shuttle border, additional warp threads in the border and additional weft in the body and pallu. These extra threads help form designs within the woven structure. The department lists silk Bomkai among the products of Sonepur and Boudh; such production associations should be kept distinct from the history of the name and its connection with Bomkai village in Ganjam.[2][7]

Berhampuri Patta brings another southern textile into view. The official directory describes its examples as silk in both warp and weft, with temple-shaped kumbha borders and an extra-weft end panel called Salari anchal. Ruchira Ghose’s Mapping Indian Textiles distinguishes the Berhampur sari from the joda worn by men. Looking at the end panel and border together helps us recognise different kinds of work within one cloth.[3][8]

In Kalahandi, Habaspuri invites a similar close reading with its own construction. Ghose describes additional warp threads forming temple motifs along the border, and additional weft designs in the pallav. Fish, flowers and kumbha are among the motifs she records. The official directory likewise describes a plain weave enriched by extra-warp and extra-weft designs.[3][8]

Placed beside one another, these descriptions offer a small vocabulary for seeing. A design may depend on colour prepared in yarn, on additional threads, or on a combination of decisions. Similar-looking motifs do not necessarily imply identical methods. The pleasure of comparison lies in learning to see the differences.

sections.heading: Kotpad and the work of colour
paragraphs: In Kotpad, Koraput district, the preparation of colour deserves a chapter of attention within the making of cloth. The Development Commissioner for Handlooms associates the tradition with the Mirgan community and describes aul-root dyes producing a palette that includes red, maroon, brown and black. Its account follows preparation, washing, drying and dyeing before weaving, and names both cotton and tussar among the materials used.[9]

Dastkari Haat Samiti’s 2017 documentation makes the designs more particular. With text by Jaya Jaitly, photographs by Chirodeep Chaudhuri and credit to artisan Gobardhan Panika and the community, it presents fish, crabs, vessels and other forms drawn from everyday surroundings. The named documentation is valuable because it brings an individual and a community into the account, alongside the finished textile.[10]

A motif is a starting point for interpretation, not permission to invent a meaning. Its name and significance should come from an identified source or from the maker’s own explanation. Similarly, the documented use of a root dye describes a process; it does not establish the fibre, dye or environmental performance of every piece offered as Kotpad cloth.

sections.heading: Before silk reaches the loom
paragraphs: Tasar, also commonly written tussar, directs attention further back in the making of a textile. Before yarn can be arranged on a loom, there is a cocoon. The basket photographed at the Odisha Crafts Museum in 2018 preserves a view of that material stage. It is a museum display, rather than a photograph of current production.

The Central Silk Board’s Keonjhar reference lists Arjun and Asan among tasar host plants, in forests and raised plantations. Its technical account distinguishes cocoon processing, reeling, spinning and preparation for weaving. Following the material therefore brings plants, silkworms and several kinds of work into a story that might otherwise begin only with a finished sari.[11][12]

The department’s weaving-centre list associates tasar textiles with Mayurbhanj, Gopalpur, Fakirpur and Mankidia. The cluster table places Rasulpur’s Gopalpur in Jajpur district. This is a different Gopalpur from the coastal town in Ganjam. Even a familiar place name needs its geographical context.[2][13]

A weaving centre does not by itself tell us where a particular cocoon was raised or where its yarn was processed. Keeping those stages separate makes the account more informative. It also leaves room for the people whose work precedes weaving to enter the textile’s recorded history.

sections.heading: Keeping the work with the cloth
paragraphs: These textiles belong together in an Odisha cultural edition because they reward comparison while resisting a single formula. Prepared colour, supplementary threads, woven lettering and the transformation of a cocoon reveal different paths towards a usable fabric. Their names locate traditions; close descriptions reveal choices within them.

For a family retaining a cherished sari, a museum recording a textile, or a reader choosing a new piece, a few details can preserve much of what a label leaves out: the maker or production group, the place of making, the fibre, the technique and the story attached to the piece. Record what is known, keep an uncertain attribution open, and ask how the cloth should be cared for.

The peacocks at the opening of this chapter will still be beautiful when we return to them. What changes is the attention we bring. We can now look beyond the finished pattern towards the decisions and people that gave it form.

chapters.title: Cloth in Everyday and Ceremonial Life
chapters.subtitle: Wearing, giving and the meanings of cloth
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Cloth changes as it moves. Spread flat, a sari displays its borders; gathered around a body, those borders turn, overlap and disappear into folds. In the opening photograph, women walk along the narrow banks of rice fields in Odisha. Their clothes differ in colour, pattern and arrangement. The scene invites us to begin with movement: walking, bending, carrying and working, rather than a garment displayed in isolation.[1]

Threads of Place followed the making of textiles. This chapter follows their use: the decisions of a wearer, the relationship expressed by a gift, and the passage of woven words into worship. These are connected histories, but their meanings belong to particular people and occasions. A textile can be beautiful to a distant viewer while carrying much more specific significance for the person who wears, makes or offers it.

sections.heading: Dress belongs to a person
paragraphs: The portrait below, identified by its source as a Koya woman in Odisha, brings cloth into conversation with adornment. White clothing frames layered necklaces; red bangles sit beside larger metal ornaments. The arrangement is the visible fact. Her name and her explanation of these objects are not supplied with the photograph, so their personal meanings remain outside our account.[2]

Looking closely at one person is a useful beginning for a cultural history of dress. A community name does not tell us everything about an individual wardrobe. Nor can a photograph establish the fibre, maker or price of a garment. What it can preserve is a particular combination: the way a fold meets a necklace, the fall of a sleeve, a gesture that changes the whole arrangement.

Adornment deserves attention in its own right. When clothing is detached from the person and labelled only by weaving technique, these relationships disappear. Here, the portrait asks us to keep the wearer in view.

sections.heading: Words worn in worship
paragraphs: At Nuapatna, the relationship between cloth and its recipient reaches into Jagannath worship. Manan Kapoor’s account for Sahapedia, drawing on weaver and textile historian Surendar Meher, describes Gita Govinda fabrics woven there for draping Jagannath. Verses from Jayadeva’s poem become part of the textile itself.[3]

The Impart encyclopedia identifies Gitagovinda khandua as silk ritual cloth with a stanza worked into the field through weft ikat. In this process, the yarn is patterned before weaving: the letters must emerge as threads are brought into alignment. Reading and making meet in a surface intended for devotional use.[4]

The photographed example lets us see that meeting. Light-coloured letters run across a red ground, surrounded by patterned bands. Its source identifies it as Gita Gobinda Khandua; it does not establish that this particular piece was used in the shrine. The distinction leaves its visual interest intact. A poem has acquired weight, texture and folds, and the act of offering cloth brings the work of a weaving community into a sacred relationship.

sections.heading: Embroidery as a relationship
paragraphs: Among the Dongria Kondh of the Niyamgiri hills, Kapdaganda brings making, wearing and giving together. Impart describes these embroidered cloths as gifts for important life events, including a bride’s gift to her husband, and gifts to parents, siblings and other close relatives. Men and women wear them on ceremonial occasions. The base fabric and the embroidery also connect different kinds of labour: the account associates the cloth with Domb weavers and the stitching with Dongria Kondh women.[5]

Kanak Rajadhyaksha’s field account for Sahapedia records women describing Kapdagonda as an expression of love. They make pieces for relatives, lovers and themselves. Her account also makes room for individual differences: not every woman embroiders, and those who do fit the work into available time. This matters in a history of dress. A celebrated community practice still consists of personal skills, choices and hours of work.[6]

Rajadhyaksha describes festival and wedding use, including women’s three-piece arrangements around the waist and neck. A textile sold elsewhere as a shawl therefore carries a history of wearing that the shop label alone cannot convey. She also records women’s explanations of particular motifs: the linga triangle refers to the mountain deity Niyam Raja, while kairi diagonals represent cultivated fields. These meanings are attributed to that account, rather than treated as a universal dictionary for geometric ornament.[6]

Giving adds another dimension to the finished surface. A border can be admired by anyone; the knowledge of who stitched it for whom belongs to a relationship. Keeping that history with the cloth allows the recipient, as well as the maker, to remain part of its story.

sections.heading: An occasion changes the cloth
paragraphs: The difference between everyday and ceremonial use can be worked into a textile’s design. Impart’s survey of Odisha ikat describes a historical distinction between shorter, simpler sari end panels for ordinary use and more elaborate patterned panels for special occasions. It also records changes in sari dimensions and end-panel arrangements over time. Dress has a history of adjustment, not a single permanent form.[4]

An occasion also changes what we notice. In a field, the arrangement of clothing can be read through movement and work. In a gift, we look for the relationship between giver and recipient. In the Gita Govinda textile, words and devotional purpose draw the eye. These examples do not yield one costume for Odisha. They show several ways in which cloth participates in life.

When a textile enters a family collection, a museum or a new market, a useful record begins with concrete questions. Who made it? Who wore it? Was it purchased, given or commissioned? What did its owner call it, and which occasion brought it out? Answers may differ even for pieces that look alike. Recording a remembered gift or a wearer’s preferred arrangement can be as valuable as naming the weave.

The photographs in this chapter leave us with three scales of attention: a line of people moving through a working landscape, one person’s arrangement of cloth and ornaments, and lettering woven across a ceremonial textile. Together with the accounts of Kapdaganda, they return us to the human life of fabric. Cloth is handled, adjusted, given and worn; those actions belong beside its pattern in the cultural record.
