chapters.title: Silver, Metal, Clay, Stone and Appliqué
chapters.subtitle: Materials, tools and the people who give them form
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: The open spaces in Cuttack filigree are part of its design. Silver wire encloses small curls and loops, allowing light to pass through an object that is still strong enough to hold its form. Looking closely changes the question from what the object represents to how its parts were made and joined.

This chapter follows that question through silver, cast and hammered metal, clay, stone and the stitched surfaces of Pipili. Each material asks something different of the maker: control of a fine wire, a mould prepared for molten metal, a hollow body shaped in clay, a measured cut or a carefully placed seam. Their finished forms belong to homes, personal adornment, worship and public display.

In the NID documentation of tarakasi, thicker wire provides a frame and finer wire fills it. Tweezers help roll, fold and twist the infill; soldering joins the parts, followed by filing and polishing. The account names Ramesh Behera as a senior Cuttack craftsman. Jewellery, ritual objects and decorative pieces share this patient construction from small components.[1]

sections.heading: Metal takes more than one path
paragraphs: Dhokra casting begins before there is a metal object to see. The Dhenkanal process recorded by NID starts with a clay core. Wax threads cover it to establish the design, and further clay layers enclose the wax. Openings provide a route for the metal and a way for air to escape. Heating removes the wax; molten metal occupies the space it has left. Once the casting has cooled, the mould is removed and the surface cleaned and finished.[2]

A raised line on the finished object therefore preserves a decision first made in a softer material. The pattern has passed through wax and clay before becoming metal. The documentation identifies Sansari Gadatia as its senior craftsman contact in Dhenkanal, giving this description of technique a named practitioner.[3]

Brass and bell-metal vessels involve another organisation of work. Impart’s account of Kansari ware describes a collaborative sequence: several artisans hammer an ingot while another turns it, with repeated heating keeping the metal workable. The coordinated blows spread the material and help maintain an even thickness. A vessel takes shape through timing and shared attention as well as individual skill.[4]

These processes deserve separate names. A cast figure, a hammered vessel and a filigree ornament may all appear in a display of metal craft, but their surfaces record different operations. Following those operations restores some of the workshop to the finished object. The preparation of a mould, the drawing of wire and the turning of heated metal are all labour, even when a polished surface makes that labour difficult to see.

sections.heading: Clay learns a shape
paragraphs: A small fish toy offers a precise lesson in clay work. NID’s documentation describes a hollow body formed on the potter’s wheel and cut free with wire. After partial drying, fins, tail, eyes and mouth are added. A wooden modelling tool helps with details; a pen cap makes impressions for the gills. Familiar tools become instruments for giving the animal character.[5]

The same documentation introduces Jayadev Rana of Barpali, Bargarh, as a maker of terracotta jewellery and crafts. Its title uses Sambalpur; the biography gives the more specific locality. Naming both preserves the record without losing the maker’s place.[6]

The museum photograph below shows another expressive use of clay: a figure with an open mouth, prominent eyes and repeated raised details. Its maker is not identified in the image record. It is reproduced as a separate example, not attributed to Rana or presented as the fish toy described above.

sections.heading: Working into stone
paragraphs: Carving requires a different kind of foresight. The NID account of stone work in Bhubaneswar begins with selecting and checking the material, including looking for cracks. Cutting establishes the broad form; hammer and chisel remove smaller pieces. Finer tools develop the details, and polishing finishes the surface. The character of the stone affects the treatment it can bear.[7]

The order matters. A face, hand or ornament must be anticipated while it is still surrounded by stone. As material comes away, the maker moves from mass towards detail. A small projection needs enough substance to survive the next cut. The finished figure can conceal the sequence of decisions that made it possible.

Sudarshan Sahoo’s work also draws attention to the institutions through which craft is shared. The Ministry of Tourism’s account credits him with establishing the Sudarshan Craft Museum in Puri in 1977. Its collection brings stone sculpture into company with other media, including wood carving, painting and filigree.[8] A named artist and a museum offer a different point of entry from an anonymous category such as “stone craft”.

The tools in these accounts also complicate a simple division between hand and machine. NID records a cutting machine alongside chiselling in stone work, just as its filigree account records wire-drawing equipment. Skill includes choosing how a tool will be used and judging what remains to be done. The presence of a machine does not tell us who conceived the form or controlled its finer details.[1][7]

sections.heading: Pipili joins colour to ceremony
paragraphs: In appliqué, a cut piece of cloth becomes part of a larger surface. NID’s Pipili account describes preparing a background, cutting motifs and joining them through stitching. For lampshades, templates help produce repeated shapes; cut pieces can be bundled for later use. The account includes machine stitching and wooden or iron rings that give the shade its form. Pattern depends on preparation as much as the visible seam.[9]

The Puri district administration connects Pipili’s cloth work with the decoration of Ratha Yatra chariots. It also lists umbrellas, bags, purses and wall hangings among the town’s products. Ceremonial use and domestic use sit within the same craft landscape, though each object has its own scale and purpose.[10]

The display photographed here makes repetition visible: circular centres, surrounding motifs and gathered borders return in different arrangements. A finished object rewards attention to these choices. Across the materials in this chapter, close looking leads back to makers, tools and sequences of work. Keeping those details in the record allows the skill to remain visible after the object has left the workshop.

chapters.title: Homes, Courtyards and Everyday Design
chapters.subtitle: Domestic spaces and the work of living
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A house meets the street before its door is opened. In the photograph from Nimeishapur, a raised frontage runs beneath a shallow roof; pillars mark a sheltered edge, and bicycles and a scooter stand alongside it. Painted walls, steps, openings and everyday belongings share the scene. Architecture is already in use.

This chapter looks at homes through those relationships: between rooms and open ground, household work and the objects it requires, a painted surface and an approaching festival. It follows selected examples from coastal villages, Mayurbhanj and Niyamgiri. These places offer different histories of building and habitation. Together they suggest that everyday design includes both the form of a house and the continuing work of making it livable.

sections.heading: Between the street and the courtyard
paragraphs: Adam Hardy’s 1999 study of Birabalabhadrapur, a Brahmin settlement near Puri, describes two facing rows of courtyard houses. Where the older pattern survived, raised front platforms connected neighbouring houses beneath the eaves. These edges provided places to sit and a route for visiting. Behind the front rooms lay courtyards, followed by further rooms and backyards.[1]

The courtyard was therefore part of a sequence. Moving inward meant passing through different levels of enclosure and between raised rooms and open ground. Hardy also records trees, cattle and domestic facilities in the rear areas. His description locates the house within the daily life of a particular settlement, rather than treating its plan as an isolated arrangement of walls.[1]

The social setting matters as much as the geometry. A study of a Brahmin settlement cannot stand for all coastal households, still less all Odisha. It offers a documented example of how a street, a shared edge and a private interior can meet. Its historical observations also leave open what residents may have altered since the study.

sections.heading: Objects make rooms useful
paragraphs: The previous chapter followed craft into the workshop. Inside a home, the same objects become part of recurring tasks. Impart’s account of Odisha’s Kansari metalware lists plates, bowls, water vessels, cups and ladles, alongside lamps and incense stands for ceremonial use. Household utility and worship can draw on the skills of the same metalworking community.[2]

A room plan alone cannot show how these things are reached, carried, cleaned or put away. To understand domestic design, we need to ask where a household keeps water, prepares food and stores its utensils, and who performs that work. These questions connect the scale of a vessel to the scale of a house. They also keep attention on the people whose repeated actions make an interior function.

sections.heading: Different homes in different places
paragraphs: Subhashish Panigrahi’s photograph identifies a Ho home in Keshpada, Mayurbhanj. A thatched building and an open-sided roofed structure stand around a broad outdoor space, with trees and woven branches marking the surroundings. The image records one household setting; the purposes of individual structures are not supplied by its caption.

Further south, Meenal Tatpati, Ashish Kothari and Rashi Mishra’s 2016 Niyamgiri study describes Dongria Kondh earthen houses arranged in parallel rows, with wooden posts and steeply sloping thatched roofs. The authors relate the low-reaching roof edges to local wind and rain.[3]

The photograph and the study concern different communities and locations. Placing them together makes variation visible without assigning every household a fixed type. Materials, available ground, building knowledge and subsequent alterations all deserve attention. A photograph can begin that enquiry, while residents’ explanations are needed to understand how a particular home works.

sections.heading: The floor becomes a ritual surface
paragraphs: The Odisha government’s account of jhoti and chita connects white rice-paste painting with household ritual. It describes women decorating walls and floors during Margasira worship of Lakshmi, when harvested grain is threshed and stored. Paddy motifs bring the crop into the painted design. The surface is prepared for an occasion, joining domestic work with devotion.[4]

The photograph from Sergarh in Baleswar shows jhoti during Manabasa Gurubara: white feet and a floral outline beside an offering of leaves and a marigold. A small area of the home carries a visible sign of observance. Its modest scale is part of its interest; cultural expression need not occupy a monumental wall.

Such work asks us to notice the person who prepares and paints a surface as well as the finished motif. Repeated household practices can be easy to overlook precisely because they are familiar. Recording the occasion, materials and maker would give a fuller history than preserving the pattern alone.

sections.heading: A home continues after it is built
paragraphs: The value of a roof is also judged during bad weather. In an account displayed by UNDP with an August 2022 date, Dongria Kondh farmer Mana Manjhi described fearing that wind and heavy rain would damage her thatched roof. Assistance for a pucca house brought relief: she felt more confident that she and her grandson would have shelter during a storm. This is a resident’s account published by a programme partner, rather than an independent assessment of the building.[5]

Repair also depends on money arriving at the right time. Reporting from Niyamgiri in June 2020, Abhijit Mohanty described income from forest produce being used for house repairs before the monsoon, alongside livestock and farm inputs. His report documented the disruption of those sales during lockdown. It connects the maintenance of a home with the seasonal economy beyond its walls.[6]

These accounts complicate the view of a house as a finished cultural object. Admiring a roofline tells us little about the cost of replacing its covering. Describing local materials does not establish whether a household can obtain them, pay for labour or make the changes it wants. The continuing life of a building belongs in its history.

Preserving knowledge of older layouts and techniques can sit alongside residents’ wishes for safer shelter, improved services or more usable space. A careful record would include both: the remembered arrangement and the reasons for an alteration. Homes carry cultural memory through things that remain, but also through decisions about what to repair, replace and make anew.

chapters.title: Rice, Millets and the Agricultural Year
chapters.subtitle: Seed knowledge seasonal work and the journey to a meal
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Before grain becomes a meal, it passes through decisions about land, water, seed and work. Odisha’s rice fields and millet plots hold knowledge of all four. This chapter follows that knowledge through the agricultural year, from choosing a crop to keeping seed for another season. The differences between places matter: a waterlogged lowland and a rainfed slope ask different things of a farmer.

Koraput offers a particularly rich window into this relationship. FAO describes an agricultural landscape in which rice, millets and pulses belong to a wider system of fields, forests and household livelihoods. Its heritage lies in the continuing work of farming communities, whose knowledge keeps crop diversity in cultivation.[1]

sections.heading: A year shaped by water
paragraphs: A farming calendar is also a map of opportunity. In their account of Koraput, Luna Panda and Sagarika Mishra identify the monsoon kharif season as the principal cropping period. Finger millet grows in rainfed uplands, sometimes alongside other millets, pulses and oilseeds.[2] The sequence of sowing, tending and harvesting therefore follows both rainfall and the crops chosen; it cannot be reduced to a single timetable for the whole state.

Water continues to determine possibilities after the main harvest. A study of farming and nutrition in Koraput, conducted within a wider project during 2013–2018, describes land commonly remaining fallow after kharif. Some households with irrigation grew vegetables in the following season and pulses before summer. The project also tested green gram and black gram after rice, and short-duration finger millet where irrigation permitted.[3]

These were interventions in particular villages, not a description of every farm in Odisha. They nevertheless reveal why an agricultural year has several possible endings. One field rests; another supports a second crop. A household’s options depend on access to water as well as seed, time and labour.

The National Rice Research Institute’s farmer guidance distinguishes drought-prone land, irrigated fields, shallow lowlands, deeper water and coastal salinity when discussing rice varieties.[4] These categories make an important cultural point: the familiar image of a green paddy field conceals very different environments and accumulated experience.

sections.heading: Seeds kept for a reason
paragraphs: A rice name can carry a history of use. MSSRF’s Koraput action plan describes Kalajeera as an aromatic lowland landrace associated with festive consumption. Its account follows farmers and researchers selecting material, improving seed supply and confronting the difficulty of marketing a larger harvest. Producing more grain did not automatically provide a dependable buyer.[5]

A 2026 study involving 150 custodian farmers in ten Odisha villages records choices grounded in cooking, taste, ritual and field performance. Farmers associated Bahal and Bojni with pakhala; Jagbandhu with rice cakes; and Kalajeera with aroma and special dishes. These are reported preferences from the study, rather than universal properties or guarantees attached to a name.[6]

This distinction matters when heritage rice enters a shop or restaurant. The name on a packet invites further questions: who grew it, where was the seed obtained, and what do growers and cooks value in it? A catalogue can preserve a spelling while losing the relationships that made the grain worth keeping.

MSSRF also documents the practical work of conservation: selecting seed, drying it and storing it in household containers. Women have substantial responsibilities in these processes. Seed exchange during visits and market journeys connects the next harvest to other households’ experience.[5] Keeping diversity alive is consequently a repeated activity, requiring people, space and attention every year.

sections.heading: Mandia and the millet field
paragraphs: Mandia, or finger millet, belongs at the centre of this story. Panda and Mishra describe its flour being made into everyday gruel in Koraput, alongside festive preparations. Their account also links declining millet consumption with changing tastes, rice supplied through the Public Distribution System and the time required for household processing.[2]

A crop may remain useful in the field while becoming difficult to bring to the table. Remembering millet as food therefore means asking how it is cleaned and milled, who does that work, and whether a family has the time and equipment to prepare it.

sections.heading: The work between harvest and meal
paragraphs: Pragati’s 2022 account describes women’s work in weeding and post-harvest processing, and the introduction of weeders, threshers and cleaners. Women’s groups received equipment and training; flour mills and food enterprises extended the effort beyond cultivation. The authors report reduced drudgery, while their account remains a programme report from its intervention areas.[2]

Equipment belongs in a cultural history of farming because it changes the experience of a working day. A useful question is not merely whether a machine exists, but who can reach it, operate it and afford its services. Celebrating inherited knowledge need not mean asking its holders to continue exhausting work unchanged.

The farming-and-nutrition study makes another connection: more kinds of production must become more kinds of food actually eaten. Its interventions combined crops with household gardens, animal foods where feasible, and nutrition awareness. The researchers examined consumption as well as production.[3] A harvest total alone cannot tell the whole story of a household’s meals.

Rice and millet need not compete for a single place in Odisha’s identity. FAO’s account of Koraput places them beside pulses and forest foods within the same livelihood system.[1] Each grain brings particular possibilities, but the people choosing, growing and preparing it give those possibilities meaning.

The next agricultural year begins before the last grain is eaten. Seed must remain available, fields must remain usable, and farmers must have reasons to continue. An edition devoted to cultural life should keep those conditions in view. The bowl on the table is the visible end of a much longer relationship.

chapters.title: The Everyday Odia Table
chapters.subtitle: Rice bowls vegetables and the choices that make a meal
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: An everyday meal is made through combinations: rice with something liquid, something green, something crisp or sharp. Odisha’s food traditions offer many ways to make those combinations. Pakhala, dalma, greens and fish are familiar points of entry, but no single arrangement represents every family or region.[1]

This chapter moves from the rice bowl to its accompaniments, paying attention to the choices that make a meal recognisable to the people eating it. A dish name helps us begin; the cook’s version tells us more.

sections.heading: Pakhala and the things beside it
paragraphs: Pakhala brings cooked rice and water together. Odisha Tourism’s general account emphasises rice fermented overnight and its association with summer. Pritisha Das’s personal account begins with cooled cooked rice placed in water and then turns to the accompaniments.[2][3] Together, these descriptions show why the word alone does not specify every detail of preparation. The treatment of the rice and the additions deserve to be named.

The liquid has its own place in the meal. Torani is the rice water; in Das’s account it includes a little curd and ginger. Her preferred plate brings together leafy greens, crushed badi, mashed potato, charred brinjal and tomato, with optional pickle. Onion, chilli and lemon supply further contrasts.[3] These are one writer’s choices, not a checklist every household must complete.

Badi also connects a stored ingredient to the meal being assembled. Chef Nisar Ahmed describes badi chura as crushed black-gram badi combined with green chilli, garlic and onion. In another accompaniment, saga badi nadia, greens are cooked with badi and grated coconut.[4] The same ingredient can therefore contribute to a dry side dish or become part of a vegetable preparation.

Think of the meal as a set of relationships. A soft mouthful of rice can be followed by a crisp bite; a mild vegetable can sit beside something sour or pungent. This way of reading the plate leaves room for a modest meal with two accompaniments as well as a larger spread. Its character need not depend on how many bowls are filled.

sections.heading: Dalma and the vegetable kitchen
paragraphs: Dalma brings lentils and vegetables into one preparation.[1] The photograph below records a particular version: its maker describes boiling the ingredients and then seasoning them with additions including cumin, curry leaves, onion and garlic-ginger paste.[5] That account belongs to this dish; it should not be turned into a rule for all dalma.

Greens deserve attention in their own right. Das describes saga bhaja as lightly spiced leafy greens, while Ahmed’s greens with badi and coconut offer another treatment.[3][4] To ask which greens were used, and how they were cooked, is already to move beyond the broad label “vegetable side”.

The photograph catches dalma in its cooking vessel, with a serving spoon resting across it. It is an apt view of everyday food: a preparation ready to be shared, rather than an arrangement designed to stand for an entire cuisine.

sections.heading: Fish and the taste of mustard
paragraphs: Fish introduces another range of preparations. In his 2021 account, Ahmed describes chuna macha besara as small freshwater fish cooked relatively dry with mustard paste. He places it beside pan-fried prawns and rohu cooked on a tawa among possible pakhala accompaniments.[4] These are documented restaurant preparations, useful examples without being a household survey.

The photograph below shows a different machha besara: fish and sliced potatoes in a gravy described by its photographer as containing mustard and dried mango.[6] The contrast matters. “Mustard fish” can name quite different textures, cuts and accompaniments. Recording those particulars preserves more of a cook’s practice than insisting on one definitive version.
Fish belongs within this range of choices, not as a requirement for an Odia meal. The vegetable preparations on the preceding pages already show several other ways to build flavour and contrast.

sections.heading: The meal changes with the day
paragraphs: Everyday eating also happens outside the home. In Cuttack, dahibara aloodum brings lentil fritters soaked in curd together with potato curry; Incredible India describes its presence at street stalls and small eateries.[7] It offers another combination of softness, sourness and spice. A cuisine’s daily life includes such purchased meals as well as what emerges from a family kitchen.

Regional variation is equally important. Odisha Tourism associates mudhi mansa, puffed rice with mutton, with Mayurbhanj.[1] Neither that association nor Cuttack’s familiar street dish turns a region into a fixed menu. They are useful invitations to notice place, and to ask what changes between homes, working days and occasions.

In a 2019 interview, chef Thomas Zacharias emphasised the regional differences he encountered in Odisha and the distinct flavours of individual preparations.[8] His observations suggest a helpful way to taste: attend to what a dish is doing, rather than judging the whole meal by the richness of its gravy or the number of spices it contains.

Access matters as much as reputation. A study of farming and nutrition in Koraput and Wardha found cereal-dominated diets at baseline and tested ways to improve dietary diversity through crops, gardens and other food resources.[9] Its findings concern particular study communities, but they caution against assuming that a celebrated food tradition guarantees varied meals for everyone.

The everyday table is consequently both a repertoire and a daily task. Someone chooses ingredients, prepares them and brings the meal together. Preserving this knowledge means recording the unassuming details: the greens available that morning, the preferred sourness of torani, the way badi is crushed, and the combinations people return to. Those details allow a cuisine to remain recognisable while its kitchens continue to change.

chapters.title: Pitha, Sweets and the Festival Kitchen
chapters.subtitle: Ingredients techniques and the foods people share
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A turmeric leaf opens to reveal a pale pitha. Elsewhere, a cake has browned slowly in its vessel, ready to be cut. Odisha’s festival kitchen works through such differences in texture, heat and time. Rice, pulses, coconut, jaggery and fresh chhena become foods whose preparation can be as memorable as their taste.[1][2]

This chapter follows the work behind those foods: grinding, filling, wrapping, steaming and baking. Festival associations give them a place in the year, while family versions and new adaptations keep the repertoire moving. The story belongs to the people who make the food as well as those who receive it.

sections.heading: A family of techniques
paragraphs: Pitha is a broad family of preparations, not one kind of cake. Lipi Das’s Traditional Rice Foods, published by ICAR’s Central Rice Research Institute in 2015, documents several ways to transform rice. In its enduri recipe, rice and black gram form a fermented batter, wrapped in turmeric leaves around a sweet filling and steamed. Its manda recipe instead makes a rice-flour dough, encloses a coconut filling and steams the shaped pieces.[1]

These two methods ask different things of the cook. Batter must spread without escaping its leaf; dough must close around a filling without splitting. The ingredient list records what goes in, but the sequence reveals the work. Soaking and grinding precede shaping, and preparing the filling is another task within the larger preparation.

Other pithas move to a hot pan or oil. Odisha Tourism describes chakuli as a thin pan-cooked preparation and gives a semolina, coconut and cardamom version of fried kakara.[2] A name can therefore identify a familiar food without settling every choice of flour, filling or thickness. The recipe belongs to a particular practice, not to an unchanging statewide formula.

Jagannath Dash’s survey of rice culture links enduri with Prathamastami and includes poda pitha among Raja foods. It also records pitha varieties across different cultural regions.[3] These associations connect the kitchen to the calendar discussed earlier in this edition. Here, the emphasis is on what an occasion asks someone to prepare: leaves to find, grain to grind, filling to cook, and portions to shape.

sections.heading: Palm fruit and the slow cooked cake
paragraphs: Poda pitha draws attention to sustained heat. Odisha Tourism describes a version in which fermented rice batter, covered with sal leaves, cooks slowly in an earthen pot.[2] The name also accommodates variation. The tala poda pitha photographed below brings palm fruit into the preparation; its photographer identifies it as a rainy-season food.[4]

Palm fruit can lead to another texture altogether. A 2016 Oriyarasoi recipe combines its extract with rice flour and a little semolina to make fried tala pitha. The writer separates the labour of extracting and straining the fruit from the shorter task of frying the batter.[5]

That distinction is easy to lose when food is described only by its final cooking time. A finished slice or fritter conceals the earlier work of turning an ingredient into something usable. The photograph invites a slower look: browned surfaces and a dense yellow interior record a preparation quite different from the leaf-steamed enduri.

sections.heading: Chhena and the sweet shop landscape
paragraphs: Chhena poda shifts the centre of attention from grain to fresh curd cheese. Odisha Tourism describes sweetened chhena baked with sal leaves in an earthen oven; its culinary trail associates the sweet with Nayagarh. The same trail connects chhena jhili with Nimapada and lists syrupy rasagola and layered khaja among Odisha’s sweets.[2][6]

These foods make a geography of taste. A place name can guide a journey or recall a purchase, but it should not erase differences between makers. The chhena poda shown here is a photographed presentation from Puri, with cut pieces and garnishes. Its appearance records one serving, not the only form in which the sweet is eaten.

Contemporary cooks add further versions. In 2021, Chef Michael published a chocolate chhenapoda recipe that mixes chocolate into the chhena before baking.[7] It is explicitly an adaptation. Naming the change allows a reader to recognise both the established sweet and the cook’s experiment, without presenting a modern flavour as an old festival requirement.

sections.heading: What travels between kitchens
paragraphs: Food can travel before it is fully made. The Oriyarasoi writer remembers a grandmother receiving extracted palm fruit from the family’s village in steel milk cans. The grandmother found the extraction physically difficult; someone elsewhere had already done that work. Years later, finding ripe palm fruit in a Bengaluru market brought the preparation back into reach.[5]

This is one family’s memory, but it opens a useful perspective on sharing. The thing passed on may be an ingredient, a prepared filling, a finished sweet or the knowledge needed to make it. A gift of food can carry labour as well as flavour. To describe it adequately, we should ask who prepared it, who sent it, and what the recipient knew to do next.

A festival kitchen also depends on practical choices. The ICAR collection’s enduri instructions allow either a steamer or a pot fitted with cloth over the water.[1] Different equipment can serve the same cooking purpose. Keeping a preparation alive need not mean reproducing every vessel or fuel arrangement exactly; it does mean understanding which steps give the food its character.

Printed recipes preserve part of that knowledge. Photographs preserve another part: the fold of a leaf, the surface of a cake, the way a sweet has been cut. Neither can replace the cook’s judgment completely. A useful family record would include the maker’s name, the occasion, the ingredients actually used and the signs by which the maker knows the food is ready.

The festival kitchen is renewed through repetition with attention. Each batch offers another chance to learn how a filling should feel, how a leaf should close, or how a browned edge should taste. Pitha and sweets remain cultural knowledge because people continue to make, share and recognise them, while leaving room for the next cook’s circumstances.

chapters.title: Sacred Food and Shared Meals
chapters.subtitle: Offerings labour and the meaning of sharing
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: An earthen pot of rice can be read in several ways: as food, as the work of cooks and potters, and as an offering returned to devotees. At Puri, Mahaprasad joins these meanings. Odisha Tourism describes it as food offered at the Jagannath temple and shared as an expression of devotion and community.[1]

The sacred meal has a life beyond its ingredients. This chapter follows the passage from preparation to offering and distribution, then turns to Ananta Basudeva in Bhubaneswar and to food observances during Kartika. The questions are practical as well as devotional: who makes the meal possible, how does it reach people, and what does sharing mean in a particular place?

sections.heading: From offering to shared food
paragraphs: Mahaprasad’s identity rests on its ritual relationship to the deity. D’source’s documentation of Puri temple pottery describes food offered first to Jagannath and then to Bimala, after which it is regarded as Mahaprasad.[2] A preparation with similar ingredients elsewhere is not made identical by its recipe alone. The offering is part of what the food means.

Rice, lentils, vegetables and milk-based preparations belong to the repertoire described by Odisha Tourism. Its account identifies earthen pots and wood-fired cooking, and locates the distribution of Mahaprasad at Ananda Bazar inside the temple premises.[1] For a devotee, receiving the food extends worship into the act of eating.

Ananda Bazar is also a place of sale. In a 2013 account of the temple economy, Abhimanyu Dash describes Suar cooks preparing food at their own cost, offering it and selling it to pilgrims. He notes that demand changes with festivals and family ceremonies.[3] Sacred significance and payment coexist here. Calling the meal shared should not imply that every portion is distributed without charge.

The ideal of eating across social distinctions is central to accounts of Mahaprasad.[1][2] It needs to be considered alongside access to the institution. Odisha Tourism’s visitor guidance states that the Jagannath temple restricts entry to non-Hindus.[4] The language of equality around food therefore does not mean unrestricted admission to every sacred space.

Keeping these distinctions visible allows a fuller account of hospitality. There is the food’s ritual status, the way it is obtained, the people with whom it is eaten, and the rules governing the place. Each belongs to the experience; none should be made to stand for all the others.

sections.heading: The people behind the pot
paragraphs: The meal begins before the kitchen fire is lit. D’source’s study, credited to Bibhudutta Baral, Divyadarshan C. S. and Aakash Sharma of NID Bengaluru, documents temple pottery at Puri. Clay is prepared, shaped and dried before firing; finished vessels are then supplied to the temple. The study also records the Kumbhar Pada potters’ association.[2]

A vessel’s plain appearance can conceal the judgment needed to make it. The potter works with clay consistency, shape and drying; the kitchen depends on the resulting object. Looking at sacred food through its containers brings a craft community into view, alongside the better-known religious institution.

Dash’s 2013 account names another chain of work. Bojhias carry Mahaprasad from offering areas to Ananda Bazar. Workers prepare vegetables and grind spices, while Suar cooks undertake the cooking. The account also describes food portions called khei received by servitors for service.[3] These details belong to that dated study, but they show why “the temple kitchen” is too broad a phrase to identify everyone’s contribution.

Devotional service is consequently also skilled labour and livelihood. A description that praises abundance without naming the work can leave its makers invisible. Equally, sales revenue alone cannot tell us what a household earns after its costs, or how regularly a worker receives an assignment.

To follow a pot to the meal is to follow several kinds of knowledge. It asks us to notice preparation, carrying and cleaning alongside cooking, and to recognise that the experience of receiving food depends on work distributed across many hands.

sections.heading: Another kitchen in Bhubaneswar
paragraphs: At Ananta Basudeva temple in Bhubaneswar, sacred food is also part of the institution’s public identity. Odisha Tourism describes its Abadha tradition and associates the Bhoga Mandapa with offerings.[5] The temple provides a second setting for thinking about food, worship and gathering, with its own history and routines.

The photograph below, taken in 2017, makes the material setting unusually visible. Earthen vessels stand in groups; firewood lies nearby; people carry, prepare and move between work areas. It is Ananta Basudeva’s kitchen, not a photograph of the kitchen at Puri.

The image brings the discussion back to effort. A sacred meal requires ingredients and fuel, but also room to work, vessels to handle and people who know the sequence. The food offered to a deity remains connected to this ordinary, demanding world of preparation.

sections.heading: Observance at the household scale
paragraphs: Sacred food also takes shape through choices about what to eat and what to set aside. The Visit Bhubaneswar account describes Habisha Dalma in connection with Kartika observance: unroasted moong, no turmeric, a restricted selection of vegetables such as elephant apple and raw banana, and pepper rather than chilli.[6] This is one documented description, not a recipe binding every household.

Benudhar Patra and Punit’s 2018 study discusses Kartika brata at Puri, particularly in relation to widows. It examines Puranic prescriptions concerning food and the observance of vows.[7] Such texts help explain religious ideals; they cannot, by themselves, tell us how every woman experiences the observance or what she eats today.

A household practice becomes more intelligible when its participant is allowed to describe it. Which restrictions does she follow? Who buys and prepares the ingredients? Does she cook for herself, join others or rely on someone’s care? These questions place agency and circumstances beside prescription, without assuming that one account represents all devotees.

The scale changes between a household pot and a temple kitchen, but both require repeated acts of provision. A meal must be planned, cooked and served; a vessel must be made or obtained. Attention to those tasks does not diminish devotion. It shows how devotion is sustained in material life.

Sacred food is therefore worth recording in more than a menu. Its story includes the offering, the maker, the carrier and the eater, as well as the conditions under which they meet. A shared meal can express belonging while also prompting questions about who can participate and whose work receives recognition.

chapters.title: Forest, Hill, River and Coast
chapters.subtitle: Gathering food and keeping it through the seasons
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A meal carries the work of places beyond the kitchen. Fruit must be recognised and gathered; a catch must reach shore; food intended for later must be dried or stored. Odisha’s forest and fishing landscapes become easier to understand when we follow those tasks and the people who perform them.

This chapter moves between local accounts: mahua use among Santhal residents near Similipal, forest-product collection in Kendujhar, fishing at river mouths and Chilika, and the work of preserving fish. Leaf cooking connects gathering with the household fire. These settings reveal different kinds of knowledge, each learned through particular materials, seasons and livelihoods.

sections.heading: Knowing the forest season
paragraphs: Jamu, kendu, bara and kantei koli appear among the fruits described by the Regional Plant Resource Centre in Bhubaneswar. Its account recalls collection for household use and exchange in village markets, and explains the purpose of its wild-fruit conservation garden. Keeping these plants in a collection preserves material for study; knowing when and how a fruit is used also requires the knowledge of people who gather it.[1]

A 2016 paper by Behera and colleagues describes mahua use among Santhal residents of Chandbill, Bangiriposi, based on 2009 fieldwork. Flowers were gathered from private and forest land in March and April, commonly by women and children early in the morning, then carried home for use or sale.[2]

Drying and storage influenced what happened next. The researchers describe households selling flowers to intermediaries because storage space and money were short.[2] Keeping a seasonal food for later was consequently a decision about household resources as well as technique.

Mishra and Pradhan’s 2018 Kendujhar study covered 120 households in six villages of Patana and Bansapal. It recorded both household consumption and sale of collected forest products, including edible and non-edible materials. Storage, collection time and pricing were among the reported difficulties.[3] Those findings locate forest foods within household work and exchange, without making every product a food or every collection a commercial harvest.

Names matter in this setting. A local fruit name, the part collected and the place of collection belong together. The broad category “forest food” is useful only if it leaves those distinctions visible.

sections.heading: Where rivers meet fishing waters
paragraphs: At Balaramgadi, the Budhabalanga reaches the Bay of Bengal. Jitu Mishra’s 2019 account describes fishing boats and trawlers at the harbour and catches unloaded for auction. River mouth, landing place and market occupy the same working landscape, although they involve different tasks and scales of fishing.[4]

Chilika offers another relationship between inland water and the coast. The Chilika Development Authority describes a lagoon whose productivity supports fish and shellfish, with freshwater inputs and seasonal changes in salinity among the conditions shaping its ecology.[5] The water is a habitat and a place of work; changes in one affect the possibilities of the other.

An IUCN account published on 11 November 2026 follows fishers in Kalupada who stay on the lagoon overnight to guard nets and catch. Children sometimes accompany their fathers and learn through participation.[6] A photograph of a boat can suggest travel, but this account adds the hours of waiting and attention that a landscape view cannot show.

sections.heading: Keeping fish and earning from it
paragraphs: Fishing work continues after a boat returns. IUCN’s November 2026 account introduces Subarna Sadhab of Pathara, who had spent nearly forty years selling fish. She travelled with other women to Balugaon and nearby markets. Her account of the physical strain of selling reminds us that the fish economy includes carrying and prolonged market work as well as catching.[6]

Drying creates another chain of tasks. In an October 2025 WorldFish report, Premalata Behera of Dalimbapur describes difficulties with open-air drying, including contamination by birds, insects and dust. She and other members of the Maa women’s self-help group received a solar tunnel dryer through a collaborative project. Training covered washing and drying, packaging, labelling and pricing.[7]

The report presents cleaner products and improved selling conditions as outcomes of that project.[7] It is a particular group’s experience, rather than a measure of every dried-fish business in Odisha. The practical lesson is that a preservation technique depends on more than sunshine: the drying space, protection of the product and the route to a buyer all matter.

Sukhua also belongs to the kitchen as a family of preparations. Tanuja Tripathy’s Kokali Sukhua Rai uses dried fish with mustard and garlic paste, onion, tomato and mustard oil.[8] This named contribution supplies a cook’s version, not a fixed recipe for every household. The vernacular fish name is retained here without assigning it a biological species.

The two accounts meet at the ingredient. The processor works to preserve fish that someone else will choose and cook. Recording the dish alongside that work gives a fuller sense of what reaches the table, while leaving room for households that prepare sukhua differently or do not eat it.

sections.heading: Leaves at the household fire
paragraphs: A leaf can form part of the cooking vessel. Away in the Kitchen’s 2024 account of patrapoda describes food enclosed in leaves, with the wrapping taking the direct heat while moisture is retained inside. The author’s home versions include fish and mushrooms prepared with an Odia-style spice paste. The ingredients change while the parcel remains the organising idea.[9]

Leaf choice and heating method need to be considered together. The same account discusses banana and other leaves, and distinguishes roasting or searing from steaming. Enduri pitha, enclosed in turmeric leaves and steamed, shows why wrapping alone cannot identify the technique. Its comparison with Bengali paturi also places Odisha’s practice beside a neighbouring culinary tradition without claiming a single origin.[9]

In Chandbill, the mahua study records flowers and rice ground into a paste, enclosed between sal leaves and fire-cooked. The authors call it cake.[2] A gathered flower, cultivated grain and leaf wrapper meet in this preparation; its recorded form belongs to that local account.

Such accounts make the leaf worth noticing before it is discarded. A food history concerned only with the finished dish would miss the wrapping material and the cook’s choice of heat. The parcel connects plant knowledge with the management of a fire, just as a drying place connects a catch with a later meal.

Across these places, continuity depends on opportunities to practise. A person needs access to the ingredients, time to do the work and someone from whom to learn. The forest collector, fish seller and cook each hold part of that knowledge. Their names and circumstances belong beside the food, so that a remembered taste does not become detached from the people who make it possible.

chapters.title: Markets, Makers and Cultural Livelihoods
chapters.subtitle: Making a living through skill and exchange
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A painted cloth, a woven sari or a bright appliqué hanging enters a market carrying hours of work. Its journey may begin in a household workshop and continue through a trader, a fair, a cooperative outlet or an online order. Each route connects making to buying in a different way.

Odisha’s cultural livelihoods become clearer when we follow these routes. This chapter moves from weekly markets and artisan villages to organised marketing and changing demand. It asks what a sale tells us, what it leaves out, and how the people who make an object can remain visible after it leaves their hands. A well-attended market and a secure livelihood are related achievements, but one does not automatically establish the other.

sections.heading: The weekly market and the artisan village
paragraphs: At Onukadelli, near Duduma, the weekly haat is identified by the Koraput district administration as a Thursday gathering attended by Bonda people and visited by tourists.[1] The meeting of trade and tourism deserves care: a market is a place where people conduct their own business, even when it also interests an outsider.

A visit can begin with what is being exchanged and how the market works. Who has brought something to sell? Who has come to buy? How far must a seller travel? These questions bring economic activity into view. Asking permission before making portraits and respecting a seller’s time allow curiosity to coexist with the ordinary work of the market.

Raghurajpur offers a different relationship between making and selling. Sucharita Sahoo’s 2014 feature for the Press Information Bureau describes a village producing paintings, palm-leaf work, carved objects and toys. It records sales through NGOs, participation in exhibitions and visits by domestic and overseas travellers.[2] The account shows several channels operating around the same place.

A workshop visit can let a buyer see an object before it is finished and hear about its making. An exhibition carries that work beyond the village. Both encounters may help a maker find customers, but they involve different demands on time, travel and presentation. The evidence of a sales channel is not yet evidence of what each household earns.

The weekly haat and the artisan village should therefore retain their different identities. One concentrates exchange on a recurring market day; the other brings visitors into a place of production. Neither can be understood fully from the visitor’s experience alone.

sections.heading: The organisations between maker and buyer
paragraphs: Utkalika’s institutional account dates the Odisha State Co-operative Handicraft Corporation to 1959 and identifies support for artisan marketing as a founding purpose. Its activities include exhibitions, raw-material support, training and product development. The organisation also describes its own online shop and partnerships with other e-commerce businesses.[3]

This is an intermediary role, but the word intermediary does not explain the terms of a transaction. A useful assessment asks what work an organisation undertakes: finding customers, displaying products, arranging transport or holding stock. It also asks when the maker is paid, who sets the price and who carries the risk if an item remains unsold.

Mission Shakti’s account of its partnership with ORMAS places women’s producer groups and self-help groups within a wider programme of market access. It names packaging, labelling, branding, buyer meetings, retail outlets and exhibitions, alongside working capital and training.[4] These activities recognise that the ability to make a product and the ability to sell it require different resources.

ORMAS also describes Pallishree Melas organised alongside events such as Rath Yatra at Puri and Balijatra at Cuttack.[5] A cultural gathering can thus become an occasion for commerce. The fair offers a meeting point, while the maker still needs to turn that encounter into a workable order, a payment or a continuing customer relationship.

Collective and institutional channels matter because they can distribute the work of reaching buyers. Their value to producers is best examined through the terms of participation and the results over time, rather than through the visibility of a stall or a brand alone.

sections.heading: What a selling price can tell us
paragraphs: The price attached to a finished sari is a price for the object at that point of sale. It is not, by itself, the weaver’s wage. To understand a livelihood, we need to know whether the maker owns the product or is paid for a particular task, what expenses they bear, and how much time the work takes.

Where a maker sells their own work, gross receipts still have to be considered alongside materials, hired labour, transport and other costs. Where someone works for a task payment, the relevant questions include the rate, the hours required and the regularity of orders. These are different arrangements and should not be combined into a single claim about artisan income.

The photograph below makes one stage of production visible. It records Sambalpuri sari weaving, but the source does not identify the weaver or his payment arrangement. His work deserves recognition without attaching an invented income to his image.

sections.heading: Changing demand and the future of making
paragraphs: Changes in marketing are also changes in what makers are asked to do. Utkalika’s account includes product development and online selling alongside exhibitions.[3] Reaching a distant customer raises practical questions about photographs, descriptions, packaging, delivery and returns. A wider audience creates possibilities, while the work of serving that audience still has to be organised and paid for.

Pipili provides a recent example of how these questions enter public policy. On 4 June 2026, the Chief Minister’s office announced the laying of the foundation stone for a Pipili Chandua Handicraft Hub. The announcement described a proposed raw-material bank and training in digital marketing and packaging, including support for women’s self-help groups.[6]

These are announced provisions, not demonstrated increases in earnings. Their eventual significance will depend on access, implementation and use. A raw-material service becomes meaningful through its availability and terms; marketing training becomes meaningful when a producer can apply it to orders that are worth fulfilling. The distinction keeps an account of cultural development grounded in the working lives it seeks to support.

Tourism likewise needs to be considered beyond visitor numbers. A useful question is whether an encounter leads to a sale on acceptable terms, repeat business or recognition of the maker. A visitor can contribute by asking who made an object, listening to the explanation of its work and recording the maker’s name when sharing it.

Cultural livelihoods continue through the ability to practise a skill and make a living from it. Markets, organisations and visitors all help shape that possibility. Following an object beyond admiration towards its terms of production and exchange gives its maker a fuller place in Odisha’s cultural story.

chapters.title: Growing Up in Odisha
chapters.subtitle: Play language reading and belonging
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A toy, a story and the language of a classroom each offer a way into childhood. They also raise questions about opportunity: who has space to play, books to choose from and a teacher who understands them? Growing up in Odisha cannot be described through a single remembered childhood.

This chapter follows play, reading and learning across a few documented settings. It brings children’s magazines and community libraries alongside home languages, oral storytelling and disability access. The common thread is participation. Children encounter cultural knowledge through other people, but they also question it, retell it and make things of their own. Their place in Odisha’s cultural life begins in the present, rather than waiting for adulthood.

sections.heading: Play and the language of learning
paragraphs: Odisha’s 2025 school curriculum framework names games including Puchi, Luchakali, Bagha Chheli and Pili Kathi among resources for foundational learning. It also proposes using clay dolls, palm-leaf toys and wooden figures in classroom activities.[1] This is a statement of educational intent, not a survey showing that every child plays the same games.

The names matter because they give local play a place in formal learning. A game learned from another child can enter a classroom; an everyday object can become something to investigate. The framework’s examples invite teachers to begin with familiar materials and experiences, while leaving room for differences between localities.

Familiarity also depends on language. In a February 2026 UNICEF account, Gowri Sundararajan describes Savitri Pingwa’s experience at Kumbhitangari in Keonjhar. Ho was the language of her home, while classroom Odia was difficult to understand. The report describes her growing participation when learning materials and teaching incorporated her home language.[2]

The same account describes bilingual materials, teacher training and contributions from community members. Savitri’s mother, Aarti, reports that her daughter shares what she has learned at home.[2] Learning moves between generations in both directions: the child receives knowledge and brings new knowledge back.

This is one reported experience, rather than a measure of every multilingual classroom. Its cultural significance is nevertheless clear. A child’s existing words and experiences can become resources for learning. Growing confident in a classroom need not require treating the language of home as something to leave behind.

sections.heading: Pages to read and stories to make
paragraphs: The history of children’s reading includes magazines as well as schoolbooks. Odia Bibhaba’s account dates the first Odia Jahnamamu to January 1956. It describes stories, mythological narratives, information and illustrations as part of the magazine’s appeal, and records a return to publication in July 1972 after an interruption.[3]

The archive also acknowledges gaps and inconsistencies in its collection. A surviving issue can show what a publisher offered children, but cannot tell us how widely it was available or how every reader responded. The publication belongs to a history of childhood without becoming a memory shared by all families.

Bakul Foundation offers a different route into reading. Its own account describes the children’s library at Satyanagar in Bhubaneswar growing from donated books and individual contributions. It presents reading alongside storytelling, workshops and meetings with writers.[4] A library can give a child the chance to choose a book beyond the one assigned for a lesson.

Bakul also reports developing Odia picture books through workshops with children and writers. It records three published manuscripts developed in Ganjam villages, with authorship credited to children.[4] That detail changes the child’s role: the reader can also become a maker whose name belongs on a book.

Access to reading therefore includes both the presence of books and the freedom to use them. An inviting picture, a familiar language and time to browse can make different kinds of entry possible. Reading aloud, looking together and composing a story are related activities, with room for children whose interests and ways of communicating differ.

sections.heading: A voice carried between generations
paragraphs: A story can be encountered before a child can read it independently. Voice, expression and timing help a telling hold its listener’s attention. The person telling it matters alongside the words: a recorded performance preserves something that a plot summary leaves out.

The image below comes from Subhashish Panigrahi’s 2014 recording of Musamoni Panigrahi telling a story in Baleswari Odia.[5] It documents an identified teller and speech variety. It does not show a classroom or a gathering of children, and should not be made to stand for every family’s storytelling practice.

Such recordings offer a way to listen across generations. A younger listener may return to a phrase, ask about an unfamiliar word or compare another version. Cultural learning can include that active response. Preserving a voice and allowing new listeners to engage with it are complementary parts of keeping a story in circulation.

sections.heading: Making room for different childhoods
paragraphs: Disability belongs within this account of play and learning. UNICEF’s guide to accessible schools focuses on removing barriers so that children with disabilities can learn alongside their peers.[6] Access involves the spaces and materials through which a child participates, rather than simply being present on an enrolment list.

A December 2025 parliamentary answer on Odisha describes support under Samagra Shiksha’s inclusive-education component, including assistive devices, transport and escort allowances, Braille and large-print materials, teacher preparation and accessible infrastructure.[7] These are provisions and approved outlays; the answer should not be read as evidence that every child has received every form of support.

For a cultural activity, the practical questions are immediate. Can a child enter the room, use the materials and communicate a choice? Can a game be adapted so that participation is meaningful? Does a storytelling session offer ways to follow it beyond spoken words alone? These questions help turn an invitation into something a child can actually use.

Location, household resources, language and disability can shape childhood in different combinations. A recollection of carefree play may be precious, but it cannot describe every child’s time or responsibilities. A chapter about growing up needs space for these differences, and for children’s own accounts of what matters to them.

The examples here suggest several openings: local games recognised in a curriculum, home languages welcomed into lessons, a library that supports young authors, and stories kept available to new listeners. Their promise rests on children being able to take part. Cultural continuity becomes richer when children can contribute in their own ways, as readers, players, questioners and storytellers.

chapters.title: Birth, Marriage, Mourning and Remembrance
chapters.subtitle: Kinship ritual and the work of memory
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A name spoken over a child, a wedding promise, a voice remembering someone who has died: life’s changes become occasions for other people to gather. They can bring joy and reassurance, but also separation, obligation and disagreement. A cultural history of Odisha must leave room for all of these experiences.

There is no single Odia sequence of rites. This chapter follows a few documented settings: family ceremonies described in the Nayagarh gazetteer, children’s tonsuring at Tara Tarini, an Odia marriage lament, and Sora practices of mourning and remembrance. Together they open questions about belonging, care and the ways a person remains part of other lives.

sections.heading: Welcoming a child
paragraphs: The Nayagarh district gazetteer describes worship of Sasthi Devi on the sixth day after birth in its account of Hindu family rites. It identifies ekoisa, on the twenty-first day, with naming and Satyanarayan Puja.[1] These are recorded customs in a district account, rather than a timetable followed by every household.

A naming ceremony draws attention to something both intimate and public. The infant is already being cared for; now a name can be spoken, remembered and used by others. The occasion gives relatives a way to acknowledge a new relationship. Looking at it in this way shifts attention from a list of ritual steps to the people who give those steps meaning.

Family observance can also meet the calendar of a shrine. Reporting from Tara Tarini in April 2024, The New Indian Express described parents accompanying children for mundan, or tonsuring, during Chaitra Yatra. The report attributed its account of the arrangements to temple officials.[2] The photograph on the opening page shows the precinct and its landscape, not a tonsuring ceremony.

The journey to a shrine makes a household milestone part of a shared place. Yet a crowd cannot tell us each family’s reasons for being there. To understand a particular visit would require listening to the people making it: what they hoped for, who accompanied them, and how they understood the offering.

Birth customs should also be read with attention to the mother’s experience. Descriptions of ritual can foreground a child’s entry into family life while leaving the work of care almost invisible. A fuller family history would ask who provided meals, rest and company, and whose recollection of the occasion has been preserved.

sections.heading: Marriage and the making of relationships
paragraphs: Marriage joins personal decisions to public recognition. The Nayagarh gazetteer places different religious forms side by side: Hindu rites including panigrahan, Muslim marriage with consent and meher, and Christian marriage with vows and rings in church.[1] Its compressed account does not capture every denomination, community or household, but it makes a single ceremonial model inadequate.

A useful account of a wedding would therefore begin with people and place. Who is marrying, in which community, and at what moment? Which actions do the participants regard as essential? Which have been adapted? Such questions allow a particular celebration to retain its character without being made to represent the whole state.

The ceremonial centre is only part of the story. An invitation, a meal or an exchange of words can matter because of the relationship it acknowledges. To describe these details well, we need more than a photograph of decorated clothing. We need the explanations of those who chose, prepared and used the objects.

We should also ask whose work makes a celebration possible. Cooking, receiving guests and arranging a gathering deserve a place in its record alongside the most visible rites. These are questions for future interviews and family archives; they should not be answered by assigning fixed roles to women, men or particular communities.

Marriage can be a moment of departure as well as celebration. The recorded kandana on the following page brings a lamenting voice into this account. It invites attention to emotional expression alongside ceremonial description. The sound of a person performing a repertoire is evidence of a different kind from a district handbook’s summary of rites.

sections.heading: A marriage lament, a remembered voice
paragraphs: Shantilata Dwibedi’s recital of an Odia marriage kandana was recorded by Sangram Keshari Senapati on 3 December 2023.[3] The image below is a preview still from that recording. It shows a named performer sharing a repertoire, rather than a bride at an observed wedding.

A recording preserves voice, pacing and expression alongside words. Here the distinction between recital and ceremony matters: a performance can carry knowledge of a form beyond the occasion with which it is associated. It can be listened to again, discussed and placed beside other tellings.

This chapter does not supply an unverified translation of the lament. A fuller edition could pair a checked Odia transcription with a translation and the performer’s explanation. That would let readers attend to her particular words, rather than assuming that every marriage lament expresses the same experience.

sections.heading: Mourning, place and continuing memory
paragraphs: The Nayagarh gazetteer records annual sraddha in its account of Hindu remembrance.[1] Other sources reveal quite different ways of sustaining relationships after death. These practices need their own names and settings, rather than being gathered into one supposedly shared belief about ancestors.

Anthropologist Piers Vitebsky recalls fieldwork among Sora communities in Odisha beginning in the 1970s. He describes mourners addressing the dead through trance mediums, with argument, tears and laughter all part of the encounter.[4] This is an account of a ritual world as participants understood it, not a claim that every Sora household shares those practices.

Stefano Beggiora’s 2016 conference abstract describes a Lanjia Saora funeral procession in Rayagada that links sacred places in and around a village. He contrasts this ritual setting with presentations at Bhubaneswar’s Adivasi Mela.[5] The distinction asks us to notice what a procession means to its participants, beyond the movements an audience can see.

Vitebsky also describes later generations adopting Christian or Hindu religious practices. Some younger Sora, he writes, have sought his earlier photographs, recordings and field notes as heritage documentation.[4] Remembering a tradition need not mean practising it unchanged. An archive can become a resource for people whose present beliefs differ from those of their grandparents.

These examples leave a question for anyone assembling cultural history: who should interpret a family’s most intimate occasions? A careful record keeps names, dates and circumstances, and makes room for participants to explain what matters. Birth, marriage and mourning belong to lived relationships. Their public documentation is most valuable when it preserves that human particularity.

chapters.title: Women as Makers and Keepers of Culture
chapters.subtitle: Authorship skill and cultural authority
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Women make Odisha’s cultural life through particular acts of skill and imagination: writing a novel, preparing a painting surface, teaching movement, telling a story. Recognising that work requires names, but also attention to the labour that does not acquire a public signature.

This chapter brings Pratibha Ray’s writing and Sanjukta Panigrahi’s performance alongside recorded storytelling, craft production and Sora ritual knowledge. These are different kinds of expertise, with different routes to recognition. Keeping culture can involve questioning an inherited story, changing its form or deciding how to pass it on. It should not be treated as a duty that women are simply born to fulfil.

sections.heading: Writing from a different centre
paragraphs: Pratibha Ray’s Yajnaseni places Draupadi’s consciousness at the centre of an inherited epic world. The English excerpt on Ray’s website follows her reflections during the Himalayan ascent: attachment, desire and the meaning of a life come under scrutiny as her husbands continue ahead.[1] The passage gives a woman inside the epic the authority to judge what she has endured.

This is one way of making culture through interpretation. A familiar story can remain recognisable while its emotional centre moves. Draupadi’s questions ask the reader to pause where a narrative of heroic progress might hurry onward. Ray’s novel belongs to the continuing life of the Mahabharata through that act of reconsideration.

Women’s literary work also becomes visible through the company in which it is read. Spark of Light, edited by Valerie Henitiuk and Supriya Kar and published by Athabasca University Press in 2016, gathers short stories by women writers of Odisha in English translation. Its contents include Reba Ray, Binapani Mohanty, Pratibha Ray and Sarojini Sahoo.[2]

The publisher describes a range of styles and concerns, including class, poverty, violence and family.[2] Such a collection allows disagreement and difference to remain visible. A woman writer may attend to domestic life, but she may also examine the wider arrangements that determine whose work, suffering or ambition receives attention.

Editing and translation are part of this cultural work. They shape which texts travel and how new readers encounter them. Crediting an author alone leaves that chain incomplete. The anthology gives readers a route back to particular stories and contributors, while its open-access edition makes the collection available beyond a single library shelf.

sections.heading: The labour within the finished object
paragraphs: A painting begins before the first visible figure. Mamata Tripathy’s 1998 study of Raghurajpur describes patta production as household work. In the division of tasks she records, women commonly prepared tamarind glue and chalk solution and polished the painting surface, while men applied the materials to the cloth.[3] These details belong to her historical study, not to an unchanging rule about who can do each task.

The preparation is consequential. A surface must be suitable for the painter’s line; its finish is part of the completed object’s material history. Calling this work mere assistance would conceal the knowledge it requires. A label that names only the person who draws the figures may tell only part of the story of how a painting was made.

Tripathy also describes household members contributing under the guidance of a senior man.[3] Participation and authority are therefore separate questions. Who knows how to make an object? Who directs its production? Whose name appears when it is exhibited or sold? A careful account of women’s craft work needs to ask all three.

The economic setting matters too. Mission Shakti’s description of its ORMAS partnership names women’s producer groups and self-help groups, with support envisaged for packaging, branding, training, buyer connections and working capital.[4] These are programme aims rather than proof of any individual maker’s income. They nevertheless acknowledge that reaching a market requires resources beyond production skill.

Recognition becomes more useful when it follows work closely: identifying contributions, recording teaching and asking how earnings are shared. Praise for a beautiful object does not answer those questions. The maker’s account of her own decisions and working conditions belongs beside the object in a fuller cultural history.

sections.heading: A storyteller with a name
paragraphs: Musamoni Panigrahi’s storytelling in Baleswari Odia was recorded by Subhashish Panigrahi on 20 January 2014.[5] The source describes a tale about a newly widowed woman who must convey family information while constrained from speaking her husband’s name. Verbal ingenuity becomes a way through a social restriction.

The recording identifies the teller as well as the tale. Her expression and timing are part of what a listener encounters; a plot summary cannot preserve them. The still below records a moment in that performance, rather than illustrating the story’s fictional widow.

A named storyteller complicates the loose description of knowledge as simply inherited. A story reaches listeners through someone’s choice of words and manner of telling. Preserving that contribution gives future listeners an individual voice to return to, and a place from which to ask about other versions.

sections.heading: Performance knowledge and the right to change
paragraphs: The Sangeet Natak Akademi’s citation for Sanjukta Panigrahi recognises a dancer who was also a teacher and choreographer. It records her training at Kalakshetra and in Odissi under Kelucharan Mohapatra, and performances in India and abroad.[6] Her work included presenting a repertoire, shaping it and helping others learn it.

Teaching makes the body’s knowledge available to another person. Choreography requires choices about how movement and expression unfold. Naming these activities gives a fuller account of artistic authority than a list of appearances or honours alone. It also reminds us to look for the rehearsal and instruction behind the public performance.

Ritual expertise belongs to a different setting. Recalling fieldwork among Sora communities in Odisha, Piers Vitebsky describes Ononti and the training of her designated successors, Taranti and Lokami. He notes women’s prominence as trance mediums in the communities he knew.[7] His account concerns particular people and religious practices, rather than a role shared by all Adivasi women.

Vitebsky also records religious change across generations and interest among younger Sora in earlier field notes, photographs and recordings.[7] Cultural continuity can take several forms. Someone may value a grandmother’s knowledge while choosing a different religious life. Documentation should allow that choice to remain visible.

The women encountered here do not occupy a single cultural role. Their work involves authorship, trained judgement, material preparation and the interpretation of relationships. Recognising them as makers means attending to what they create and decide. Recognising them as keepers means valuing the work of transmission without asking them to hold every tradition still.
