chapters.title: Caste, Labour and Access to Cultural Life
chapters.subtitle: Making learning belonging and recognition
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A cultural tradition can depend on someone’s labour without giving that person equal authority or recognition. To understand Odisha’s cultural life, we must ask who makes and serves, who can learn, and who is allowed to enter, speak or decide.

This chapter follows those questions through craft production, temple access, devotional arguments and Dalit writing. These settings cannot be reduced to one history. Together, however, they show why celebrating cultural achievement also requires attention to its social conditions. Caste hierarchy has been challenged within Odisha’s literary and religious worlds, while struggles over participation have continued. The makers and critics of culture belong within the same account.

sections.heading: Skill inheritance and the opportunity to learn
paragraphs: In her 1998 study of Raghurajpur, Mamata Tripathy describes patta painting as a household craft, with materials prepared and work shared among family members. She also records painters from communities beyond the Chitrakaras entering production as markets changed.[1] Her account shows a relationship between occupation and community that was being remade, rather than a permanent correspondence between birth and skill.

The distinction matters when a visitor hears a craft described as hereditary. A family can carry a valuable history of teaching, remembered designs and practical knowledge. That history deserves recognition. It does not establish that artistic ability belongs naturally to a caste, or that someone from another background cannot learn.

Tripathy describes training and workshops as opportunities for exchanging ideas. She also records competition and the involvement of middlemen, sometimes to artisans’ disadvantage.[1] An expanding market could bring new participants while producing new pressures. Her study belongs to a particular historical setting; it cannot establish the earnings or opportunities of today’s households.

To follow these relationships further, an account of a workshop would need to distinguish ownership, teaching, preparation, painting and sales. A person’s visible task does not reveal who owns the materials, sets the price or receives payment. The photograph opening this chapter records skilled painting, but supplies none of that information about the individual shown.

Cultural credit can begin with precise description. Who prepared the surface? Who taught the design? Whose labour made the finished work possible? These questions help recognise collaboration while leaving room to examine unequal control. They also keep an account of inherited expertise from becoming an endorsement of inherited social rank.

sections.heading: A doorway is also a social boundary
paragraphs: Article 17 of the Constitution of India abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.[2] This establishes a public principle against which exclusion must be judged. A cultural description should not turn discrimination into an unquestioned custom merely because it occurs around a revered institution.

An answer in the Lok Sabha on 6 September 2011 provides a specific Odisha record. Drawing on information from the state government, it reported two temple-entry incidents during the preceding five years: at the Jagannath temple in Keredagada, Kendrapara district, and the Kali temple at Nuapada village in Puri district. It stated that Scheduled Caste people had been barred and that cases had been registered.[3]

The answer also said that such incident data were not maintained centrally. Its two reported cases are therefore neither a complete count of exclusion nor evidence about those temples’ present arrangements. The record establishes that access was contested at named places and that the state acknowledged the disputes.

Entering a cultural space is only one dimension of participation. Learning its repertoire, receiving a performing role, sharing a meal and helping govern an institution raise further questions. Service may be highly skilled and essential without carrying the same authority as deciding how that service is organised.

These distinctions help us read claims of cultural unity carefully. A story about equality, a legal principle and a person’s experience of welcome are different kinds of evidence. Each matters. Placing them beside one another lets us ask where an ideal has become practice, where it has been resisted and whose testimony is needed to understand the difference.

sections.heading: Devotion as a language of challenge
paragraphs: Balaram Das’s Lakshmi Purana makes food and hospitality part of an argument about hierarchy. P. C. Mohanty and Swadhin Mohanty’s account describes Jagannath and Balabhadra enduring hardship after Lakshmi leaves them, and reads the narrative as an appeal against caste discrimination.[4] That moral argument should not be mistaken for proof that exclusion disappeared.

Bhima Bhoi’s legacy offers another public language of equality. At a meeting in Sambalpur on 2 March 2024, President Droupadi Murmu highlighted social equality in his work and called for wider translation of his writings.[5] This is evidence of how his legacy is invoked in public life today.

The memorial at Khaliapali gives remembrance a physical setting. Such places invite a further question: how can honouring a poet keep the challenge of his ideas audible, alongside the ceremonies through which he is remembered?

sections.heading: Speaking as a maker of the record
paragraphs: Dalit writing changes the position from which cultural life is described. In a 2019 interview with Jaydeep Sarangi, Basudev Sunani recalls his early concern with poverty and his later engagement with caste discrimination and Ambedkar’s thought. He describes this development as part of his own thinking and creative work.[6]

Sunani identifies poverty, migration, starvation and protest as concerns of his first poetry collection, published in 1995. He also discusses a substantial work on Dalit cultural history based on years of fieldwork, and his editing of Odia Dalit literature.[6] His account brings poetry, historical research and the work of assembling other voices into the same creative life.

He questions the limited attention paid to marginalised people in much contemporary writing.[6] The criticism asks more of literary culture than sympathetic representation. It asks who is writing, whose experience shapes the terms of discussion and which works reach readers. A poet can be an interpreter of society as well as someone whose experience is interpreted by others.

This interview is one writer’s position, not a statement for every Dalit author. Its importance lies partly in that specificity. Naming a speaker and locating an argument gives readers something they can examine and respond to, rather than an anonymous category presented as having a single voice.

A fuller cultural record would place such voices alongside accounts by makers, performers, teachers and people who have challenged exclusion. It would ask about remuneration and access to training as carefully as it asks about artistic form. Odisha’s cultural achievements become more intelligible when the people who sustain them can also question their conditions, claim credit for their work and participate in deciding what comes next.

chapters.title: Places to Learn Together
chapters.subtitle: Shared reading libraries and voluntary learning
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A place to learn together needs more than a collection of books. It needs someone to welcome a newcomer, a reason to return and time in which a question can be asked. Reading aloud, browsing a shelf and learning to type Odia each create different relationships between people and knowledge.

This chapter follows Bhagabata Tungis, Bakul’s library work and a volunteer digitisation workshop. Their purposes and histories differ, but each makes learning a shared activity. The important continuity is the work of gathering people around something worth understanding. The future of such places depends on who can participate, who sustains them and how their activities respond to the people who use them.

sections.heading: The book heard in a shared room
paragraphs: Historian Pritipuspa Mishra describes Bhagabata Gharas or Tungis as places where palm-leaf manuscripts were housed and communal readings took place. In her account of nineteenth-century Odia literary culture, these spaces also served as village libraries and sites for panchayats.[1] A text had a social life beyond its owner or the person able to read it independently.

Reading aloud changes the scale of access. A single copy can reach several listeners; explanation and discussion can accompany the words. The gathering becomes part of the text’s circulation. This helps us understand why the history of books cannot be written entirely through printing presses, sales or individual literacy.

The photograph on the opening page shows a Bhagabata Tungi in a Bhubaneswar temple precinct in 2016. Its devotional objects and painted lettering locate it within a religious setting. It does not show a reading session, and cannot tell us how often people gathered or who participated. A photograph of a room is an opening into its history, rather than a complete account of its use.

A shared institution should also be understood through its local arrangements. Who kept the manuscripts safe, opened the room and led the reading? Who could interrupt with a question? Were people of different ages and social backgrounds equally welcome? Those questions require testimony about particular places, rather than an assumption that every gathering worked in the same way.

The Tungi offers a history of learning through listening and meeting. Its relevance today need not depend on calling it an early version of every modern institution. Its devotional purpose, collections and local relationships deserve to remain visible in their own terms.

sections.heading: A library made through participation
paragraphs: Bakul Foundation describes its Bhubaneswar library as growing from an online appeal for books, individual donations and voluntary effort. Its education page presents the Satyanagar space as a free library with storytelling, author interactions and creative workshops.[2] The account shows how a collection can become a setting for repeated encounters.

The organisation also reports mobile-library activity and work with schools. Under its BLISS initiative, it distinguishes helping children learn to read from encouraging those already able to read, placing enjoyment at the centre of both.[2] These are related tasks, but they call for different kinds of attention from a volunteer.

A child who struggles with a page may need patient help with words. Another may need the freedom to abandon an uninteresting book and find a better one. A shared reading space can accommodate both. Its value is partly the room it gives readers to develop preferences, rather than measuring every encounter as a completed lesson.

Bakul’s account also describes workshops that produced Odia picture-book manuscripts, including three developed in Ganjam villages and published with children credited as authors.[2] Here the library’s educational work leads towards making books. A participant can contribute something for another person to read.

Book donations begin a process that still needs daily care. Collections must be arranged, damaged copies repaired and activities prepared. Volunteers need guidance and reliable ways to share responsibility. These practical matters help explain why a successful appeal and a lasting library are different achievements. Bakul’s published account documents its approach; the experience of any particular reader would need to be heard directly.

sections.heading: Learning to build a digital collection
paragraphs: A Centre for Internet and Society report from December 2014 describes an Odia Wikisource workshop in New Delhi, organised with community volunteers and The Intellects. Pankajmala Sarangi and Sitikantha Kheti shared their experience, while Subhashish Panigrahi demonstrated Odia input and book digitisation.[3]

The report records a handbook explaining the project and keyboard layout, and plans for further workshops and digitisation sessions. It also describes Sarangi’s involvement in proofreading the Odia Bhagabata.[3] A text associated with collective listening could become the focus of another shared task: checking and preparing it for readers online.

The meeting illustrates how a digital collection depends on people learning together. A keyboard layout becomes more usable when someone can demonstrate it and answer a question. The group photograph records that gathering; it does not by itself establish the later completion or accuracy of the texts discussed.

sections.heading: What makes renewal meaningful
paragraphs: In October 2025, PTI reported the Odisha government’s stated intention to revive Bhagabata Tungis across the state.[4] An announcement expresses a commitment; it does not establish that every proposed space is functioning. Assessing renewal requires attention to activities, people and continued use as well as buildings.

The IFLA–UNESCO Public Library Manifesto of 2022 offers a useful principle for public libraries: equality of access and services responsive to local needs. It recognises lifelong learning and participation in cultural life as part of their purpose.[5] This is an international statement of aims, not a report on implementation in Odisha.

For a future community learning project, we propose beginning with the people who might use it. Children, older residents, people with disabilities and speakers of different languages may need different materials and arrangements. Asking when they can attend and what they want to learn would give the programme a firmer basis than choosing activities on their behalf.

A modest programme could combine a dependable reading hour with practical help, a book discussion or a session led by a local maker. This is a proposal for adaptation, not a claim that all Tungis or libraries already offer these activities. A devotional gathering and a general public library may share resources while retaining distinct purposes.

The measure of a learning place is also the confidence it gives someone to return. A child choosing a book, an adult practising a new skill and a volunteer learning to teach all contribute to its life. Keeping such a place open means sustaining the relationships that let people become participants, and eventually help others take part.

chapters.title: Changing Towns and Rural Lives
chapters.subtitle: Work mobility and the choices that shape a place
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: Change in Odisha can be read through the distance between a home and a workplace, a school and a seasonal journey, or a workshop and its buyers. Town and countryside meet in these relationships. A village does not stand outside modern life, and a growing city carries older places and attachments within it.

This chapter follows the planned capital at Bhubaneswar, the schooling of children in migrant families, craft livelihoods at Raghurajpur and a farmer’s account from Koraput. Together these examples show why cultural continuity depends on practical conditions: space to gather, time to learn, reliable work and a voice in decisions about the future.

sections.heading: A capital grows beside an older town
paragraphs: Bhubaneswar’s City Development Plan traces the new capital to planning begun in 1948 under Otto Koenigsberger. It describes neighbourhood units, an administrative centre and markets. Government departments moved from Cuttack after the Secretariat building was completed in 1956; offices and institutions helped draw further residential and commercial development.[1] The capital’s growth joined a political decision to many smaller decisions about where people would work and live.

The same planning history records the incorporation of neighbouring revenue villages as the urban area expanded. This matters because a city can grow around a place without all its residents having moved. A familiar locality becomes part of a larger administrative and economic landscape. Its name may survive even as the relationships around it change.

The older temple town offers another scale of belonging. India’s 2014 Tentative List submission for Ekamra Kshetra describes a landscape of temples, tanks and ritual connections.[2] The submission is a proposal for recognition, not proof of World Heritage inscription. Its account nevertheless helps us see why a monument cannot be understood entirely apart from the spaces around it.

The opening photograph of Mukteswar records one part of that older landscape. It cannot show the experience of every resident or the effects of subsequent development. To understand a changing neighbourhood, we would also need accounts of everyday routes: where people shop, meet neighbours, find work and take children to school.

These different scales belong in the same history. A capital can be described through plans and institutions, but its cultural life also depends on the places residents can continue to use. The question is how change is experienced, and whose experience is included in the record.

sections.heading: A working season and a school year
paragraphs: The Odisha School Education Programme Authority describes seasonal migration from western Odisha after the kharif season and Nuakhai, often in October or November. Its account includes parents travelling with children for work at brick kilns outside the state. The agency also records seasonal hostels at places of origin from 2006–07, intended to help children remain in school.[3] These are descriptions of an educational response, not evidence that every child received support.

Here the agricultural year, the festival calendar and the school year overlap. For a family, the timing of work can determine whether a child travels or remains behind. Cultural participation is therefore connected to wages and care: being present for a gathering or a lesson requires arrangements that make presence possible.

A hostel changes the organisation of family life as well as access to a classroom. Assessing it properly would mean listening to children, parents and carers about safety, companionship and contact during separation. An official objective tells us what an institution is meant to achieve; it does not substitute for those experiences.

Migration itself needs to be described precisely. The Census of India’s 1991 migration table for Odisha distinguishes employment, business, education, marriage, movement with family and other reasons.[4] These categories remind us that leaving home is not one kind of event. They should not be used as current statistics or as explanations of a particular person’s decision.

A young person leaving for study and a family travelling for seasonal labour may both keep connections with a village, but their opportunities differ. A cultural history should make room for those differences. It should also ask about people who remain: who cares for relatives, tends a home and keeps shared activities going while others are away?

sections.heading: A workshop connected to wider markets
paragraphs: In a 2014 account of Raghurajpur, Sucharita Sahoo described craft production in homes, support for training and marketing through organisations, and artisans taking work to fairs within and beyond Odisha.[5] The village was already connected to buyers elsewhere. Its rural setting did not make its artistic life economically self-contained.

The photograph below, made in 2018, shows an artisan displaying her work at a painted doorway. Her name is not recorded in the source. The image brings a maker into view, but tells us neither her earnings nor her wishes for the next generation. A fuller account would let her explain how she learned, how work reaches buyers and what makes continuing worthwhile.

For younger makers, continuity must leave room for choice. Training can keep a skill available; a sustainable livelihood can make practising it possible. Neither requires us to imagine that every child should inherit the same occupation.

sections.heading: Having a say in what changes
paragraphs: In May 2025, Associated Press reported Sunita Muduli’s account from Putpondi village in Koraput. A Paraja farmer, she described late rains and reduced production. The report also documented women mapping local resources and the changes they wanted to see, with support from a rural development organisation.[6] Their work made local knowledge part of a discussion about the future.

This example places a resident’s explanation beside the plans and institutional accounts encountered earlier. The authority to describe change should include people whose daily work gives them knowledge of a place. Their priorities may be expressed through a field, a water source or a route used repeatedly, rather than through a famous landmark.

Generational change deserves the same attention. Instead of deciding in advance that young people have abandoned a tradition, we can ask what learning it requires and what choices are available. Instead of assuming that staying preserves a way of life, we can ask whether those who stay can influence the conditions in which they live.

A useful local record could bring together a dated map, photographs and conversations with residents of different ages and occupations. People should be able to decide how their names, images and accounts are used. Recording both agreement and disagreement would help future readers understand why a change was welcomed by some and resisted by others.

The future of cultural life is shaped in ordinary decisions about work, education and shared space. Remembering a place well means attending to these decisions as carefully as to its buildings and celebrations. It also means allowing its residents to imagine lives that differ from those of earlier generations.

chapters.title: Radio, Recordings and Television
chapters.subtitle: Voices performances and audiences across media
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A voice can reach a listener who has never seen the singer or the stage. A recording can return that voice to another day. Television adds a face, a setting and a choice of what the camera allows us to see. Each medium changes the relationship between a performance and its audience.

In Odisha, these relationships connect writers, musicians, dancers and the people who prepare programmes for transmission. This chapter follows AIR Cuttack, recorded songs and literary readings, and the growth of Odia television. Their histories overlap: a performer can work across several media, while a familiar story acquires a different shape in each.

sections.heading: The studio and the imagined stage
paragraphs: Jose Jacob’s account of an engineer-guided visit dates AIR Cuttack’s inauguration to 28 January 1948. It describes an initial temporary studio at Madhapur House and a transmitter at Killa Fort. During his 2008 visit, Jacob observed specialised spaces for talk, drama, music and playback, with computers used alongside reel-to-reel tapes.[1] His account makes the practical work of broadcasting visible as well as its beginnings.

For a radio dramatist, the absence of a visible stage is a creative condition. A change of voice can announce an arrival; a pause can suggest hesitation. Music and other sounds can help a listener imagine distance or a change of scene. The script must give performers and listeners enough to build that world together.

Gopal Chhotray’s work belongs within this exchange between writing and performance. The Library of Congress describes his long association with AIR Cuttack and credits him with helping revive Gitinatya, or plays in verse.[2] His career shows how a literary form could continue through new opportunities to write for voices.

Dancer Kumkum Mohanty recalls another kind of collaboration. For Kumar Utsav Samiti programmes in Cuttack, students from different dance institutions worked with AIR artists. Bhubaneswar Mishra composed music and AIR staff played instruments including violin, flute and harmonium. In her account, AIR recorded and broadcast the music, while the dances themselves were not filmed.[3]

That distinction matters. A surviving soundtrack can preserve the musical part of an event without preserving its movement, costumes or audience. Mohanty’s recollection helps restore the relationships around the sound. It also reminds us to describe an archive according to what it actually holds, rather than treating one surviving part as the whole performance.

sections.heading: What a recording carries
paragraphs: In a 2018 interview, lyricist Devdas Chhotray contrasted the studio with the stage. A singer before an audience can repeat or emphasise a phrase in response to listeners; a radio recording has a different immediate setting. He remembered his first recorded ghazal being composed and sung by Akshaya Mohanty for AIR Cuttack, and said such songs were classified as adhunika, or modern songs.[4]

The programme category mattered because it placed an experiment within an existing listening world. A song could draw on a form associated with another language while finding its own words and manner in Odia. The recording preserved one version of that encounter, not every way the singer might later perform it.

Devdas also described making the album Nua Luha Puruna Luha with Susmita Das and Omprakash Mohanty.[4] Here the album offered another setting for collaboration and for returning to a musical approach. Broadcast schedules and recordings were connected parts of creative work, with different ways of reaching listeners.

A recording also allows us to return to spoken literature. The Library of Congress catalogue links Gopal Chhotray’s readings from Pheria, Parakalama and Sei phula.[2] These are author readings, not a collection of original AIR drama broadcasts. Their value lies partly in the opportunity to hear how a writer gives pace and emphasis to words on a page.

A disc, a tape and a digital file are different carriers of recorded sound. To understand any particular item, we need its credits and history: who wrote and performed it, when it was recorded, and whether it is complete. A label, sleeve or catalogue entry can preserve information that listening alone cannot supply. Keeping those details with the sound helps later listeners distinguish a new rendition from an older recording.

sections.heading: Odia stories on television
paragraphs: Mrinal Chatterjee’s history places Odisha within the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment of 1975–76, with programmes produced at Cuttack for districts including Dhenkanal, Sambalpur and Phulbani. He traces the move of production to the Bhubaneswar studio complex in 1992.[5] Educational television and later entertainment belonged to different stages of this development.

Prasar Bharati dates its Odia satellite service to 2 October 1993 as DD-5, its renaming as DD-6 to August 1994, and round-the-clock broadcasting to April 2001. Its programme catalogue includes Katha Sarita and Gopala Rahasya.[6] Stories could now be shaped through actors, framing and editing as well as through voice.

sections.heading: The work behind a shared screen
paragraphs: Television’s expansion brought more settings in which Odia programmes could be made. Chatterjee records OTV’s beginnings in Bhubaneswar and Cuttack in 1997, and the subsequent growth of private broadcasting.[5] A channel’s arrival created another schedule, but the programmes still depended on people assembling stories, images and sound for viewers.

Fakira Mohan Nahak’s recollection of ETV’s Rath Yatra coverage on 12 July 2002 describes teams working in Puri and Hyderabad. He names field leadership, engineering and panel production among the coordinated roles.[7] The account turns a live broadcast into a history of work: what reaches the screen depends on decisions and connections that the viewer may never see.

A televised festival is also a particular view of a larger event. The camera can bring a distant detail close, while commentary gives it an explanation. Viewers elsewhere can follow the procession without being in Puri. Yet the screen cannot reproduce every sound, movement or personal reason for attending. These are different ways of participating, each worth understanding.

For programmes encountered again online, the original broadcast date and the upload date should remain distinct. An excerpt may preserve a memorable scene while leaving out the rest of a serial or performance. Identifying the episode, contributors and source makes it easier to appreciate the work and harder to mistake a fragment for a complete record.

The history of these media therefore includes more than familiar voices and faces. It includes writers, accompanists, engineers, editors and the listeners and viewers who remember programmes. Preserving credits alongside recordings gives those contributions a better chance of remaining visible. It lets future audiences encounter the work with some understanding of the people and circumstances that made it possible.

chapters.title: Odia Cinema and the Worlds It Makes
chapters.subtitle: Literature households and the work behind the screen
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A film makes a world through people, places, voices and the time it asks us to spend with them. A family meal can reveal an argument without naming it. A familiar landscape can become the setting for someone else’s hopes. Watching in Odia also brings the sound of the language into that encounter.

This chapter follows a few routes through that larger world: the first Odia talkie, the movement of literature to the screen, household stories, and the labour of making and preserving films. These examples offer different ways of looking at Odisha. They also invite us to notice the people behind the images, whose work continues beyond a film’s release.

sections.heading: Stories finding a screen
paragraphs: Kapilas Bhuyan’s historical account for the Press Information Bureau identifies Mohan Sundar Deb Goswami’s Sita Bibah as the first Odia talkie. It distinguishes an earlier Calcutta showing from the formal release at Laxmitalkie Cinema in Puri on 28 April 1936. Bhuyan records fourteen songs sung by the actors.[1] Story, performance and music were already closely connected at this beginning.

The choice of a familiar story gave cinema a relationship with audiences who could know its characters before entering the hall. Yet a film still had to organise that familiarity through recorded performances and a sequence of images. The encounter belonged to a new setting, even when its material had a longer life.

Literature provided further routes. Mrinal Sen’s filmography credits Kalindi Charan Panigrahi with the story of Matira Manisha, his 1966 Odia film. Its synopsis describes two brothers whose attitudes towards inherited land diverge.[2] The source places family obligations beside changes in agrarian life, allowing a household dispute to open onto a wider social world.

Adaptation involves decisions about what can be seen and heard. A novelist can explain a thought directly; a filmmaker might place two people in a room, let one remain silent, or return to an object that has acquired meaning. These possibilities make the relationship between book and film worth exploring without expecting them to work identically.

An adaptation can also lead a viewer back to its author. Keeping the source work visible in credits, introductions and discussions gives that journey a starting point. The film need not exhaust the book’s possibilities. It can become one reading of a work that other readers, performers and filmmakers may approach differently.

sections.heading: The household as a larger world
paragraphs: Nirad Mohapatra’s Maya Miriga follows an extended middle-class family in a small town. The Il Cinema Ritrovato programme describes its gradual disintegration and draws attention to the restrained performances and Bhaskar Chandavarkar’s music. It also reproduces the director’s reflections on affection, responsibility and the desire for personal freedom within the joint family.[3]

This is a useful way to approach the title of this chapter. A film’s world need not be geographically large. The expectations shared inside a household can carry questions about education, status and independence. We can ask who has room to choose, whose work supports others, and how a decision that seems promising to one person may unsettle someone else.

Another father-and-son story appears in Anupam Patnaik’s Pratikshya. The 2022 IFFI account identifies Gourahari Das’s short story as its inspiration. Its central character, Sanjay, seeks a government job while the family faces debt and his father’s serious illness. The possibility of employment through compassionate appointment brings a troubling pressure into their relationship.[4]

The premise turns an economic hope into an intimate conflict. It asks what happens when the wish for security becomes entangled with the fate of someone loved. Such a story can be rooted in a recognisable social setting while leaving viewers to consider feelings that are difficult to acknowledge.

These films should retain their differences. Their households, styles and moments of production are not interchangeable portraits of every Odia family. Together, however, they show how cinema can make ordinary relationships worthy of sustained attention. A pause, an exchange or a decision may reveal something that a broad description of social change leaves out.

sections.heading: Parbati Ghose and the work of adaptation
paragraphs: The Gour–Parbati archive dates Chha Mana Atha Guntha to 1986 and identifies Fakir Mohan Senapati’s novel as its source. It credits Parbati Ghose as producer and director, as the performer playing Saria, and as Shrabani, the name used for screenplay and dialogue.[5] Several kinds of creative responsibility met in her work on this film.

The same record names Ashok Swain for camera, Nagen Barik for sound, and Asim Basu and Sarat Sahoo for art. It describes filming in Olosingh and acknowledges the villagers and Kalyani Patnaik’s hospitality.[5] These details widen the picture of authorship. A screen world also depends on technical skill, places to work and people willing to help a production take shape.

sections.heading: Keeping a film available to be seen
paragraphs: A completed film has another life to negotiate: reaching viewers and remaining available after its initial release. At IFFI in 2022, Anupam Patnaik spoke about the difficulty of sustaining an industry with limited theatre access.[4] His account is a filmmaker’s assessment at that moment, rather than a current inventory of cinema halls. It nevertheless connects the making of stories with the practical question of where people can see them.

Preservation presents a different challenge. Film Heritage Foundation describes locating deteriorated reels of Maya Miriga’s original camera negative in 2021. Repair, scanning and restoration used that material together with a surviving 35 mm print held by NFDC–NFAI. The foundation credits laboratories, restoration specialists and the director’s family in a process lasting almost three years.[6]

The 2024 Il Cinema Ritrovato programme placed the restored film before a festival audience.[3] Recognition and survival are separate achievements: a celebrated film can still depend on fragile materials and sustained effort to remain viewable. The restoration makes this dependence visible without diminishing the original filmmakers’ work.

For a viewer, careful identification is part of that renewed encounter. A restored version, a trailer and a short online extract offer different experiences. Recording the source and version helps a discussion stay close to the work actually seen. Credits also let us follow the contributions of actors, writers, composers and technicians into other films.

Odia cinema’s worlds are made by these connections as well as by what appears within the frame. Books find performers; households become stories; crews turn locations into scenes; preservation brings older work to another audience. The pleasure of watching can lead us further into each of those relationships, and towards films we have yet to discover.

chapters.title: Archives, Libraries and the Digital Page
chapters.subtitle: Keeping words available, making room for readers
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A book may survive without being available. Someone remembers its title; a library catalogue records it; a copy rests in a cupboard. Yet the person who wants to read it cannot reach its pages. Between survival and use lies a chain of work: keeping, describing, copying, checking and helping another reader find a way in.

In Odisha, that work connects manuscripts and printed volumes with reading rooms, volunteer collections and digital libraries. The screen adds another doorway. What passes through it depends on earlier acts of care—and on the people who continue to make a preserved page intelligible.

sections.heading: The work before the website
paragraphs: Odia Bibhaba offers a particularly revealing history of this labour. Its account describes Srujanika as a volunteer collective rooted in science and education. Project Rebati, begun in 2004, joined work on Odia computing with the preservation of printed material. The digital Purnachandra Odia Bhasakosha appeared in 2006, followed by collections of dictionaries, periodicals and individual writers’ works.[1]

The equipment belongs to the story. Srujanika describes developing a camera-based copying system and using open-source software. Before a reader could download a volume, someone had to arrange the pages, obtain usable images and process them. Earlier distribution on discs and flash drives also reminds us that the digital archive did not begin with a browser window.[1]

This history has changes of responsibility as well as achievements. In a post dated 23 May 2021, Srujanika announced that its digitisation work had ended and described work beginning under SOA University’s PPRACHIN programme, using its equipment and experience. It said website management would continue for the time being. That dated statement records a transition; it does not establish the present staffing arrangement or imply that the collection disappeared.[2]

An archive therefore needs more than a successful launch. Someone must answer a query, repair a broken route to a volume and explain what a collection contains. The visible page rests on less visible continuity. A useful question is not simply how much has been scanned, but whether a reader can identify the edition, follow its sequence and return to the same passage later.

sections.heading: What a collection can—and cannot—show
paragraphs: A periodical preserves a conversation differently from a collected volume. A poem appears beside an essay; an editorial shares an issue with advertisements or correspondence. Their proximity is part of the evidence. Reading only a detached passage can conceal the company it kept and the audience to which it first spoke.

Odia Bibhaba’s Utkal Sahitya collection identifies the magazine’s beginning in 1897 under Biswanath Kar and describes writing on religion, philosophy, culture, politics and science. Its range invites a reader to follow connections across subjects rather than regard literary history as a shelf of isolated masterpieces.[3]

But a catalogue entry is a promise of a route, not proof that every issue survives. The responsible reader checks the volume and issue dates, the available pages and any indication of gaps. An absent search result cannot settle whether a word was never printed: the relevant issue may be missing, or the page may be present only as an image.

A scanned page and a searchable text also offer different kinds of help. The image retains visible layout, marks and damaged edges. A transcription makes words easier to search, quote or enlarge, but introduces decisions about letters, spacing and uncertain readings. Keeping the image close to the transcription lets readers examine those decisions.

The same care applies to editions. A scan of a later reprint is evidence of that reprint; it should not silently become a photograph of an original newspaper sheet. Author, title, edition, date and page number are modest details with a large purpose. They allow another person to retrace a reading and disagree with it on shared ground.

sections.heading: Readers who help make the text
paragraphs: Digital preservation also creates occasions for people to learn together. A Centre for Internet and Society report documents an Odia Wikisource workshop in New Delhi in December 2014. Its photograph places the digital page in an ordinary social setting: people around tables, working in a room lined with books.[4]

The image is a useful reminder that a readable text is made through attention. Comparing a transcription with a page asks for patience, language knowledge and a willingness to leave uncertainty visible. A corrected letter may look like a tiny contribution. Across a book, such acts determine whether another reader can trust what appears on screen. Participation has value when the source remains available for checking.

sections.heading: A place to read, a way to return
paragraphs: The library remains a physical invitation as well as a collection. Bakul Foundation’s account of its Library Movement describes donated books, individual contributions and volunteer work. It presents its Bhubaneswar library as free to readers and describes storytelling, author interactions and creative workshops. Its work with Odia picture books also connects access to the making of material that children can enjoy.[5]

These activities answer a question that digitisation alone cannot resolve: who feels able to begin? A child may need someone to read aloud. An unfamiliar catalogue may need explanation. A person using a phone may struggle with a large file or a page whose letters cannot be enlarged clearly. Availability becomes meaningful through the conditions in which reading happens.

For a small collection, a practical beginning is a clear record of what is held, where it came from and what can be consulted. A digital copy should carry its source and any known gaps. Backups, dependable filenames and a named person responsible for the collection help keep that record usable. These are suggestions for care, not a claim that every collection already follows them.

Access and reuse also need separate descriptions. A page that can be read or downloaded does not, by that fact alone, explain permission to republish it. The work, its edition, a photograph and a recorded performance may carry different notices. Readers need the applicable terms beside the material, with uncertainty acknowledged rather than replaced by a blanket claim.

An archive is most generous when it makes return possible: return to a source, to an overlooked writer, to an unfinished question. The digital page extends that possibility. Libraries and the people who sustain them give it a welcoming place in everyday life.

chapters.title: Languages on New Screens
chapters.subtitle: Ho Santali and Odia in digital everyday life
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A message reaches a phone, but its letters appear as empty boxes. A book is visible online, but its words cannot be searched. A keyboard displays familiar letters, yet the person using it still needs help composing a sentence. These are different difficulties, and solving one does not automatically solve the others.

For Ho, Santali and Odia, digital participation involves writing systems, usable tools and people willing to teach and contribute. The question reaches beyond whether a language appears on screen. It concerns who can write, correct, read and circulate knowledge there—and whose choices shape the result.

sections.heading: A language is more than its lettering
paragraphs: Ho and Santali have histories that cross the boundaries of Odisha. Their digital lives cannot be understood through a single state or a single writing practice. The Unicode Standard identifies Warang Citi as a script devised by Lako Bodra for Ho. It also records Ho writing in Odia, Devanagari and Latin letters. For Santali, it identifies Ol Chiki with Raghunath Murmu and notes other scripts used to write the language.[1]

These distinctions matter when someone prepares a learning resource or a digital collection. A speaker may understand a story while being unfamiliar with the script in which it is presented. Choosing a script is therefore also a choice about readers, teaching and the paths through which a text will circulate. It should begin with the people expected to use it.

Unicode supplies a shared system for representing characters in digital text. It does not assign one script exclusively to one language. Its own explanation stresses that several languages may share a script, while a language may be written in more than one.[2] Encoding makes exchange possible; it does not determine what a community should write or settle differences in usage.

For Ho digital work, the practical questions follow from this distinction. Which writing practice do intended readers know? Can they enter the letters on the devices they use? Who will check a lesson, a local name or an explanation? A successful demonstration on one computer cannot answer all three. The value of a resource becomes clearer when a reader can use it independently, and when a knowledgeable contributor can correct it without surrendering control of the language to an outside editor.

sections.heading: Letters that can travel
paragraphs: The tools involved have separate jobs. Character encoding represents the text; a font supplies the visible forms of its letters; an input method lets a person enter them. These parts must work together. A page can contain correctly encoded text while the device lacks a suitable font. Equally, text that looks right in an older font may need conversion before it can travel reliably into another system.[2][3]

O Foundation’s Santali resource page makes these differences concrete. It brings together Ol Chiki fonts, input methods and a converter for text typed with older fonts. It credits individual makers, including Pooja Saxena for the Guru Gomke typeface and Jnanaranjan Sahu for the listed Unicode converter. Such credits reveal a field of design and maintenance behind what may look like a simple act of typing.[3]

The page also names Sarjom Baha as a phonetic input method for Wikimedia projects. A keyboard arrangement can help someone begin, but familiarity still takes practice. The useful test is a real task: entering a name, composing a question or correcting a paragraph. Instructions should meet people at that level rather than assuming that installing a tool completes the work.

In a multilingual household or classroom, movement between scripts may be ordinary. A person can read one language, speak another and use a third for study or employment. Digital design should leave room for those combinations. Clear language labels, readable text and an easy way to change input methods can support them. These are practical design aims, not evidence that all devices or platforms already serve every reader equally well.

sections.heading: People who make a digital public
paragraphs: In an interview published by Wikimedia’s Diff in February 2025, Santali contributor Ramjit Tudu describes building contacts among editors and receiving support from the Odia community. The account places workshops and collaboration alongside the Santali Wikipedia launch in 2018. It also describes outreach to writers and universities, and the importance of social media for a geographically dispersed community.[4]

This is a history of relationships as well as pages. An experienced contributor helps another person make a first edit; a writer introduces a source; a discussion resolves an uncertainty. The Odia workshop photograph below records another such learning setting. It does not measure the reach of either language online, but it makes visible the people whose effort a website can easily hide.[5]

sections.heading: From a page image to a usable text
paragraphs: Odia Wikisource offers a different view of digital participation. A 2014 account by Subhashish Panigrahi describes volunteers retyping books or using optical character recognition, usually shortened to OCR, to turn scanned images into editable text. It also discusses converting writing from older font systems. These are related forms of work, but they begin with different materials.[6]

A scan is a picture of a page. OCR attempts to recognise the printed characters in that picture. Conversion, by contrast, can begin with text already stored digitally in an older encoding. Neither operation removes the need to check the result. A damaged letter, an unfamiliar name or an unusual spelling may require a reader who understands both the source and its context.

Correction is consequently part of authorship’s supporting world. A useful edition keeps a route back to the page it follows and makes uncertain readings visible. It should also distinguish a faithful transcription from a modernised spelling or a translation. Each can help readers, but each makes a different promise.

Access involves more than letters. A long download may be difficult on a limited connection. Someone may prefer listening, need larger type or rely on another person to explain an unfamiliar interface. Recording a voice adds possibilities, while also requiring agreement about attribution, circulation and future use. Community participation should include decisions about what remains unrecorded or outside public circulation.

New screens offer room for everyday correspondence, learning and literary experiment. Their strongest promise is the possibility of sustained use: people writing to one another, finding material worth reading and helping newcomers take part. The tools matter because they can support those acts. The direction belongs to the people whose languages give the screen its meaning.

chapters.title: Modern Art, Photography and Public Heritage
chapters.subtitle: Making images and learning to look
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A painting, a museum label and a photograph of a temple each direct attention. They select something for us to see, while leaving other things outside the frame. Odisha’s visual life includes this work of interpretation as well as the objects and places being represented.

Modern artists give inherited forms new purposes; illustrators build worlds on a page; public murals address people passing in the street. Museums and heritage walks arrange encounters with the past. Looking closely at these practices reveals how culture becomes public—and why a familiar image should still invite questions about its maker, setting and audience.

sections.heading: Modern art across places and materials
paragraphs: Jatin Das offers one route into this field. The National Gallery of Modern Art, Mumbai, records his work Lovers as a pen-and-ink image of a seated couple. Its catalogue identifies his birth in Mayurbhanj and training at the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay, and draws attention to his interest in the human body and the possibilities of line.[1] The record connects a particular work to a life that moved between places.

This is a useful starting point for looking at modern art from Odisha. Regional belonging need not mean that every picture illustrates a recognisable monument, costume or festival. Gesture, tension, intimacy and the handling of a material can matter as much as the subject’s location. A work may carry relationships with home without becoming a diagram of local identity.

Sculpture expands those possibilities into physical space. The President’s Secretariat’s 2025 profile of Odisha-born Adwaita Charan Gadanayak describes his work with abstract sculpture and identifies the Police Memorial in New Delhi among his projects.[2] Such work asks viewers to consider mass, surface and placement as well as likeness. A public memorial also connects artistic decisions with the institutions and collective memories that commission it.

Collecting can propose another relationship between forms. JD Centre of Art’s collection account brings modern art and Jatin Das’s own work together with traditional arts, textiles, hand fans, films and books.[3] That range invites comparison without making the objects interchangeable. A fan has a history of use; a painting has its own material and exhibition history. Bringing them into conversation is a curatorial choice, not proof that their differences have disappeared.

sections.heading: Images in books and on public walls
paragraphs: Illustration reaches many readers before they enter a gallery. In a picture book, an image helps establish who is present, how a place feels and what happens between one page and the next. It can extend a sentence or tell something the words leave unsaid. Decisions about line, colour and sequence are therefore part of the storytelling.

Bakul Foundation describes work with children’s authors and illustrators to create Odia picture books. Its education account also records the Udayanath Award for children’s book illustration, begun in 2015.[4] This places illustration within a network of writers, artists, readers and encouragement. The making of a book involves more than supplying decoration after a story is finished.

A public wall has a different audience. People encounter it while travelling, working or waiting, often without having chosen to look at art. Bakul’s arts account describes a Wall of Peace painted after the violence in Kandhamal, involving professional artists and students. It records the same wall being repainted as the Wall of Water on World Water Day in 2013.[5] The changing surface documents successive attempts to address public concerns.

Such an example also raises questions that remain useful beyond one project. Who chooses the subject? Whose account of a place becomes visible? Who maintains the work after its opening? A mural may invite reflection, advertise an institution or make an ordinary route more memorable. Calling it public art should begin discussion about its relationship with the public, rather than end that discussion.

Artists, illustrators and participants need names in this history. A city’s visual identity is made through individual labour and collaboration, even when the finished image is later described simply as local culture.

sections.heading: The photograph and its missing name
paragraphs: The photograph below shows an artisan displaying work in a painted doorway in Raghurajpur. It brings together a person, an object and a working environment. The photographer is credited, but the source does not identify the artisan by name. That absence matters: the image lets us see more than its accompanying record allows us to know.

A photograph can preserve a meeting, a surface or a moment of change. It also reflects where someone stood and when the shutter was pressed. Its date is not automatically the date of the building or artwork it depicts. Careful captions distinguish observation from identification, acknowledge missing information and keep the maker’s credit attached as the image travels.

sections.heading: Museums and walks as acts of interpretation
paragraphs: A museum brings objects into new relationships. Odisha Tourism’s description of Kala Bhoomi, the crafts museum in Bhubaneswar, presents galleries of carving, terracotta, metalwork and textiles alongside opportunities to encounter artisans at work.[6] The description suggests a way of connecting a finished object with processes of making. It should not be read as a guarantee that a particular demonstration is available on every visit.

A display also depends on words. A label can identify a maker, place, material and use, or reduce a complex object to a broad category. The sequence of rooms encourages some comparisons and makes others less likely. Visitors can ask how objects were acquired, what is known about their histories and whether the people represented have helped explain them.

Outside the museum, a heritage walk arranges a sequence through inhabited space. The Bhubaneswar Development Authority’s account of Ekamra Heritage Walks links temples with surrounding settlements, rituals and festivals.[7] This is a broader invitation than looking at isolated monuments. Streets, water, shops and patterns of everyday movement also shape how a place is understood.

A route remains a selection. The guide’s explanation, a resident’s memory and a written record may emphasise different things. Their differences can make a walk more thoughtful when clearly acknowledged. Worship and work continue while visitors look; a doorway or courtyard does not become freely available for photography simply because it appears along a heritage route.

Public heritage grows through these encounters between making, showing and interpreting. It asks for accurate credits, room for different memories and attention to the people who inhabit celebrated places. A painting can unsettle a familiar view; a photograph can preserve a detail; a walk can return that detail to its surroundings. Each offers a way to look again.

chapters.title: Keeping Culture Alive
chapters.subtitle: Learning work and the next generation
chapters.author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs: A song continues when someone learns to sing it. A skill continues when there is time to practise, material to work with and a reason to return tomorrow. A language continues in questions, jokes, disagreements and ordinary conversation. Cultural life depends on these repeated acts, often carried out far from a stage or a commemorative occasion.

This book has followed many such worlds across Odisha. Its closing question is practical: what helps people carry knowledge forward? The answer includes teaching and memory, but also livelihoods, access and choice. Keeping culture alive means attending to the conditions in which people can continue to make it their own.

sections.heading: Learning begins with someone being welcome
paragraphs: UNESCO’s account of cultural transmission emphasises continuing practice and learning between generations. It recognises that living heritage changes as people pass it on.[1] This helps us understand why a recording, an exhibition or a festival can support a tradition without replacing the relationship between someone who knows and someone who is learning.

That relationship needs a language in which questions are possible. In a February 2026 report, UNICEF describes Savitri Pingwa’s experience at Kumbhitangari in Keonjhar, where Ho-speaking children encountered difficulties with lessons conducted in unfamiliar Odia. The account describes teaching that connects their home language with Odia learning materials.[2] It is a particular reported experience, but it gives the wider question of access a human scale.

Learning Odia and respecting Odisha’s other languages can be parts of the same commitment. A child should be able to bring a familiar word into a classroom without being made to feel that home knowledge is an obstacle. An adult beginner, too, needs room to hesitate, mispronounce and try again. Shame rarely makes a dependable teacher.

In a family or neighbourhood, a useful beginning might be one story, a short song or the name of a tool. Ask who uses it and when. Let a willing practitioner demonstrate, then allow time for another person to attempt the task. These are proposed ways to begin, not a programme shared by every community.

The invitation also needs practical support. Timing, seating, cost, transport and care responsibilities influence who can attend. A gathering that welcomes everyone in words can still exclude people through its arrangements. Listening to those who do not return may teach organisers as much as counting those who came.

sections.heading: The livelihood behind the skill
paragraphs: The loom pictured at the opening of this chapter makes a simple point visible: cloth requires work. Behind a finished object lie learned movements, tools, materials and time. Praise for a tradition does not by itself pay for any of them. Asking young people to continue skilled work also means taking their prospects and choices seriously.

Utkalika’s institutional history describes a mandate to support handicraft marketing, alongside activities involving raw materials, training and product development.[3] The range is instructive. A maker may need help reaching a buyer, obtaining supplies or developing a product, rather than another invitation to perform authenticity for an audience. An organisation’s stated activities, however, do not establish what an individual worker earns.

For an organiser commissioning a demonstration, the practical response is to discuss preparation, materials, travel and payment beforehand. Teaching is work even when the session is short. Credit should identify the contributor as they wish to be named, and a photograph should not substitute for an agreed fee. These are working principles for a respectful arrangement.

Continuity also needs room for invention. A weaver, performer or illustrator may adapt a form for a new setting while retaining relationships with earlier practice. The interesting questions concern what changes, why it changes and who makes the decision. A new design is not automatically a loss, just as a familiar appearance is not proof that working conditions are sound.

No generation owes another a predetermined occupation. Someone may leave a family craft and remain connected through language, patronage, research or teaching. A meaningful cultural future gives practitioners reasons and opportunities to continue, while allowing people to choose the shape of their own lives.

sections.heading: Memory with a voice and a name
paragraphs: The still below comes from a recording of Musamoni Panigrahi telling a story in Baleswari Odia.[7] Naming the speaker, the language variety, the recorder and the date gives the image a recoverable setting. The record preserves a particular telling; it cannot contain every occasion on which the story has been shared.

UNESCO’s ethical principles place communities in the leading role in safeguarding their heritage and emphasise dialogue and continuing informed consent.[4] For a local recording project, that means discussing the audience and proposed uses before recording begins, then keeping those understandings open to review. A person may welcome a family copy while declining a public upload. The ability to make that choice is part of cultural care.

sections.heading: Something worth returning to
paragraphs: A community archive can begin modestly: a named recording, a dated photograph, a notebook of expressions or a scanned publication. Each needs enough description for another person to understand its source. Keep a family recollection identifiable as a recollection; keep unanswered questions beside the answers. Different memories need not be forced into a single authoritative version.

Odia Bibhaba’s account of Srujanika’s digitisation work shows how collecting, copying and organising printed material can create routes back to literature.[5] Such projects also remind us that saving a file is only one step. Someone must maintain the collection, help readers find it and carry its explanations forward when responsibility changes.

A place to meet can give that work an everyday audience. Bakul Foundation describes libraries sustained through donated books, contributions and volunteer participation, with storytelling and other activities around reading.[6] Its example suggests the value of a dependable invitation. The important question for a new group is what it can sustain after its opening event.

A possible beginning is four small meetings. Read something together, invite a willing contributor, make one carefully described record and review what happened. Ask participants what they learned, what made attendance difficult and whether they want to continue. Share the organising work and agree how contributors will be supported. This is a proposal for a manageable trial, not a measure of an existing programme’s success.

Odisha’s cultural life has never belonged to a single voice or form. Its future will also contain disagreement, movement and new work. We can help by making knowledge easier to approach, recognising the labour that sustains it and giving younger people room to respond. A fitting end to this book is therefore an invitation: learn something carefully, share it with someone willing, and make time to meet again.
